# THE CUSTODIANS OF THE LIBRARY
## Of the Vatican, to the Students of Alchemy
### To think rightly.

*Since many followers of alchemy of every social class are found in these times, investigating the hidden causes of natural philosophy so that they might extract what is commonly called the "philosopher's stone" from the riddles of written texts, and wrest it from the hands of Arnald of Villanova <note>original: "Raynaldi"</note>, Raymond Lull <note>original: "Raymundi"</note>, Geber <note>original: "Geberis", the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note>, and certain monks—not to mention even the highest theologians—the more ingenious by interpreting perversely, the more prone by affirming ambiguities, the more foolish by believing in fantasies, the more ready by experimenting, and the wasteful by pouring out and losing their money. They end up wasting their time, making vain promises, babbling bombastic words, and being held in derision and mockery by all; in the end, instead of finding the stone, they squander their wealth. Hence an art so rare—indeed, a science so supernatural—is held and believed to be a mere illusion and deception.*

*Nor is it any wonder, since the students of this divine discovery constantly read Geber and admire him as if he were their supreme authority <note>original: "Aristarchum", referring to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a famous ancient critic; used here to mean an unquestionable guide.</note>. They cling to him, stay awake over him, and devote themselves to him, just as Alexander the Great <note>original: "Alexander macedo"</note> used to do with the "Education of Cyrus" <note>original: "pediae Cyri", referring to the Cyropaedia by Xenophon, which Alexander the Great reportedly kept under his pillow.</note>. And yet, that author overflows with infinite errors, and is circulated in a form that is blind, crippled, and indeed altered; like a Scyllan satyr, he does not speak but merely grinds his teeth. He does not teach, but rather un-teaches, and [seduces] the fledgling mind—*

<summary>This page contains a preface from the Vatican Library custodians addressing the errors and frustrations of contemporary alchemists. It criticizes the blind devotion to corrupted texts by authors like Geber, which leads to financial ruin and the loss of the art's reputation.</summary>

<keywords>Vatican Library, alchemy, Philosopher's Stone, Arnald of Villanova, Raymond Lull, Geber, Cyropaedia, Alexander the Great, natural philosophy, manuscript corruption</keywords>

# KEEPERS OF THE LIBRARY
->Of the Vatican, to the Students of Alchemy,<-
->to be truly wise.<-

**S**ince many followers of alchemy of every social class are found in this age, who examine the hidden causes of natural philosophy so that they might extract the (commonly) so-called <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term><note>The legendary substance believed to transform base metals into gold and grant eternal life.</note> from paper labyrinths, and wrest it from the hands of <term>Arnaldus</term><note>original: "Raynaldi", likely Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note>, <term>Raymund</term><note>original: "Raymundi", likely Ramon Llull, a polymath whose name was frequently attached to alchemical works he did not write.</note>, <term>Geber</term><note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of alchemy; however, most Latin "Geber" texts were actually written by a 13th-century European author known as Pseudo-Geber.</note>, and several monks (not to mention even the highest theologians); the more clever by interpreting perversely, the more inclined by affirming ambiguities, the more foolish by believing in fantasies, the more eager by experimenting, and the wasteful by pouring out and losing their wealth—they all end in this: they waste their time, make empty promises, babble bombastic words, and are held as a joke and a derision by everyone, so that at last they squander their money in pursuit of a stone:

hence an art so rare, indeed a science so supernatural, is held and believed to be an illusion and mere deception.

Nor is it a wonder, since the students of this divine invention constantly read Geber and admire him as if he were their <term>Aristarchus</term><note>Aristarchus of Samothrace was the most famous literary critic of the ancient world; the author implies alchemists treat Geber as an infallible authority.</note>: they cling to him, watch over him, and devote themselves to him, just as <term>Alexander the Macedonian</term><note>Alexander the Great.</note> used to do with the *Education of Cyrus*<note>A famous biography of Cyrus the Great by Xenophon, which Alexander the Great supposedly kept under his pillow.</note>. And since that author overflows with infinite errors and is circulated as something blind and mangled—indeed, as something else entirely—and like a <term>Scyllan satyr</term><note>Likely an allusion to a "Silenus," a figure that appears monstrous or nonsensical on the outside; here, it describes a text that grinds its teeth in confusion rather than speaking clearly.</note>, he does not speak but grinds his teeth; he does not teach but "un-teaches," and [misleads] the developing mind...

<summary>This preface from the Vatican Library keepers warns students that alchemy has fallen into disrepute because practitioners rely on corrupted and nonsensical texts, particularly those attributed to Geber.</summary>
<keywords>Vatican Library, alchemy, Geber, Philosopher's Stone, Arnaldus de Villa Nova, Ramon Llull, Alexander the Great, textual criticism</keywords>

# I N D E X

*...of those who deceive,* <note>The OCR begins with a fragment "-tium," likely completing a word like "prestigiantium" (deceivers) or "stultitium" (fools) from the previous page.</note> *enveloping and overthrowing them in a mist of darkness. We have decided to meet your vain labors and expenses by healing the wounds of this art, applying a salve to bleary eyes, eliminating disharmony, and restoring more beautiful limbs—just as was done for* **Pelops** <note>In Greek myth, Pelops was cut into pieces and served as a feast for the gods, but was later restored to life with an ivory shoulder replacing a missing piece.</note>—*so that at last, like* **Medea’s boiled ram**, <note>The sorceress Medea demonstrated her power to restore youth by cutting up an old ram and boiling it with herbs, from which a young lamb emerged.</note> *it may seem to be reshaped, grow young again, be animated, shine, and be returned entirely to itself. We bring forth* **Machaon** <note>A legendary healer and son of Asclepius, who served the Greeks during the Trojan War.</note> *from the Vatican Library as if from the Trojan Horse.*

*He who, toiling at this cure, has watched most attentively, and—rescuing what was given up for dead from the gates of* **Proserpina** <note>The Queen of the Underworld; to rescue something from her gates means to bring it back from certain death or oblivion.</note>—*has restored it to life, light, purity, and to you: favor this charming man, and admire him as he discourses so learnedly and profoundly. His words promise and bestow secret doctrine; his sentences are pearls; and his precepts offer and grant* <term>pure gold</term> <note>original: "obrizum", a term for gold that has been refined and tested for purity.</note>.

*How much you—most of whom are seekers of nature's riches—owe to our diligence, you yourselves shall judge (if the hard-won knowledge of so rare, so hidden, and so heavenly a treasure ever reaches you). For we have supplied the* **lamp of Cleanthes** <note>Cleanthes was a Stoic philosopher who worked as a water-carrier by night so he could study by day; his lamp symbolizes tireless scholarly labor in the dark.</note> *to those walking through Cimmerian darkness, and we have led out and brought into the light those who were cast down into the* **cave of Trophonius** <note>A reference to a Greek oracle; visitors to the cave were said to be so overwhelmed by the experience that they lost the ability to laugh, symbolizing deep, terrifying confusion.</note>.

*In the meantime, read often: drink this in and toil over it, and keep the gods appeased by your persistence, so that this most secret truth—covered by so many lies and obscurities, called by every name in the world, held by few through books yet always beloved, perceived by even fewer through a teacher, and nevertheless never abandoned: [granted] to the very fewest through revelation in...*

The text frames the Vatican Library as the source of this purified, "resurrected" secret doctrine.</summary>

FIRST.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE SUMMARY BY GEBER, THE MOST PERSPICACIOUS PHILOSOPHER
## Preface regarding the perfection of the mastery in its own nature.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'T' featuring two nude putti interacting with a wooden staff or branch, set against a background of foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>

ALL our <term>science<note>In this context, *scientia* refers to alchemy, viewed by medieval scholars as a rigorous branch of natural philosophy.</note></term>, which we have abbreviated from the sayings of the ancients in various compilations within our volumes, we shall here gather into a single Summary. Know therefore, dearest son, that in this work, the entire operation of the art—in general chapters and universal discussion—is sufficiently contained without any omission. ## On the impediments by which the craftsman of this work is hindered.

### Chapter 1.

<margin>The classification of impediments.</margin>
THEREFORE, there are two impediments occurring in this work: natural inability, and a lack of necessary funds <note>original: "impense," referring to the high cost of materials, fuels, and specialized equipment.</note>, or the distraction of labor <note>original: "occupationis laboris," meaning being too busy with other work to focus on the alchemy.</note>. We say, however, that natural inability is multifaceted. Namely, on the part of the craftsman’s own organ <term>organ<note>original: "organi." In medieval Aristotelian thought, the body and its senses were viewed as the "instruments" or organs through which the soul interacts with the material world.</note></term> and on the part of the soul itself. Regarding the craftsman’s organ, it is multifaceted: because the organ may be weak or entirely corrupted. Regarding the soul’s inability, it is also multifaceted: either because the soul is perverse in its organs, having no uprightness or reason within itself because of the organs—such as the soul of a madman or a fool—or because it is over-imaginative <note>original: "fantastica." In this context, it refers to a mind that is too easily swayed by "phantasms" or unstable mental images, preventing steady focus.</note>, improperly and easily receptive to opposite forms, and suddenly extending from one known thing to its opposite, and from one universal truth to its likely opposite.

<margin>A soul that is perverse and imaginative.</margin>

It specifically warns that a "perverse" or "fantastic" mind—one that lacks steady reason or jumps erratically between ideas—is incapable of the work.</summary>

## On the impediments concerning the body.
### Chapter 2.

<margin>A body that is mutilated or poorly affected.</margin>
I have already defined for you in general terms the impediments to this work. But now, I speak to you in this chapter with more specific language and greater clarity, and I shall relate all those impediments to you most fully and in order. We say, therefore, that if a person does not have his complete organs <term>organs<note>original: "organa." In medieval philosophy, this refers to the physical "instruments" of the body, such as hands for working and eyes for observing, which the soul uses to interact with the world.</note></term>, he will not be able to reach the completion of this work. For instance, if he were blind, or had his extremities cut off, he cannot be successful because he is not assisted by the limbs through which this art is perfected, which serve as the ministers of nature. Furthermore, if the craftsman’s body is weak and diseased—such as the bodies of those suffering from fevers <note>original: "fabricantium," likely a variant or error for "febricitantium" (fever-stricken), given the context of illness.</note> or of lepers whose limbs fall away, or those struggling in the final stages of life, and those in the feebleness of a decrepit age—they do not reach the completion of the art. By these natural physical incapacities, therefore, the craftsman is hindered in his intention.

## Concerning impediments occurring by chance. Chapter 4.

We have reduced the impediments of this art to two chapters, namely all those things that delay the final goal, which arise from the fundamental principles according to the nature of the practitioner of this precious business. It is expedient, therefore, to describe only those impediments that come from the outside, arising from accidental occurrences and chance, by which this glorious work is hindered.

We have seen certain clever and ingenious men, by no means ignorant of the works of nature, who follow nature wherever possible in their principles and works. Their investigation is not delusional <note>original: "fantastica"</note> in any of the things which are regulated by the actions of nature beneath the lunar circle <note>In the medieval worldview, the "lunar circle" or sublunary sphere refers to the Earthly realm where things are subject to change, decay, and the four elements.</note>. 

<margin>Poverty and want.</margin>
Yet these men, weighed down by extreme poverty, are forced to set aside this most excellent mastery <term>Magisterium: The "Great Work" or the completion of the alchemical process.</term> due to a lack of resources for their needs. 

There are also many others (besides those just mentioned) who are curious, but are held back by the various cares and anxieties of this world. 

<margin>Cares and the oppression of business.</margin>
They occupy themselves entirely with every secular business, and from such people, our precious science flees. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the preceding chapters what the impediments are that hold one back from this art.

### Concerning the impediments arising by fortuitous chance. Chapter 4.

We have reduced the impediments of this art—all of which delay the end result—to two chapters, which arise from the radical principles according to the nature of the practitioner of this precious business. It is expedient, therefore, to describe only the impediments occurring from the outside, from fortuitous contingencies and accidents, by which this glorious work is hindered. We have seen, therefore, certain shrewd and ingenious men, by no means ignorant of the works of nature, following nature where possible in principles and works; through these, their investigation is not fantastical in all things regulated by the actions of nature beneath the lunar circle <note>original: "infra lunarem circulum"; referring to the "sublunary sphere," the earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens.</note>. <margin>Poverty and want.</margin> These men, however, oppressed by extreme poverty, are forced by a lack of means to set aside this most excellent mastery <term>Mastery: or *magisterium*, the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work.</term>. There are also many others (besides those just mentioned) who are curious, but are detained by the various cares <margin>Cares and the oppression of business.</margin> and anxieties of this world, occupying themselves entirely with every secular business, from whom this precious science of ours <note>original: "scientia nostra præciosa"; a common way alchemists referred to their craft.</note> flees. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the preceding chapters what the impediments are that withdraw one from this art.

## On what the practitioner <term>artifex</term> <note>Latin: "artificem"; while often translated as "artist," in this context it refers to the alchemist or skilled craftsman of the "Great Work."</note> must consider.
### Chapter 5.

<margin>The practitioner must be learned and studious.</margin>
We conclude, therefore, from the preceding points, that it is necessary for the practitioner of this work to be learned and advanced in the sciences of natural philosophy <note>The study of nature and the physical universe, the precursor to modern science.</note>. This is because, no matter how naturally deep his intellect may be, and even if he has achieved a desire for this craft and for natural philosophy, he will not reach its goal except through formal teaching <note>Latin: "doctrina"; implying that innate brilliance is insufficient without the study of established tradition.</note>. For whatever is not attained through natural talent, the deficiency is remedied through instruction.

<margin>He must also excel in natural talent and diligence.</margin>
It is also necessary for the practitioner to be aided by the deepest investigation and natural diligence <term>industria</term> <note>Latin: "industria"; a combination of hard work, cleverness, and resourcefulness.</note>. For no matter how much knowledge he has acquired through teaching, unless he is aided by natural diligence, he will not be invited to such precious banquets <note>A metaphorical reference to the successful completion of the alchemical process and its rewards.</note>. By his own diligence, he might correct an error in an instant for which he would otherwise know no remedy if he were grounded only in theory. Likewise, he might quickly remedy an error using the science acquired through teaching which he could not avoid by natural diligence alone; for art is aided by talent, and talent is similarly aided by art.

<margin>He must be of a constant will.</margin>
It is similarly necessary for him to be of a constant will in his work, so that he does not attempt first this and then that; for our art is not brought to completion <note>Latin: "perficiter"; meaning to be perfected or finished.</note> through a multitude of different things.

<margin>Note.</margin>
*For there is one Stone, one medicine, in which the mastery <term>magisterium</term> <note>Latin: "magisterium"; the highest level of alchemical achievement, often used to describe the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note> consists. To this we add no external thing, nor do we take anything away, except that in its preparation we remove what is superfluous.*

# FIRST BOOK

What we have written for you in this little book is open and manifest: do not unfairly criticize us, nor bring <term>blasphemies (blasphemias)</term> <note>original: "blasphemias"; here meaning slanderous or irreverent accusations against the author</note> against us, but attribute any failure to your own ignorance and presumption.

<margin>The Art is certainly not suitable for the poor.</margin>

Therefore, this <term>knowledge (scientia)</term> <note>original: "scientia"; in this context, it refers to the systematic study of alchemy and natural philosophy</note> is not well-suited to a poor or needy person; rather, it is his enemy and adversary. Do not strive to reach a deceptive goal for your labor, but be intent only on the completion of the work. For our <term>art (ars)</term> is preserved within the power of God, and He grants it to whom He wills and withholds it as He pleases—He who is glorious, sublime, and filled with all justice and goodness.

<margin>Deceptions are to be avoided.</margin>

For perhaps, as a punishment for a deceptive work, He might deny you the art and cast you into the path of error, and from error into <term>unhappiness (infœlicitas)</term> and perpetual misery. Most wretched and unhappy is he whom God, after the end of his work and toil, refuses to let behold the truth; for he always concludes and ends his life’s span in sorrow. Such a man, set in perpetual labor and besieged by every misfortune and <term>unhappiness (infœlicitate)</term>, loses all the consolation, joy, and delight of this world, consuming his life in sorrow without any profit.

<margin>Observe all the accidents that occur during the execution of the work.</margin>

Strive likewise, when you are engaged in the work, to fix in your mind all the signs that appear in any <term>decoction (decoctio)</term> <note>original: "decoctione"; the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or change its state</note>, and to investigate their causes. These, then, are the things necessary for a <term>craftsman (artifex)</term> <note>original: "artifici"; the practitioner or adept who performs the alchemical operations</note> who is fit for our art. But if any of the things we have recounted are missing, let him not attempt this art.

# On the Persuasions of the Sophists.
## Chapter 6.

<margin>
Part 2 of the first Book.
</margin>

<margin>
The first argument: from the ignorance of the proportion of the elements, which is found to be diverse and specific in each species.
</margin>

Since, in the summary of this our book, we have already set forth all the impediments to this work and have given you sufficient instruction for adhering to the art, it is now fitting—according to the intention of our proposal—that we dispute against the <term>Sophists</term> <note>original: "Sophistas." In this context, Sophists are not just philosophers, but those who use clever but fallacious logic to argue that alchemy is impossible, or those who practice fraudulent, "imitation" chemistry.</note> and the ignorant. We shall do this first by setting forth their own reasons, just as we promised at the beginning that we would determine them. Lastly, by addressing them all, we shall demonstrate to the wise through clear proof that these arguments contain no truth.

There are, indeed, various people who deny and attempt to destroy the art. Some do so simply, while others strive to reject it based on the premises of the underlying cause. For there are some who assert that the art does not exist as we have described, strengthening their own opinion <term>sophistically</term> in this way:

They argue that the species and diversities of things are distinct because the proportions of the elements to one another in their mixture are diverse and distinct. For example, a donkey is different in species from a man because it possesses a very different proportion of the elements in its composition; the same logic can be applied to all other diversities of things, and therefore also to minerals. They argue that if the proportion of the ingredients—by which the form and perfection of a thing is achieved—is unknown, then how can we know how to form a mixture or determine what is to be mixed? They claim that we are ignorant of the proportions of the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "solis," referring to gold.</note> and the <term>Moon</term> <note>original: "lunae," referring to silver.</note>, as well as the elements themselves; therefore, we must be ignorant of how to form them. From these points, they conclude that this art is useless and impossible. They also argue against our <term>magistery</term> <note>original: "magisterium," the master-work or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> in another similar way...

## <unclear>In what way qualities are formed in mixed bodies</unclear>

<unclear>Since</unclear> <unclear>in this part of natural science</unclear> <note>Natural science, or "physica," was the study of the natural world and its laws.</note> <unclear>we are going to treat those things which exist in mixed bodies,</unclear> <note>In ancient and medieval science, a "mixed body" is a substance made by combining the four elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note> <unclear>which are derived from the elements, we must consider what differentiates them.</unclear> <unclear>For the qualities found in mixed bodies do not all relate in the same way to the blending of the elements from which the mixture is formed.</unclear> <unclear>For some qualities flow from the very essence and form</unclear> <note>In this context, "form" refers to the organizing principle that makes a substance what it is.</note> <unclear>of the mixture itself, while others enter the mixture by "accident"</unclear> <note>An "accidental" quality is a property that can change without changing the fundamental nature of the thing, such as its temperature or color.</note> <unclear>from the elements. In these qualities, a two-fold difference is found:</unclear> <unclear>one is essential, which proceeds from the form of the mixture; the other is accidental,</unclear> <unclear>which depends on the specific proportion and stability of the elements themselves.</unclear> <unclear>For in mixtures, besides the four primary qualities,</unclear> <note>The four primary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> <unclear>which are derived from the elements, we see that there are other qualities</unclear> <unclear>which arise from the form of the mixture, and which proceed from such a composition and proportion</unclear> <unclear>of elements that there is in mixtures a certain stability and power</unclear> <note>original: "virtus," referring to an inherent capacity or efficacy.</note> <unclear>which is not found in the elements themselves. Thus, we must therefore consider</unclear> <unclear>what the difference is between these qualities and how they exist in mixed bodies.</unclear>

<term>Mixed bodies</term> (original: *corporibus mixtis*): Substances created by the combination of elements.
<term>Qualities</term> (original: *qualitates*): The characteristics or properties of a substance.
<term>Elements</term> (original: *elementis*): The fundamental building blocks of matter (earth, water, air, fire).
<term>Mixture</term> (original: *mixtionem*): The process or result of blending elements.
<term>Essence</term> (original: *essentia*): The fundamental nature of a thing.
<term>Form</term> (original: *forma*): The internal principle that gives a thing its specific identity.
<term>Proportion</term> (original: *proportione*): The specific ratio of elements within a mixture.

<margin>
2. Argument from ignorance of the method of mixing.

...destroying our [position]: for they say: even if you knew the proportion of the elements, you are still ignorant of the method of their mixing with one another: because nature procreates these things in caverns and mines and hidden places: therefore, since you are ignorant of the method of their mixing, you are specifically ignorant of how to perform this. Again,

<margin>
3. Argument from ignorance of the balancing of heat.
</margin>
they argue similarly: Even if you knew this properly, yet in the action of mixing you would be ignorant of how to balance the active heat <note>original: "calorem æquare agentem"; in medieval science, heat was the primary "active" quality that transformed matter.</note>, by means of which this thing is perfected. For nature has a certain quantity of heat by which it brings metals into being, the measure of which you do not know.

<margin>
4. Argument from ignorance of the other causes of metals.
</margin>
Similarly, you are ignorant of the other differences of nature’s acting causes <note>The "acting" or efficient causes refer to the external forces—like planetary influence or subterranean vapors—that philosophers believed moved matter toward its final form.</note>, without which nature could not perfect its intent: these being unknown, the whole method of the art's operation will similarly be unknown. Furthermore, I lead you to a reason based on experience.

<margin>
5. Argument from experience: this art is not discovered by wise philosophers and princes, therefore it does not exist.
</margin>
For this science has been sought for so long by wise men, that if it were possible to reach it by any path, they would have completed it a thousand times over. Similarly also, since the philosophers <note>In this context, "philosophers" usually refers to the ancient authorities like Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> have not dared to hand it down in their volumes, nor do we find manifest truth in them: it is probable enough from this that this science does not exist. Similarly also, many Princes and Kings of this world, having infinite treasure and an abundance of philosophers, have desired to discover this art: yet they have not been able to reach the fruit of this most precious art <note>The "precious art" refers to alchemy, specifically the transmutation of base metals into gold.</note>; this is surely a sufficient enough argument that the art is frivolous. BOOK 2

## On the refutations of the arguments of the Sophists.
### Chapter 8.

<margin>The purpose of the Art <term>Art</term> <note>In this context, "Art" refers to alchemy, the practical application of human skill to natural materials.</note> is not to imitate nature in its primary principles, but it takes its principles <gloss>from</gloss> nature.</margin>
OUR intention, therefore, is not to follow nature in its primary principles, nor in the proportion of the elements to be mixed, nor in the manner of their mutual mixing, nor in the balancing of the thickening heat, since all these things are impossible for us and entirely unknown. It remains, therefore, to destroy the arguments of the Sophists <note>original: "Sophistarum"; here referring to skeptics who used clever but fallacious arguments to deny the possibility of alchemy.</note> who deny that this sublime Art can exist.

<margin>Refutation of the first four arguments:</margin>
If they should say, therefore, that we are ignorant of the proportion of the elements and the manner of their mutual mixing, and the balancing of the heat that thickens metals—and many other causes and accidents involved in nature’s actions—we certainly grant this to them. But they do not for this reason destroy our divine science, because we neither wish to know those things, nor are we able, nor can they pertain to our work. Instead, we adopt a principle for ourselves and another method for the generation of metals, in which we *can* follow nature.

<margin>Refutation of the fifth argument.</margin>
If they should also say that the Philosophers and the princes of this world have longed for this science and have not found it, we reply that they lie. For we read that certain princes—though few, and especially the ancient and wise ones, and some found in our own time—have already investigated this science through their own industry. But they did not wish to hand it down to such people either by word of mouth or in writing, since they are unworthy. Therefore, because they have not seen anyone possessing this science, an error has fallen upon their minds, so that they believe no one has found this knowledge. To this, they also argue fantastically,

## Concerning the solutions to the persuasions of the Sophists. Chapter 8:

<margin>The purpose of the Art is not to imitate nature in its first principles, but rather it adopts the principles of nature.</margin>
Our intention, therefore, is not to follow nature in its first principles, nor in the proportion of the elements to be mixed, nor in the manner of their mixing with one another, nor in the balance of the thickening heat—since all these things are impossible for us and entirely unknown. It remains, then, to demolish the arguments of the Sophists <note>The author uses "Sophists" to describe skeptics who use clever but fallacious logic to argue that alchemy is impossible.</note> who deny that this sublime art can exist.

<margin>Solution to the first four arguments.</margin>
Therefore, if they say that we are ignorant of the proportion of the elements, the manner of their mixing together, the balance of the heat that solidifies metals, and many other causes and accidents <term>accidents|In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential qualities of a thing, like color or smell, as opposed to its "essence."</term> that govern the actions of nature—we certainly grant this to them. However, they do not, for this reason, destroy our divine science <note>original: "scientiam divinam," a common term for alchemy as a sacred art.</note>; for we neither wish to know those things, nor are we able, nor are they necessary for our work to succeed. Instead, we adopt a starting principle for ourselves and another method for the generation of metals, in which we are able to follow nature.

<margin>Solution to the fifth argument.</margin>
Furthermore, if they say that the philosophers and the princes of this world have desired this science and have not found it, we reply that they are lying. We read that certain princes—though few, and especially the ancient ones, as well as wise men found in our own time—have already investigated this science through their own industry. But they did not wish to hand it down to such people either by word of mouth or in writing, as they are unworthy. Therefore, because they have not seen anyone in possession of this science, an error has fallen upon their minds, leading them to believe that no one has discovered this science. To this end, they also argue fantastically,

### FIRST BOOK.
C

<margin>Solution to the sixth argument.</margin>
...fantastically, asserting that our powerlessness <note>The author is addressing critics of alchemy who claim humans lack the power to create natural substances.</note> prevents us from imitating nature even in "weak" mixtures—such as the biological makeup of a donkey or an ox—and therefore, we surely cannot do so in "strong" mixtures <note>In this context, "weak" mixtures refer to perishable living tissues, while "strong" mixtures refer to durable minerals and metals.</note>. We say that their error is manifold: first, because there is no logical necessity in their way of arguing that forces us to concede our Art does not exist. They try to bolster their fantasy and error using arguments based on "similarity" or "from the greater" <note>original: "a simili, uel à maiori." These are rhetorical devices suggesting that if a person cannot do a small thing, they cannot do a larger thing.</note>, which do not provide certainty, but only a likelihood in most cases. We also demonstrate their error through another path, by showing that they fail to see any true similarity between the weak composition of animal mixtures and the firm, strong composition of mineral forms.

<margin>A most beautiful and truly philosophical doctrine concerning the subtle form.</margin>
This is because in animals and other living things, where the physical composition is "weak" (perishable), the "proportion" <term>proportio: the specific ratio of elements—earth, air, fire, and water</term> is not the only thing that brings the creature to perfection. It is not merely the mixable parts of that proportion, nor the qualities of those parts, nor the chemical mixture resulting from their mutual "action and passion" <note>Action and passion: the Aristotelian idea of elements acting upon and reacting to one another.</note>—that is, the gathering of their physical qualities. Rather, according to the opinion of many, it is the **soul**—which comes from the hidden depths of nature, such as from the **fifth essence** <term>essentia quinta: the "quintessence" or celestial element, distinct from the four earthly elements</term> or from the **prime mover** <note>The "Prime Mover" refers to the original source of motion or God in Aristotelian philosophy.</note>.

<margin>The Soul of the World, or the spirit diffused throughout the universe, perfecting all things.</margin>
We state this according to the consensus of many, though we remain ignorant of the hidden nature of this soul. Therefore, regarding such living things—even though their physical mixture is "weak"—we do not know how to bring them to perfection because we do not know how to infuse that perfecting principle: the **soul**.

<margin>The perfection of animals consists in the soul, which is infused.</margin>
Through this, it is certainly clear: the reason we cannot "perfect" (create) an ox or a goat is not due to a failure in mixing the physical elements, but rather from our inability to infuse the soul. We are indeed capable of making both weak and strong physical compositions by following the natural course of nature...

<summary>The author argues that while alchemists can replicate the physical "mixtures" of nature, they cannot create life because they lack the ability to infuse the "soul" or "quintessence." This distinguishes the chemical creation of minerals (which have strong forms) from the biological creation of animals (which require an animating spirit).</summary>

<margin>Note: The solution to the eighth argument, by conceding that nature acts over a long period of time.</margin>

Similarly, we ourselves do not change metals, but rather nature does, for whom we prepare certain materials through <term>artifice<note>original: "artificium"; here referring to the skilled application of alchemical knowledge and laboratory techniques.</note></term>. For nature acts of its own accord, while we are merely its administrators. And if they argue by another reasoning to sophistically strengthen their opinion—namely, that nature takes thousands of years to perfect metals, while you cannot live for thousands of years—

<margin>The preparation and establishment of <term>principles<note>original: "principiorum"; the fundamental components or "seeds" of matter according to alchemical theory.</note></term> is completed by nature over a very long time, and therefore human art cannot replicate that part; but once those principles are established, art is perfectly capable of extracting, preparing, and purifying them, and does so in a short time.</margin>

We say that although nature, acting upon its principles (according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers), reaches perfection in thousands of years, we cannot follow those specific starting principles. Therefore, whether nature perfects this in thousands of years, or more, or fewer, or even in a single moment, their persuasion does not hold: because we neither can nor wish to imitate nature in its primary principles. We see, for example, that nature does not bake stones into <term>lime<note>original: "calcem"; calcium oxide, produced by heating limestone in a kiln.</note></term> even in thousands of years, yet man does this in a short time through his natural ingenuity using <term>accidental heat<note>original: "accidentalem calorem"; heat applied from an external source, like a furnace, as opposed to the "natural" internal heat of the earth.</note></term>. Thus, in purifying metals through human ingenuity and skill, they are reduced to a pure and nobler substance in a short time, because nature cannot rectify their defects so quickly. We have already settled this in the preceding brief rebuttal, and we shall demonstrate it more fully in the following sections.

<margin>Solution to the same 8th argument: stating that while nature may take a long time to arrange the principles, it perfects and introduces the <term>form<note>original: "formam"; the essential nature or identity of a substance.</note></term> in an instant.</margin>

However, according to the opinion of certain clear-sighted and insightful men, nature achieves its intent suddenly—that is, in a single day, or even less time. Even if this is true, we still cannot imitate nature in its primary principles, which we will demonstrate more clearly through evidence. <margin>What has been said thus far, and what will be said hereafter.</margin>
We have therefore sufficiently recounted, my dearest son, the fantasies of the Sophists <note>In this context, "Sophists" refers to people who use clever but deceptive or fallacious logic to argue against the possibility of alchemy.</note>. After that determination, we shall also speak of the principles themselves insofar as they are the foundations of this, our <term>magistery</term> <note>original: "magisterij" — the "Mastery" or Great Work; the complete process of alchemical transformation.</note>. SOME, therefore, assuming the Art is to be found in sulfur <note>original: "Sulphure"</note>, have spent great labor; yet, being ignorant of the perfection of its preparation, they have left that very perfection incomplete. For they believed that mere cleansing and purification constituted the entire perfection of the preparation. This cleansing is achieved through sublimation <term>Sublimation: The process of heating a solid substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used by alchemists to purify materials</term>. Consequently, it entered their minds to estimate that sublimation alone was the perfect way to prepare sulfur; they were led to believe the same regarding its companion, namely arsenic <note>original: "Arsenico"</note>.

When they reached the stage of projection <term>Projection: The final stage of the alchemical process where the "medicine" or "stone" is cast upon a molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver</term>—which is the intended moment of transformation—they saw the substance burn up and vanish. It did not linger within the "bodies" <note>In alchemical texts, "bodies" refers to the solid metals, such as lead or copper, as opposed to the volatile "spirits."</note> for any length of time. In fact, the metals were left even more impure than they were before the projection was attempted.

Because they saw this delusion at the completion of their work, and because the idea that this science could be found in sulfur alone had revolved in their hearts for a very long time—yet they had not found it there—they argued that it could not be found in anything else either. Therefore, since they find it neither in this nor in any other substance,
<margin>
A rebuke of the
stated opinion.
</margin>
they argue that it can never be found at all. Responding to them briefly, we say that they perceive little in this matter and know very little, because they assume that sulfur alone is our medicine. Even if this were a true assumption, they are nevertheless deceived in the manner of preparation, because they believe that sublimation alone is sufficient.

# On the Inclination towards the Inspiration of Things. Chapter IX.

-> L <-

<meta>catchword: They are</meta>

But if the <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurius"; here referring to the philosophical principle of volatility and soul, not just the common metal.</note> of <term>sublimation</term> <note>original: "sublimationis"; the process of vaporizing a solid to purify it.</note> is worked with two weights of mercury, and if that be for the purpose of manifestation, it acquires perfection insofar as it leaves those weights behind again through the sublimation. And in the sublimation, by discerning them into one through the perfection of sublimation—of which it is said—it happens in this manner by sublimation in the fire. Therefore, it is impossible for it to be seen in this way: that such a sublimation proceeds in its own substance and proper nature. For in that substance, these things are seen through the sublimation of the <term>elements</term> <note>original: "elementa"; the four basic components of matter: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> into their own proper places, as we shall explain.

Although this may be caused by the spirits, it is then that the intention and the knowledge are realized. For that is to be seen, and seen through their <term>bodies</term> <note>original: "corpora"; the "fixed" or solid metallic parts of a substance.</note>; here it will strive to remain in the substance, and it leaves the bodies in other materials which they were before. Therefore, without perfection, and only from that point, is it inspired by God in the higher intellects, and it is said to happen within them. Because of the revelation of the authors, it is clear that through <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "sulphure"; the active, combustible, and "masculine" alchemical principle.</note> alone the <term>solution</term> <note>original: "solutio"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</note> occurs in the regeneration of the kind. From these things, it is said that their work cannot be seen to seek this in such a way. Wherefore it is not seen, nor are they seen anywhere in these things, and because of this, it would never be seen.

And regarding the essence, which comes briefly from them—and in this, one takes but a small amount—the result appears to be that they say solids here can be <term>medicines</term> <note>original: "medicinas"; in alchemy, these are the elixirs or tinctures used to "heal" or transform base metals into gold.</note>. However, it is true and certain that from these things, the bodies of mutation are received into the joined subjects; these bodies are sufficient in their being for that purpose only by means of sublimation.

For they are like a boy who, from the very beginning of his birth until his old age, is shut up within a house; he does not think that the breadth of the world extends beyond that house, or beyond what his own eye can behold. <margin>In all spirits, there is the same method of preparation.</margin>
<margin>All these things are to be understood concerning philosophical matters.</margin>

...they carried on, yet did not know how to complete it. For they were ignorant of how to seek the **ingression** <note>original: "Ingressionem"; in alchemy, the "entry" or penetration of a transformative substance into a base metal to change its nature.</note>, which is the final perfecting act. In all spirits likewise, there is the same method of preparation, except that in **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento uiuo"; mercury.</note> and **tutty** <note>original: "tutijs"; zinc oxide usually found as a crust in furnace chimneys, used in making brass.</note>, we are excused from the greater labor of removing the "burning" quality <note>original: "adustionis"; refers to the combustible or corrosive impurities (sulfureity) that "burn" the metal rather than perfecting it.</note>. These substances do not possess a combustible and flammable sulfureity, but only **flight** <note>original: "fugam"; volatility, or the tendency of a substance to evaporate or escape when heated.</note>. **Magnesia** and **Marcasite** <note>These terms in medieval alchemy often referred to various metallic ores or sulfides; Marcasite was often iron pyrite, while Magnesia could refer to various dark or magnetic minerals.</note>, however, possess every kind of sulfureity: more in the case of Marcasite, and less in Magnesia. Yet all of them possess flight. **Quicksilver** and **sal ammoniac** <note>original: "armoniacum sal"; ammonium chloride, prized for its ability to sublimate and its role in cleaning metals.</note> have the most flight; sulfur has less; its companion <note>likely referring to arsenic</note> has even less; fourthly, Marcasite has even less; fifthly, Magnesia has less still; and sixthly and lastly, Tutty has the least of all. Nevertheless, each of these participates in "flight," some more and others less; and therefore, because of their flight, a powerful delusion overcomes certain experimenters in their operations of preparation, and similarly in their **projections** <note>original: "proiectionibus"; the act of casting the alchemical "medicine" or Elixir onto molten metal to effect transmutation.</note>. Therefore, they themselves argue and struggle as if they were working with sulfur, and we respond to them as if they were indeed working with sulfur. There are also

others, priding themselves on their experiments, who strive to **fix** <note>original: "figere"; the process of making a volatile "spirit" stable and resistant to fire so it does not evaporate.</note> spirits into bodies <note>original: "corporibus"; the solid metals.</note> without any other preparation preceding this. But this same delusion similarly brings them trouble and desperation, and they are compelled by it to believe that this science does not exist, and to argue against it. Indeed, the cause of their confusion is their own excessive haste; for in the melting of the bodies, they let the spirits go, so that they do not adhere to the metals. On the contrary, the spirits flee from the harshness of the fire, while only the bodies remain in it, because they cannot endure the pressure of the "wickedness" <note>original: "impietatis"; here used metaphorically to describe the destructive force of the fire or the impurities that prevent the union of spirit and metal.</note>...

### BOOK ONE.

They cannot endure the fire of that <note>original: "impietatis ignis," likely referring to the "merciless" or destructive nature of intense, untempered furnace heat</note> impiety because of their flight <note>referring to "volatility," the tendency of a substance to evaporate when heated</note>, which has not been removed from them. <margin>The Lesser Art.</margin> Similarly, a delusion sometimes occurs because the <term>bodies</term> <note>the solid metals or minerals</note> themselves flee the fire along with the spirits; <margin>The error of certain others who fix spirits into bodies.</margin> and this happens when the spirits, not being <term>fixed</term> <note>rendered non-volatile or stable under heat</note>, have not adhered inseparably to the deep interior of the bodies, because the quantity of the volatile substance overcomes the quantity of the fixed.

## Concerning those who suppose the art exists in bodies, stones, salts, aluminous substances, boraxes, or growing things.
### Chapter 11.

<margin>The error of those who place the art as hidden within lead and tin, which are soft bodies.</margin>
However, certain people have placed that art in "bodies" <note>metals in their solid state</note>, yet when they came to the actual work, they were deceived. They judged both types of <term>tin-metal</term> <note>original: "stagnum"; in medieval alchemy, this term often covered both tin and lead alloys</note>—namely the leaden and the white—to greatly resemble and approach the nature of the Sun <note>gold</note> and the Moon <note>silver</note> through their pure whiteness. They believed the leaden type indeed resembled the Sun much, but the Moon little; whereas the white type resembled the Moon much, and the Sun but little. <margin>Concerning the various preparations of tin.</margin> Therefore, some of these men, judging tin (which they called Jupiter) to be much like the Moon, and believing it to differ only in its "cry" <note>original: "stridore"; the "tin cry" is the distinct crackling sound made when bending a bar of pure tin</note>, its softness, and the speed of its melting, thought it was easily melted and similarly soft due to an excess of its internal humidity. They believed it possessed that "cry" because of the "fugitive" <note>volatile or unstable</note> substance of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>mercury</note> falling between its parts. Consequently, they exposed it to fire, and by <term>calcinating</term> <note>original: "calcinantes"; the process of heating a metal until it oxidizes into a powder</note> it, they kept it in the fire as long as it could endure, until it was turned white in its <term>calx</term> <note>the powdery metallic oxide remaining after heating</note>. Afterward, though they attempted to "wrap" it to protect it, they were unable to <term>reduce</term> <note>the chemical process of turning a metallic oxide back into a solid metal</note> it, and so they judged the task to be impossible. Furthermore, some of these men did manage to reduce something from that powder, but they found the same "cry" as before, the same softness, and the same speed of melting. Therefore, they believed this goal was impossible to reach by this path, and they were led into disbelief, thinking that the art of "hardening" <note>making a soft metal like tin as hard as silver or gold</note> that metal could never be found. Some of these men, however, calcinated and reduced the metal repeatedly, attempting to remove its dross <note>scoria or impurities</note> with greater...

# BOOK ONE.

...by the expression of fire they calcined <term>calcination</term><note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state or remove impurities, often resulting in a powder or "calx."</note> and reduced it; and so, frequently repeating the work upon it, they saw it hardened and without its characteristic "cry" <note>original: "stridore"; the "cry of tin" is a distinctive crackling sound produced when bending the metal, which alchemists sought to remove to make the metal more like silver.</note>. However, because they did not entirely remove the speed of its liquefaction <term>liquefaction</term><note>The melting point or the process of a solid metal turning into a liquid state.</note>, their minds erred, and they judged that success could not be reached. 

Thus, some of these practitioners, wishing to grant it hardness and a delay in melting by administering two [other] metallic bodies, fell into a delusion: 

<margin>Tin breaks the bodies that are mixed with it.</margin>

they found that it would break whatever two bodies were mixed with it, and that preparation did not help them. Therefore, when they could prepare it neither with hard substances nor with fire, they excused themselves regarding the long delay in discovering the art; because they called it impossible, and believed it so, they argued persistently against the art, claiming it did not exist. 

Because of this, and because those adding many medicines <term>medicines</term><note>In alchemical theory, a "medicine" or elixir is a chemical agent intended to "heal" or transmute a base metal into a noble one, like gold or silver.</note> saw that they produced no change and were not suitable for them—but rather corrupted the work and acted against their purpose—they cast aside their books, turned their heads away, and finally called the art frivolous. ...that the **Art** is found in salts and alums, nitres and boraxes <term>boraxes: original 'bauracchijs', referring to various mineral salts used as fluxes in metallurgy</term>. They can, indeed, experiment with these, but we believe the Art is least of all to be found in them. Therefore, if after their experimentation they find little use for transmutation—namely through dissolving, coagulating, and roasting—they should not therefore discard the Art, as it is a necessary part of science <note>original: 'scientia', meaning a structured system of knowledge</note>. It is possible, however, for some alteration to be found in all of these minerals, but it is a very remote possibility and extremely laborious.

Furthermore, it is proven that seeking the Art in all other "growing things" <note>referring to the plant kingdom</note> is even more laborious. For this reason, some seekers place the Art in all vegetables. They claim it is possible in theory, but not for them in practice; they would sooner fail from the sheer exhaustion of the labor than the work could possibly be perfected. Thus, even if such people do not find the Art through their own efforts, they argue that the Art cannot be found by *any* amount of labor.

All those previously mentioned who are in error have established their own single "medicine" <note>original: 'medicina', the alchemical agent or 'Elixir' used to effect change</note> and have assumed no other exists besides it. All of these have now been refuted. Many others, indeed an almost infinite number, attempt to create a composition of all these things, or of certain mixtures under a different method of creation. They proceed ignorantly and without true knowledge. Their error extends into infinity, because the diversity of how things can be mixed is infinite, and the number of things to be mixed is itself infinite. In both of these infinities, one is bound to err infinitely—sometimes by having too much of an ingredient, and sometimes too little. For these people, correction is impossible.

But we, wishing to avoid long-windedness and wordy speeches, do not wish to dwell upon these infinite errors. Instead, we shall deliver this universal science in brief sayings.

-># THE BOOK<-

...vigor <note>original: "strenuitatem," completing the word from the previous page</note> through the smallest parts: with a heat in minerals equal to that hidden in the earth's bowels, multiplied and equalized according to the proper course of nature, according to the requirements of their essence, <margin>The opinion of some who deny that the principles of metals are immediately quicksilver and sulfur.</margin> according to the opinion of certain ancients. Others, however, have spoken differently, because the principle was not Quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term> in its own nature, but rather altered and converted into its own earth; and Sulfur was similarly altered and changed into earth. For this reason, they said that the principle was something other than the "stinking spirit" and the "fleeing spirit" <term>spiritus fugies: a volatile substance that evaporates or "flees" when heated</term> in the intention of nature. 

<margin>The first reason for the stated opinion.</margin> And the reason by which they were moved was this: they do not find in silver mines or those of other metals anything that is Quicksilver in its own nature, or anything that is Sulfur similarly in its own nature. Rather, they find each of these separately in their own proper mine and nature. 

<margin>The second reason for the stated opinion.</margin> Similarly, they also affirm this through another reason, namely: there is no transition from one contrary to another except through a middle state <term>dispositio media: an intermediate phase or condition necessary for a substance to transform from one extreme (like liquid) to another (like solid)</term>. Therefore, since this is how it happens, they are compelled to admit and <margin>Earth mixed with water is the root of all metals if it is balanced by the power of the heavens and changed. It does not pass directly into metals, but is first converted into vitriol; from vitriol a vapor is raised again, from which metals arise.</margin> believe that there is no transition from the softness of Quicksilver to the hardness of any metal, except through a state that is between their hardness and softness; but in the mines they do not find anything in which this middle state is preserved. 

For this reason, they are compelled to believe that Quicksilver and Sulfur in their own nature are not the principle by the intention of nature, but rather something else: which follows from the alteration of those essences in the root of nature into an earthy substance. And this <margin>Note the manner according to which metals are made by these philosophers.</margin> is the method: since first each of them is converted to an earthy substance, and from both of these earthy natures...

# BOOK ONE

### D ij

<margin>
Know that this smoke coming forth from vitriol <note>original: "uitriolo"; a term for sulfate minerals often associated with metallic formation</note> is the quicksilver and the sulfur of the philosophers, and when it is raised and received by the outermost sulfur, and the stones [become] metals are procreated, because it takes on fixation <note>The process by which a volatile substance becomes solid or stable</note> and hardens.
</margin>

...is resolved a very thin smoke by the multiplied heat in the bowels of the earth, and this double smoke is the immediate matter of metals. However, this smoke, cooked by the tempered heat of the <term>mineral vein</term> <note>original: "minerae"; refers to the natural site or ore-body where minerals grow</note>, is converted into the nature of a certain earth. Therefore, it undergoes a certain fixation, which the flowing water dissolves through the bowels of the mineral vein and the sponginess of the earth, and it is uniformly united in a natural and firm union. Therefore, those holding this opinion have said that

<margin>
Flowing water and vapor of the earth, or the substance of the outermost [thing].
</margin>

water flowing through the passages of the earth finds a dissolvable substance from the substance of the earth in its bowels, and dissolves it, and is uniformly united with it, until the dissolved substance of the earth and the dissolving flowing water become one in a natural union; and all elements come to such a union according to their due and natural proportion, and are mixed in their smallest parts until they make a uniform mixture. And this mixture, through successive <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decoctionem"; a "cooking" or ripening process driven by the Earth's internal heat</note>, is thickened in the mineral vein and hardened, and becomes metal.

<margin>
A critique of the said opinion.
</margin>

And these authors are also close to the truth, yet they do not grasp the pure truth. Now that we have determined in a general discourse the natural principles of metals, it remains now that we set down a chapter for each principle. Since, therefore, there are three: Sulfur, Arsenic, and <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argentum uiuum"; Mercury</note>.

The three principles of metals: incoming sulfur, arsenic (or sulfur in the earth), and quicksilver; see the same on page 51, on the back.

## BOOK On Sulfur. Chapter 13:

<margin>Definition of sulfur [mentioned] above.</margin>
<margin>The same [is found] above on pages 14 and 17.</margin>
WE SAY, therefore, that **Sulfur** is a fatness <note>original: "pinguedo"; in alchemy, this refers to an oily, combustible principle or "sulfur of the philosophers" rather than just common brimstone</note> in the mineral of the earth, thickened by a tempered <term>decoction</term> <note>A slow "cooking" or ripening process believed to happen naturally within the earth over long periods</note> until it becomes hardened and dry; and when it has been hardened, it is called Sulfur. Indeed, Sulfur has a very strong composition and is of a uniform substance in all its parts, because it is homogeneous; therefore, its oil is not taken away from it by distillation, as it is from other things that contain oil.

<margin>The effects of Sulfur in calcination.</margin>
Those, therefore, who seek to <term>calcine</term> <note>original: "calcinare"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder or "calx"</note> it without losing any of its substance that is worth caring for, labor in vain. This is because it is not calcined except through great industry, and much of its substance is dissipated; for out of a hundred parts, you will scarcely preserve three sufficiently after its calcination.

<margin>The effects of Sulfur in fixation.</margin>
Similarly, it cannot be <term>fixed</term> <note>original: "Figi"; the process of making a volatile, vaporous substance stable and resistant to heat</note> unless it is first calcined. Nevertheless, it can be mixed [with other things], and its flight <note>original: "fuga"; the tendency of a volatile substance to evaporate or sublimate when heated</note> can be somewhat delayed, and its burning can be restrained; when mixed, it is calcined more easily. Therefore, he who seeks to draw out a work from it should not try to draw it out by preparing it on its own, because the work is perfected when it is mixed, and without that, the <term>magisterium</term> <note>original: "magisterium"; the "mastery" or the specific alchemical process/elixir used to transform metals</note> is prolonged until one reaches despair.

<margin>If sulfur and arsenic are prepared together, they become a tincture.</margin>
And when combined with its companion <note>referring to arsenic, as noted in the margin</note> it becomes a <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tinctura"; a potent substance capable of "dyeing" or transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note>. It gives a complete weight to each of the metals, and it purifies them of foulness and makes them bright, and perfects them with the mastery, without which it provides none of these things, but rather corrupts and blackens them. Therefore, do not use it without the mastery itself. He who also seeks to mix it in the preparation...

### Concerning the Bay. Chapter VI.

We have presented in those more general chapters [the way] in which we will treat the shapes of islands and peninsulas: it follows, therefore, that we will not speak rashly about their use and forms, as the subject requires; a **bay** <note>original: "sinus"</note>, therefore—which is also called a **recess** <note>original: "recessus"</note>—is properly a portion of the sea, led into such narrowness that it is surrounded by land on three sides, being open only by a fourth entrance; moreover, the sea there seems to those who sail upon it, or who observe it, to withdraw itself as if from the side, and they seem to enter in this manner: bays, <unclear>unless they differ entirely, all have this [quality], that those entering into them</unclear> [find] a freer entrance and a narrower port <note>original: "portum," here meaning a harbor or sheltered water</note>, and they seem to return as if into themselves, and to be formed again.

<term>Bay</term> (Sinus): A coastal body of water that connects to a larger main body of water.
<term>Recess</term> (Recessus): A synonym used here for an inlet or a bay that "recedes" into the land.
<term>Sea</term> (Maris): The salt water that covers most of the earth.
<term>Land</term> (Terra): The solid part of the earth's surface.
<term>Island</term> (Insula): A piece of land surrounded by water.
<term>Peninsula</term> (Peninsula): A piece of land almost surrounded by water or projecting out into a body of water.
<term>Port</term> (Portus): A maritime facility where ships may dock; used here to describe the protected nature of a bay.
<term>Geography</term> (Geographia): The study of the physical features of the earth.

## On the Moon. Chapter 18.

<margin>
Definition and nature of the Moon, that is, of silver.
</margin>
<margin>
Through the Moon <note>In alchemy, "the Moon" is the standard name for Silver.</note>, they dye things white; or, they mean by this the external sulfur which hardens mercury and which is mixed with the Sun <note>The "Sun" refers to Gold.</note> or enclosed within it; which, being refined by a subtle art, is thickened and fixed with arsenic into a stone.
</margin>
Having finished the chapter on the Sun, let us speak now of the Moon using its fitting name, Silver. We say that Silver is a white metallic body, of pure whiteness, clean, hard, resonant, enduring in the refining-ash <note>original: "cinericio," referring to cupellation, a process where silver is refined in a dish made of bone ash</note>; it is extensible under the hammer, and capable of being melted and heated by fire. It is, therefore, a tincture <note>An essence used to "color" or transform the quality of a metal.</note> of whiteness, and it hardens Jupiter <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note> through artifice, and converts it to itself, and is mixed with the Sun, and is not broken; but in an examination without artifice, it does not persist with it. He who knows how to refine it further, and after refining to thicken it and fix it when joined together, stays with it in the struggle and does not completely let it go.

<margin>
The same in chapter 13 on sulfur: as seen below on pages 34, 53, 85, 86.
</margin>
However, upon the smoke of sharp substances—such as vinegar, salt ammoniac, and verjuice <note>The acidic juice of unripe grapes.</note>—a wonderful celestial color is formed. It is a noble body, but diminished from the nobility of Gold. Its ore is found in specific deposits; and sometimes it has an ore confused with other bodies, and that variety is not as noble.

<margin>
The silver of the common people is calcined <note>Reduced to a powder by heat.</note> and dissolved without profit, and therefore it cannot be the material of the Elixir.
</margin>
It is likewise calcined and dissolved only with the greatest labor and with no benefit.

<margin>
Definition and nature of Saturn, or lead.
</margin>

It flees the refining-ash and the cement <note>A reference to lead's tendency to oxidize or evaporate during the high-heat processes used to purify gold and silver.</note>; it is soft, easy to work in all its dimensions, and extensible with very little pressure.

<margin>
Moon: i.e., the definition and nature of silver.
</margin>

<margin>
Through the "tinted moon" [silver] toward white, one should understand in this <unclear>place</unclear> the extreme substance to be taken, which is purely hardened, and which is mixed with the Sun's [gold's] <unclear>enclosed</unclear> essence, and which is refined by subtle art, thickened, and fixed with arsenic into a stone.

<margin>
The same mentioned in the pages above, 4, 5, 7, and 8.
</margin>

Having concluded the chapter on the Sun <note>Gold</note>, let us now speak of the Moon, using the fitting name, Silver. We say that Silver is a white metallic body, of pure whiteness, clean, hard, ringing when struck, and enduring in the cupel <note>original: "cinericio"; a shallow ceramic dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</note>. Under the hammer, it is extendable, capable of being heated, and easy to melt. It is, therefore, a tincture of whiteness; it hardens Jupiter <note>Tin</note> through the craft, converts it to its own nature, and mixes with the Sun [Gold]. It is not destroyed by fire, but in a standard test without the aid of art, it does not remain united with the gold. He who knows how to refine silver further, and after refinement to thicken it and fix it in association with gold, will find that the silver stays with the gold during the "battle" <note>the intense heat of the furnace</note> and does not leave it entirely. Furthermore, when exposed to the fumes of sharp substances—such as vinegar, sal ammoniac <note>original: "salis ar."</note>, and verjuice <note>original: "agrestæ"; the acidic juice of unripe grapes</note>—it creates a wonderful sky-blue color. It is a noble body, though it falls short of the nobility of Gold. Its ore is found in distinct deposits, though sometimes it is found confused with other substances, in which case it is not as noble. It can be calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and dissolved, but only with the greatest effort and with no practical benefit.

<margin>
Common silver is calcined and dissolved without benefit, and therefore it cannot be the material for the Elixir.

## Concerning Saturn. Chapter 19.

<margin>
Definition and nature of Saturn or lead.
</margin>

Let us now provide the chapter on Lead, and say that it is a metallic body, livid <note>bluish-gray</note>, earthy, heavy, and "mute" <note>producing no sound when struck</note>. It is soft and easily yielding in every dimension, and can be extended with very little pressure.

<margin>Lead is not the closest metal to gold.</margin>
...expandable, and easily meltable without a dissoluble ignition. As certain fools think, they say that lead in its own nature is very close to Gold. But because they are stiff-necked, devoid of all reason, and unable to recognize any logic in the most subtle things, they judge them according to their senses as far as they are able. Because they see that it is heavy, and silent <note>original: "mutum"; referring to the "thud" lead makes when struck, as opposed to the ring of other metals</note>, and does not rot, they believe it to be very close to gold. But all of this is erroneous, and will be more openly disproven by us in the following business at greater length.

<margin>Philosophical lead is the <term>magnet</term><note>In an alchemical sense, a substance that attracts or holds certain properties</note> of metals which, through preparation, passes into philosophical tin and silver.</margin>
Lead, therefore, contains much earthy substance, and for that reason it is washed; and through washing it is turned into Tin <note>original: "Stagnum"</note>. Through this, it is evident that Tin is more similar to the perfect metal <note>Gold</note>. Lead is likewise scorched and becomes <term>Red Lead</term><note>original: "Minium"</note>, and by placing it over the vapor of vinegar, it becomes <term>White Lead</term><note>original: "Cerusa"</note>. And although lead itself is not very close to Silver, we nevertheless easily form Silver from it through our craft; and it does not keep its own weight in transformation, but is changed into a new weight. And it acquires all of this in the <term>Mastery</term><note>The "magisterium" or the Great Work of alchemy</note>.

<margin>See book 4, the chapter on <term>cupellation</term><gloss>refining metals in a hearth of ash</gloss> etc.</margin>

## On Mars. Chapter 22.

<margin>The definition and nature of Mars, which is iron.</margin>
<margin>The Mars of the philosophers is an added sulfur <note>original: "sulphur superueniens"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Sulfur in the mastery easily becomes red, but with difficulty white.</margin>
<margin>A comparison of all the philosophical bodies to their end, namely the elixir.</margin>
Indeed, the account of Mars <term>Mars: the alchemical name for Iron</term> and its whole secret is derived from the work of nature: for it is a metallic body, very leaden in color, with a little red, participating in an impure whiteness; it is hard, capable of being heated to a glow <note>original: "ignibile"</note>, but not fusible by ordinary melting; it is extendable under the hammer, and very resonant. Furthermore, Mars is difficult to work <note>original: "durae tractionis"</note> because of the powerlessness of its melting: for if it is melted without a medicine <note>A "medicine" is an alchemical agent used to "heal" or transform a base metal into a noble one.</note> changing its nature, it joins with the Sun <term>Sol: the alchemical name for Gold</term> and the Moon <term>Luna: the alchemical name for Silver</term>, and it cannot be separated by the trial of separation without great industry. But if it is prepared, it is joined and cannot be separated by any artifice, provided its fixed nature is not changed, and only its uncleanness is removed from it. It is, therefore, easily a tincture <note>A "tincture" is a substance that can impart its color and quality to another.</note> of redness, but a tincture of good whiteness only with great difficulty. And when it is joined without being altered, it does not change the color of what it is joined to, but increases it in quantity. Among all the bodies, therefore, Jupiter is transformed into a more splendid, brighter, and more perfect solar and lunar state...

-># BOOK<-
<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<margin>
Twofold infections of the spirits: oiliness and earthiness. <note>original: "Infectiones spirituum binæ, unctuositas, et terreitas"</note> The same [author] in the Book of Investigation, chapter 27.
</margin>
...[they] act; for one [reason], because the oiliness <term>unctuositas: a greasy or oily quality attributed to sulfur that was believed to cause substances to burn or turn black</term> of Sulfur—whose property is to be easily inflamed and blackened by fire, and consequently to be corrupted once blackened—has not been removed from them. But the other cause is earthiness <term>terreitas: the gross, solid, or "earthy" impurities that weigh down a substance and prevent it from becoming a pure spirit</term>, which was likewise not separated from them. However, in those things where a perfect color is not achieved, the cause is earthiness alone, which produces a leaden <note>original: "liuidum"</note> hue. Burning <term>adustio: the scorching or "combustion" of a substance that renders it impure</term> can also create a leaden color; therefore, we have devised ways to cleanse these from the burning oiliness, and to rid all of them of earthy superfluity.

<margin>
The power of sublimation, and its necessity for purifying spirits from earthiness and oiliness.
</margin>
And to this we can arrive through no other mastery except by sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into a gas, then allowing it to solidify again, leaving impurities behind</term> alone. For when fire is raised, it always elevates the more subtle parts, and thus leaves behind the coarser ones. From this it is clear that by sublimation the spirit is cleansed from the earthiness that hindered its entry <note>the ability of the alchemical spirit to penetrate and "tinge" a metal</note> and gave it an unclean color. Indeed, experience makes it known enough to you through your own sight that they have been freed from it. For you see them to be more shining and more transparent, and that they more easily enter and penetrate the density of [metallic] bodies, and do not make them foul as before. That burning is removed through sublimation is clear by experiment: for Arsenic, which before its sublimation was impure due to burning, does not allow itself to be inflamed after its sublimation, but only recedes <note>meaning it evaporates or sublimes</note> without flaming. And you will find this same result in the experiment with Sulfur.

<margin>
Only spirits adhere to metals with their alteration; therefore the elixir must be made from spirits.
</margin>
Since, therefore, we have seen in no other things but spirits <term>spiritus: volatile substances (like Mercury, Sulfur, or Arsenic) that could "fly" from the fire</term> the ability to adhere to bodies with alteration <note>changing the fundamental nature or color of the metal</note>, we are excused by no other means than the necessity of having prepared them with their purification <note>original: "mundificatione"</note>.

It emphasizes that only these purified spirits have the power to penetrate and permanently alter the nature of metallic bodies to create the Elixir.</summary>

The proof of the administration of dregs <term>faeces: the solid residue or "dregs" left behind after a substance is heated or filtered; in this context, it acts as a stabilizing base</term> in their proper proportion is this: a material should be chosen with which the spirits to be sublimated <term>sublimation: the process where a solid substance is heated into a vapor and then collected again as a solid</term> are most compatible, and with which they may mix most deeply. For that nature to which they are more closely united is more powerful in retaining the dregs of the substances to be sublimated than a nature to which they are not.
