The proof that the administration of dregs is necessary is that if the sulfur or arsenic to be sublimated is not joined with the dregs of some fixed thing, then it would necessarily ascend <note>meaning: "vaporize and rise up the neck of the vessel"</note> with its entire substance, unpurified. Indeed, those who are practiced in sublimations know through experience that we speak the truth.
<margin>This reasoning must be carefully noted by those who mix various kinds of things and wretchedly end everything in smoke. In the Great Work, however, nothing foreign enters.</margin>
The proof that the administration of such dregs (with which the substances to be sublimated are compatible and united in their depths) is necessary is this: if the dregs were not mixed down to the smallest particles <note>original: "per minima," referring to the smallest possible units of matter</note>, then the same thing would happen as if they had no dregs at all—namely, that their entire substance would ascend without any purification. For if they ascend with their whole substance when without dregs, then they must similarly ascend when sublimated from dregs with which they are not united. Experience, however, knows this to be necessary; whoever has seen and known this realizes that when he has sublimated from a foreign substance, separate from their nature, he has sublimated in vain, so that he finds them in no way purified after their ascension. <margin>
On the size of the sublimation furnace.
</margin>
Errors similarly occur regarding the furnace itself. A large furnace provides a great fire, while a small one provides a small fire—provided that the wood and the vent holes <note>original: "foramina auricularum," literally "holes of the ears," referring to the air intakes or vents that allow the furnace to breathe</note> are properly proportioned to them. Thus, if one places a large quantity of the substance to be sublimated into a small furnace, the furnace will not be able to provide enough heat to raise the vapors. But if a small quantity is placed in a large furnace, the sublimation will be ruined due to the excessive heat.

On the same regarding the thickness of the walls.
</margin>

### Concerning the Dregs and the Furnace. Chapter 3.

<margin>Again, the fire must correspond in proportion to the dregs.</margin>
It is therefore profitable for us to guide the craftsman in those matters where everyone is liable to err through ignorance regarding the sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then collects as a solid again</term> of these two spirits <note>original: "spirituū"; in alchemy, "spirits" usually referred to volatile substances like sulfur, mercury, or arsenic</note>. <margin>Concerning the sublimation furnace regarding its size.</margin>
One similarly happens to err regarding the furnace. For a large furnace gives a large fire, while a small one gives a small one, provided the wood and the openings of the "ears" <term>auricularum: the side-vents or air holes of a furnace used to control draft</term> are proportioned to them. If, therefore, the craftsman places a large quantity of the thing to be sublimated into a small furnace, he will not be able to provide a sufficient fire to elevate the substance. If, however, he puts a small amount into a large furnace, he will destroy the sublimation because of the excess of heat.

BOOK 7

## On the thickness of the furnace. Chapter 4.

<margin>Practical instructions on the thickness of the furnace walls.</margin>
The method for determining the thickness of the furnace is this: if you require a large fire, the thickness should be greater, measuring the width of a full hand-span from the thumb to the opposite side of the palm. <note>original: "mensuram extensionis palmæ cum pollice suo"</note> If you require a medium fire, the thickness should be the width of the palm alone. If, however, you require a smaller fire, the furnace should be shaped to the thickness of two fingers.

## On the proportion of firewood. Chapter 5.

<margin>Practical instructions on the material used to kindle the fire.</margin>
Similarly, a specific proportion should be observed regarding the wood used, because solid wood produces a strong fire, while spongy wood produces a weak one. Dry wood yields a large fire that ends quickly, while green wood produces a small fire that lasts a long time. Likewise, solid wood is long-lasting, whereas spongy wood provides a fire that is easily extinguished. Therefore, by considering the distance of the <term>aludel</term> <note>An aludel is a pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in the process of sublimation, where a substance is heated into vapor and then solidified.</note>, the size of the "ears" <note>The "ears" (auricularum) likely refer to the air-vents or draft holes in the furnace walls.</note>, the thickness or thinness of the furnace, and the variety of wood, one can master all the variations of fire through true experience.

<margin>Practical instructions on the duration of the fire.</margin>
By adjusting the width of the vents or the furnace window through which the wood is inserted, and by managing the variety of wood used—including how much is added or removed—one can determine the exact duration of the fire. This allows for specific knowledge of how long each degree of heat can be maintained with consistency. This investigation is extremely useful and necessary for your work.

## On the Sublimation of Mercury.
### Chapter I.

Now indeed let us come to the sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify chemicals</term> of Mercury <term>Mercury: also known as quicksilver; in alchemy, it represents the fluid, transformative principle of matter</term>, so that we may hand down the method by which it is deposited into a crystalline substance. And because much experience is needed for the subtlety of this matter, we have set down our chief purpose and this book so that no one may be led astray by their own errors. 

First, therefore, take two pounds <note>original: "lb." (libra), a unit of weight roughly equal to 327 grams</note> of Mercury extracted from the surface of the earth, which you must clean with salt until it shines brightly like a mirror. Then place the washed Mercury on top, having cleaned it of all water with a linen cloth so that it is pure and dry; and afterward, reduce the vitriol and common salt to a powder and pour them over the mercury so that it is covered. Afterward, let it be sealed with the lute of wisdom <term>luto sapientiæ: a specialized airtight sealant made of clay, lime, and organic fibers used to seal alchemical apparatus against high heat</term>.

The method of removing its superfluous wateriness <term>wateriness: refers to "aqueitas," the internal moisture or volatility of a substance that alchemists sought to stabilize</term> is this: when it is mixed with the calces <term>calces: the powdered remains of a mineral or metal after it has been burned or "calcined"</term> from which it ought to be sublimated, let it be ground. *The furnace for high-intensity heat is one whose* <term>supports<note>original: "spondilia"; structural columns or supports for the furnace body</note></term> *are two cubits high. In the middle, there should be a* <term>grate<note>original: "rota" (wheel); a circular perforated plate used as a fire-grate</note></term> *perforated with very small and numerous holes, securely sealed with* <margin>The grate to be placed in the middle of the furnace.</margin> *clay. The tops of these holes should be narrow and the bottoms wide, so that ash and coals can fall through them more freely, leaving the holes constantly open for the intake of fresh air. Indeed, the free and abundant intake of air through the lower holes is the reason for the great heat produced throughout the furnace; practice with it, and you will find it to be so.*

<margin>
The reason for the design of the aforementioned vessel regarding its length.
</margin>

*The reason for the length of the vessel is so that a large portion of it may extend far beyond the fire and be cooled. In this way, the vapors produced during* <term>sublimation<note>The alchemical process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then collected as it cools back into a solid form</note></term> *may find a place to cool and adhere, rather than finding a way to escape and be lost. This is well known to the practitioner who, having performed a sublimation in a short* <term>aludel<note>A pear-shaped pot or tube used as a condenser in the sublimation process</note></term>*, found nothing of the sublimated material because, due to the shortness of the vessel, the heat was uniform throughout. Therefore, the substance to be sublimated remained constantly in a state of vapor and did not adhere, but instead gradually vanished through the pores of the vessel. Consequently, in all sublimations, the vessel should extend for the greater part of its length into a cool area.*

<margin>
The reason for glazing the aforementioned vessel.
</margin>

*The reason for glazing the vessel is so that the rising vapors do not find the walls of the aludel to be porous and escape by penetrating through them. Thus, the area where the vapors ascend is glazed so that their path of escape is blocked. However, the bottom of the aludel is not glazed, because it sits in the intense heat of the fire, which would melt the glazing. If the glaze were to melt, both the bottom of the vessel and the material being sublimated would be liquefied and turned into* <margin>The property of glass; by "glass," understand mercury.</margin> *glass. For it is the property of glass to melt all things and convert them into its own nature.*

We say, therefore, that we take a "body" <note>original: "corpus"; usually referring to a base metal like lead, tin, or copper</note> which is intended to be purified. ## On the threefold distillation, namely by 
## Alembic, Chemistry, and Filter.
### Chapter 12.

<margin>Distillation and descent agree, because through both we draw out the purer part from the impure.</margin>
<margin>The nature and definition of distillation.</margin>
<margin>The species of distillation.</margin>
It is therefore fitting that, following our purpose, we deliver a discourse on Distillation together with its causes. Distillation is, therefore, the elevation of watery vapors within its vessel. Distillation is certainly diversified. For one kind is through fire. Another, however, is without fire. That which is done by fire is found to be of two types. One is by elevation in an alembic <note>original: "alembic." An alembic is the upper part of a still, consisting of a gourd-like lid where vapors condense before being led down a tube.</note>. Another is by descent of "Chemistry" <note>original: "Chimiæ." Here referring to a specific apparatus for downward distillation, often used for extracting heavy oils from woods or resins.</note>, through which oil is drawn out from vegetable matter. <margin>The cause and purpose of distillation in general.</margin> The general reason for the invention of any distillation is the purification of a liquid substance from its dregs and its cloudiness, and its preservation from decay <note>original: "putrefactione." In alchemy, this refers to the decomposition of a substance into a lower or useless form.</note>. For water does not sustain the sharpness of fire in the same way that ashes do. Therefore, through the method using ashes, it happens that colors and coarser earthy parts are raised. But with the method using water, more subtle parts—colorless and approaching the nature of simple wateriness—are raised. <margin>In this place, if you pay close attention, you have the practice of the entire separation of the elements of the Elixir.</margin> Therefore, a more subtle separation occurs through the method performed with water than through that which is drawn out by ashes.

Experience has shown this to be true; one who had distilled oil using ashes received the oil in the receiver barely changed. Wishing, therefore, to separate its parts, he was forced by necessity to distill it through water. Then, by repeating this process, he separated the oil into its purest elementary parts, such that he extracted the whitest and clearest water from the reddest oil, while the redness of that oil remained entirely in the bottom of the alembic. <margin>"Vegetable" denotes Quicksilver.</margin> Through this mastery, therefore, one reaches the vegetable <note>original: "uegetabilis." ## On Calcination, Chapter 13.

<margin>The nature and definition of calcination.</margin>
<margin>The cause and purpose of calcination.</margin>
Therefore, following the account of distillation, let us deliver a discourse on Calcination. <term>Calcination</term><note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air, typically to remove volatile components or to oxidize it into a powder.</note> is, then, the pulverization of a dry substance by means of fire through the removal of the moisture that binds its parts together. The reason for its discovery, however, is so that the burning, corrupting, and defiling sulfurousness <note>original: *sulphureitas adustiua*; in alchemy, this refers to the combustible principle within metals that was believed to cause them to tarnish or decay.</note> may be destroyed by fire. It varies, indeed, according to the variety of the things to be calcined.

<margin>The types of calcination.</margin>
For bodies are calcined, and spirits are calcined, as well as other things external to their nature, though with a different intention. Because there are "imperfect bodies" of two kinds: namely, the hard ones, such as <term>Venus</term><note>Copper</note> and <term>Mars</term><note>Iron</note>, and the soft ones, such as <term>Jupiter</term><note>Tin</note> and <term>Saturn</term><note>Lead</note>, all of which are calcined, it was necessary for them to be calcined with both specific and general intentions.

<margin>The general intention of calcination is to consume the burning sulfurousness from imperfect bodies.</margin>
Nevertheless, one reason why they are calcined is so that that burning sulfurousness, which corrupts and defiles, might be destroyed; for everything in which there is burning sulfurousness is burned up by fire, and it cannot be destroyed without calcination. This is because the body itself is solid, and due to its solidity and the way the sulfurousness is hidden within the continuity of the substance of <term>Quicksilver</term><note>original: *Argentum uiui*; Mercury, which alchemists believed was a primary component of all metals.</note>, it is protected by it from being burned away. Therefore, it was necessary to separate the metal's continuity so that the fire, reaching more freely to every tiny part of it, might be able to burn the sulfurousness out of it, so that the continuity of the Quicksilver within it would no longer protect it.

<margin>And to cleanse them of their earthiness.</margin>
And there is likewise a common intention in that purification of "earthiness." <note>original: *terreitas*; refers to the non-metallic or impure dross found within a substance.</note> For it has been found that through the repetition of calcination and their "reduction," <note>The process of restoring a calcined powder back into its metallic state.</note> bodies are cleansed...

<summary>This page defines calcination as the use of fire to reduce dry substances to powder by removing their binding moisture. It explains that the primary goal is to strip away "burning sulfurousness" and "earthiness" from metals like copper, iron, tin, and lead.</summary>
<keywords>calcination, sulfurousness, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Quicksilver, earthiness, imperfect bodies, alchemical purification</keywords>

<margin>The purpose of the calcination of both types of lead <note>In alchemy, "both leads" usually refers to common lead and tin (often called "white lead").</note>.</margin>
as we will soon write in the following sections. The special **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</term> of **soft bodies** <term>soft bodies (corpora mollia): metals with low melting points, specifically tin and lead.</term> is done so that, with these two objectives, the intent of that calcination is to harden them and subject them to fire. This is achieved through the clever repetition of calcination upon them, which we should explain in the following tradition. For we have found through this ingenuity that they are clearly hardened. Yet, **Jupiter** <note>original: "Iupiter"; the alchemical name for the metal Tin.</note> is hardened more clearly and quickly. [The reason for the discovery of the calcination of **spirits** <term>spirits (spirituum): volatile substances like mercury, sulfur, or ammonia that vaporize when heated.</term> is

<margin>The purpose of the calcination of Spirits.</margin>
so that they themselves may be better **fixed** <note>"Fixation" is the process of transforming a volatile, evaporating substance into a stable solid that can withstand heat.</note> and more easily dissolved in water. For every type of calcined material is more fixed than that which is not calcined, and is of easier **solution** because the calcined parts are more refined by the fire, mixing more easily with water and being converted into liquid; anyone who is experienced knows this.
<margin>Note the thinning of substances through solution.</margin>
The calcination of other things was required for the preparation of spirits and bodies, which we will determine more extensively in the following section. However, none of these things [the preparations] are yet of the final perfection.

<margin>The method for calcining soft bodies—namely tin and both types of lead—either by fire alone or with salt.</margin>
The method of calcination is therefore diverse because of the diversity of the things to be calcined. For bodies are calcined differently than spirits or other things, and even the bodies differ among themselves. Similarly, they are calcined in various ways. [For **soft bodies** have one general method for the purpose of calcination: specifically, that both can be calcined by fire alone, and both similarly by the sharpness of salt, whether they are prepared or not.

<margin>How tin and the "lead of the philosophers" are calcined by fire alone.</margin>

<margin>All these things which the philosophers write about Jupiter and Saturn are to be understood as referring to the mass already dissolved. because **Saturn** easily returns from its calx back into a metallic body. **Jupiter**, however, returns to metal with great difficulty. Therefore, lest the craftsman err in the processing of Saturn, after its first pulverization—which should be done at a moderate fire—he must take care that it does not revert to metal before its calx is perfected. This requires a careful tempering of the fire and a gradual, cautious increase of heat until the substance is "fixed" in its calx and cannot easily return to a solid metal state; only then can a greater fire be applied to perfect the calx. ...his powder <note>original: calcem; the ash-like residue left after heating a metal</note>, it might happen that he does not reduce <note>restore to metallic form</note> it; instead, he may find it in its previous state, or turned into glass, and then judges its reduction to be impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of Jupiter, he will not reduce it; but if he uses a great fire, it is not certain that he will reduce it, but it is possible he will lead it into vitrification <note>turning into glass</note>. And the reason for this is that Jupiter, in the depths of its nature of Quicksilver <note>original: Argenti uiui; mercury</note>, contains a fugitive substance shut within it. If it remains for a long time in the fire, this substance will flee, leaving behind a body deprived of moisture. This body will be found to turn into a glassy melt rather than a metallic one. For everything deprived of its own moisture provides no melting except that which turns to glass. Therefore, it is necessarily required that one reduces it quickly with the greatest force of fire and hastens speed; for otherwise, it is not reduced. Let him who wishes to know this practice it.

# BOOK

<margin>
On the calcination <note>the process of heating a substance to a high temperature to reduce it to a powder</note> of Venus <note>alchemical name for copper</note> and Mars <note>alchemical name for iron</note>.
</margin>

<margin>
Here you have the practice of calcining the metal from which the elixir <note>a transformative substance sought by alchemists</note> is drawn.
</margin>

This occurs because Saturn <note>lead</note> possesses a more fixed moisture and a greater earthiness <note>original: terreitatem; the elemental quality of "earth"</note> than Jupiter <note>tin</note>. Regarding Venus <note>copper</note> and Mars <note>iron</note>, the method is the same, yet it differs from the first two because of the difficulty of melting them. The method is to place them as thin plates in a strong fire. The intention is not to melt them, due to their high quantity of earthiness and the large measure of burning and fugitive sulfur they contain. In this way, they are easily brought into lime <term>lime: original "calcem," referring to the powdery oxide or ash left after heating a metal</term>. This is because the continuity of the Quicksilver <note>mercury</note> substance is interrupted by the great amount of earthiness mixed within it, and thus porosity is created in them. Through this porosity, the passing sulfur can fly away, and the fire reaching it can burn and lift it. By this means, the metal is left behind, its parts are made smaller, and it is converted into ash through the disruption of its density. The experience of this is manifest: for when a plate of Venus <note>copper</note> is exposed to fire, it will give off a sulfurous flame and produce a pulverizable scale on its surface. This happens because the sulfur near the surface necessarily burns away more easily.

<margin>
Furnace for the calcination of hard metals.
</margin>

The design of the furnace for this calcination is the same as the distillation furnace, except that it should have only one hole at its top, through which it may freely release smoke. The materials to be calcined should be placed in the middle of the furnace so that they receive the fire freely from all sides. 

<margin>
Vessel for the calcination of hard metals.
</margin>

The vessel itself should be made of earth <note>clay or ceramic</note> and shaped like a shallow bowl <note>original: paropsidis; a Roman-style side-dish</note>.

### BOOK 2

<margin>Many differences in coagulation:</margin>
...due to the multiplicity of those things to be coagulated. For one substance requires the coagulation of <term>quick-silver<note>original: "Argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the old name for mercury.</note></term>, while another requires a dissolved me-
<margin>Concerning the coagulation of quick-silver.</margin>
dicine <note>In alchemy, a "medicine" refers to the "elixir" or "philosopher's stone" in its liquid or powder state, used to heal "sick" or base metals.</note>. Furthermore, there is a twofold coagulation of the quick-silver itself. One is through the removal of all the innate moisture from it. The other is through the thickening of that moisture until it is hardened. To coagulate it, however, is an extremely difficult and laborious task, which is only achieved through the depth of sharp industry; and we shall relate every method <note>original: "ingenium"; meaning a clever device or specialized technique</note> of that coagulation.

<margin>1st error of those coagulating mercury by keeping it in a temperate fire.</margin>
Certain people thought the method of coagulation would be through keeping it in a temperate fire. When they believed they had coagulated it, they found that after removing it from the fire, it flowed just as it did before. Because of this, they were brought into a stupor and great wonder, arguing that this goal could not be reached.

<margin>2nd error of those coagulating mercury through long perseverance in a strong fire.</margin>
Others, however, assuming by necessity from natural principles that any moisture is converted into dryness by the heat of fire, attempted to continue its preservation in the fire with persistent urgency. Through this continuation, they reached a point where some converted it into a white stone, others into a red stone, and others into a yellow stone which had neither fusion nor <term>penetration<note>original: "ingressio"; the ability of an alchemical substance to merge with and transform a base metal.</note></term>. Because they could not judge the cause of this diversity, they threw it away.

<margin>3rd error of those coagulating mercury with mixed, but foreign, medications.</margin>
Others, attempting to coagulate it with medicines <note>additives or chemical reagents</note>, did not reach the goal. Instead, an illusion happened to them: either because they did not coagulate it, or because it was invisibly thinned out by them, or because their coagulation did not take the form of any metallic body, but rather the form of quick-silver mixed with lead. And the cause of these things they likewise did not know—

### SECOND [BOOK]

<margin>The 4th error of those who coagulate mercury with impure medicines.</margin>

<margin>The cause of the aforementioned errors regarding the coagulation of mercury.</margin>
Therefore, it is helpful for us to explain the causes, so that the craftsman may discover the mastery of that coagulation. As we have already sufficiently explained, the substance of Quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</term> is uniform; for this reason, it is not possible to remove its watery nature in a short space of time by keeping it in the fire. 

<margin>Cause of the 1st error of those coagulating mercury.</margin>
Too much haste, therefore, was the cause of the first error. Since mercury is of a subtle substance, it withdraws from the fire; therefore, an excess of fire was the cause of the error for those from whom it flees <note>The author uses "flees" to describe the process of evaporation or sublimation where mercury turns to vapor and escapes the vessel.</note>.

<margin>Cause of the third error. Substances that coagulate quicksilver.</margin>
It mixes easily with Sulfur, Arsenic, and Marcasite <term>A mineral, often iron pyrite, which alchemists believed shared a "nature" with metals</term>, because of a commonality in their nature. Therefore, it appears coagulated through these substances, yet not in the form of a solid metallic body, but rather as Quicksilver mixed with lead. Since these substances are fugitive <term>Volatile; substances that evaporate or vanish when exposed to heat</term>, they cannot hold the mercury in the "battle of the fire" until it reaches the nature of a solid body. Instead, they flee together through the heat of the fire: and that is the cause of the error for those who coagulate in this way.

<margin>That quicksilver has a superfluous humidity. The same author in the book *On Investigation* and often elsewhere.</margin>
Similarly, Quicksilver certainly has a humidity closely united to it, which cannot be separated from it except by a cautious "violence" of fire, or by keeping it in its own fire.

<margin>Cause of the second error.</margin>
And its "own fire" is that which, by being increased according to the requirements of the metal's tolerance, removes its humidity without leaving behind enough of a part for metallic fusion <note>The ability of a metal to melt into a liquid state.</note>. When this humidity is removed, it does not melt; and this is the cause of error for those who coagulate it into that non-fusible stone.

<margin>That quicksilver has sulfurous parts naturally mixed in. The same author on page 37 and often elsewhere.</margin>
Similarly, it has sulfurous parts naturally mixed with it...

Therefore, because of the diversity of the medicine, an illusion occurs in its solidification: sometimes it becomes Lead, sometimes Jupiter <term>Tin</term>, sometimes Venus <term>Copper</term>, and sometimes Mars <term>Iron</term>. This happens because of impurity. But sometimes it becomes the Sun <term>Sol: Gold</term>, and sometimes the Moon <term>Luna: Silver</term>, which must result from purity and the careful consideration of the colors.

### CHAPTER IV.
### On Coagulation.

We shall define Coagulation as the action of heat upon dry matter, by which that same matter—whether it be a spirit <term>Spirit: in alchemy, a volatile substance that can evaporate, like mercury or sulfur</term> or an earth—is reduced to a state of fixation <term>Fixation: the process of making a substance stable in fire so that it no longer evaporates</term>, or rather to a specific consistency. The subject of the action of Coagulation is dry matter, yet not so dry that it does not still retain some radical moisture <note>original: "humiditatem radicalem"; in alchemical theory, this is the essential "inner" liquid that holds the substance's form together and prevents it from crumbling into dust</note> within itself. It is through this moisture that Coagulation is said to be "in potential" to achieve the consistency of its form. The result of Coagulation, arising from two matters coalescing into a single body, even causes one to extinguish the other: just as Spirit and Earth coalesce into one body. This result will always remain locked away, so that it may never again be extracted unless the Coagulation is dissolved <note>This refers to the alchemical cycle of "solve et coagula"—dissolve and solidify.</note>.

Coagulation is, moreover, either material or formal. Material coagulation is that by which matter is reduced into a certain consistency. Formal coagulation, however, is that by which the "form" remains within that same dry matter, and thus reduces it to fixation, or rather to a certain consistency. And so, through this, Coagulation is nothing other than fixation and the act of fixing, whether in potential or in act. Fixation "in potential" is that which is called "consistent," and it is said to cling to the dry and the non-dry; it is fixed in a certain way because it is fixed by its own nature, but not yet fully within itself. That which is fixed "in act" is that which has been made fixed, or solid. The matter of Coagulation is that body in which the fixation exists—such as earth—and which is called "fixed." There are two types of Coagulation: namely, union and consistency.

<vocab>Coagulation, Dry matter, Fixation, Fixation (the process), Heat, Spirit, Consistency</vocab>

# On the Coagulation of Mercury by Precipitation
## Chapter 17

<margin>The first method of coagulating mercury in a urinal-shaped vessel.</margin>
<margin>Regarding this vessel, see page 34 and the figure below.</margin>
Mercury is therefore coagulated <note>In alchemy, coagulation refers to the process of turning a liquid or volatile substance into a solid or stable form.</note> through frequent precipitation using the violence of intense heat. For the harshness of the fire easily removes the mercury's "wateriness" <note>its volatile, liquid nature</note>. This is achieved using a vessel of great length; in this long space, the mercury finds a place to cool and a surface to cling to and rest upon along the interior sides. Because of the vessel's height, it finds no way to escape, but is instead repeatedly driven back down to the bottom by the great heat of the fire. Through many such repetitions, it eventually becomes <term>fixed|the state where a substance is stable and no longer evaporates when exposed to fire</term>.

<margin>The second method of coagulating mercury in a flask.</margin>
<margin>You will find the second figure for this vessel below.</margin>
It is similarly coagulated by being kept for a long duration in its own fire within a glass vessel. This vessel should have a very long neck and a belly shaped like a flask <note>original: "ampullæ"</note>. The neck must remain open throughout the process so that its moisture can eventually evaporate.

<margin>The third method of coagulating mercury through a medicine.</margin>
<margin>The medicine that truly coagulates mercury is purified and clean sulfur.</margin>
It is also coagulated by a <term>medicine|In this context, a "medicine" is a chemical reagent or agent of transformation</term> suitable for it, which we will describe more clearly in what follows. Here, however, we shall state our full intention regarding it, based on what we have discovered through our own experiments. That medicine is the substance which adheres most deeply to the mercury and is mixed with it at the most minute level before the mercury can escape.

<margin>Metals cannot bond deeply with mercury so as to coagulate it.</margin>
One must, therefore, gather this medicine from things compatible with it. These substances include all "bodies" <note>the alchemical term for metals</note>, Sulfur, or Arsenic. However, because we do not see any metal in its natural state coagulate the mercury—rather, the mercury flees from them, no matter how compatible they may seem—we consider that no solid metal adheres to it deeply. Therefore, it is necessary that the medicine be of a subtler substance and a more liquid melting point...

As for the method of coagulating dissolved substances, it is done using a flask buried in ashes up to its neck over a tempered fire, until the "wateriness" <note>original: "aqueitas," the volatile liquid component</note> evaporates.

according to the variety of things to be fixed: which are, namely, certain "bodies" diminished from perfection, such as <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for Lead</note>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>Tin</note>, and <term>Venus</term> <note>Copper</note>; and according to the diversity of the "spirits" themselves, which are <term>Sulfur</term> and <term>Arsenic</term> in one degree, and <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury</note> in another. In the third degree are <term>Marcasite</term> <note>Iron pyrites or similar metallic ores</note>, <term>Magnesia</term> <note>A term often used for various minerals, including manganese or magnesium ores</note>, and <term>Tutty</term> <note>Zinc oxide collected from the flues of furnaces</note>. ## On Fixation and its Methods, Chapter 18.

<margin>
The nature and definition of fixation.
The cause and purpose of fixation.
The types of fixation.
</margin>
**FIXATION** is the appropriate stabilization of a substance that escapes from the fire. <note>original: "FIXIO est rei fugientis ad ignem conueniens adaptatio." Fixation is the process of making a substance non-volatile so it does not evaporate when heated.</note> The reason for the goal of fixation itself is so that every tincture and every alteration may be made permanent during the process of changing, and not be altered further. It is also diversified in a similar way, according to the variety of things to be fixed: which are, namely, certain bodies diminished from perfection, such as <term>Saturn</term> <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note>, <term>Jupiter</term> <note>The alchemical name for Tin.</note>, and <term>Venus</term> <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note>; and according to the diversity of the <term>spirits</term> <note>In this context, "spirits" refers to volatile substances that easily vaporize.</note> themselves, which are <term>Sulfur</term> and <term>Arsenic</term> in one degree, and <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note> in another; and in a third degree, indeed, <term>Marcasite</term>, <term>Magnesia</term>, and <term>Tutia</term> <note>Zinc oxide or zinc ore.</note>: all the aforesaid are dissolved, coagulated, and fixed, along with similar substances.

<margin>
Fixation of imperfect bodies through calcination.
</margin>
Therefore, these bodies that are diminished from their perfection are fixed through their <term>calcination</term> <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve oxidation or a change in state.</note>: since through this process they are released from their volatile and corrupting sulfurous nature. We have already sufficiently demonstrated this calcination in its own discourse.

<margin>
Fixation of sulfur and arsenic, etc., first by their frequently repeated sublimation.
</margin>
Sulfur and Arsenic are fixed in two ways: namely, by the repetition of <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process where a solid turns directly into a gas and then back to a solid, used here to purify and stabilize the material.</note> over them in <term>aludel</term> <note>A series of pear-shaped earthenware pots used as condensers.</note> vessels, until they remain stable. From this, one achieves the goal of hastening their fixation, so that you may contrive a method for multiple sublimations and repetitions in a short time. This is done with two aludels and their double covers, in this order: that they should never cease the act of sublimation until they have been fixed. Therefore, when the substance has ascended in one aludel, let it be cast into the other, and so let it be done in alternating turns; also, the aludels should never be allowed to sit idle adhering to the joints, but should be in a continuous rising of the fire.

<margin>
Regarding this vessel, you have the third figure.
</margin>

## On Ceration. Chapter IV.

**Ceration** <term>Ceration: derived from the Latin 'cera' (wax); the alchemical process of softening a hard substance until it reaches a waxy consistency, making it easier to melt or merge</term> is therefore the reduction of a hard, non-meltable substance to a state of **liquefaction**. To this end, let the intention of the mind be directed: that the **anointing** <term>anointing: or 'unction' (unctio), refers to the addition of a moist or oily principle to a dry, "brittle" substance to change its physical properties</term> of fixation or liquefaction—the qualities by which these two states are determined within a body—may be increased so that the substance does not simply flow away <note>In this context, to "flow away" means to leak out of the vessel or dissipate uselessly rather than transforming</note> in the fire.

The reasoning is as follows: hard substances are scarcely meltable even when the fire is blown for a very long time; they are barely fused and are withdrawn from the alchemical operations because they lack this "anointing" within their bodies and are instead dry. For where there is anointing, a transformation occurs immediately. 

We see this, for instance, with leather: if placed in a fire without being softened, it is soon burned up. If, however, you grease <note>original: *unxeris*—to anoint or smear with oil or fat</note> the leather, it certainly flows and softens more easily. In this same way, substances that the fire cannot melt are moistened within their bodies until they are brought to a state of fusion; afterward, the heat of the fire should be gradually increased so that they may be **fixed** <term>fixed: the process of 'fixation' makes a substance stable and resistant to evaporation or further change when heated</term>. 

In this way, we achieve the goal of our works: the substance does not fly away <note>that is, it does not evaporate or escape the vessel as vapor</note> under the impulse of the fire, and the pure, meltable matter—though once fleeting <note>original: *fugax*—referring to a volatile substance that "flees" the heat</note>—will not have escaped.

<summary>This chapter defines ceration as the process of softening hard materials into a waxy, meltable state by adding an "oily" principle or unction. This prevents dry substances from burning and allows them to be stabilized so they do not evaporate during the heating process.</summary>
<keywords>ceration, liquefaction, anointing, unction, fixation, alchemy, metallurgy, volatility, Geber</keywords>

<margin>The fixation of <term>marcasite|a term used historically for iron pyrites or other glittering minerals</term>, magnesia, and <term>tutia|impure zinc oxide collected from furnace flues</term>.</margin>
The fixation of Marcasite, Magnesia, and Tutia is performed such that when, after their first sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note>, we have obtained the part we desire from them, we discard their dregs. We then repeat the sublimation upon them, continually returning that which ascended to the top back to that which remained at the bottom for each of these substances, until they are "fixed" <note>rendered stable and no longer volatile under heat</note>. The description of the vessels for this has already been provided.

## On Ceration. Chapter 19.

<margin>The nature and definition of ceration.</margin>
**CERATION**, therefore, is the softening of a hard, non-fusible <note>unable to be melted</note> substance until it reaches a state of liquefaction. From this it is clear that the reason for its invention was so that a substance—which previously could not penetrate or alter a "body" <note>usually referring to a base metal</note> because it lacked the ability to melt—might be softened so that it could flow and achieve penetration.

<margin>The cause and goal of ceration.</margin>
<margin>The opinion of some regarding ceration is refuted.</margin>
<margin>See pages 52, 70, and the back of page 56.</margin>
Some have therefore thought that ceration ought to be performed using liquid oils and waters. But this is an error, entirely removed from the natural principles of this mastery, and is proven false by the manifest works of nature.

For we do not see nature having placed in metallic bodies themselves a moisture that is quickly ended; rather, she provides a moisture that is long-lasting, intended for the necessity of their softening and melting. 

<margin>In metals there are two types of moisture: one is external, the other internal and "radical" <note>essential or fundamental</note>, as Albertus <note>referring to the medieval scholar Albertus Magnus</note> says. The first is consumed by strong fire during <term>calcination|the process of reducing a metal to powder through heat</term>; the other resists fire and thrives in fire like a <term>Salamander|a mythical creature believed to be unharmed by flames</term>. It is through this [internal moisture] that the ceration of the <term>Elixir|the transformative substance sought by alchemists</term> is achieved.</margin>
If nature had placed such [temporary] moisture in them, it would necessarily follow that these bodies would be totally deprived of moisture by a single heating. Consequently, after one such heating, any body would be unable to be hammered or melted. Therefore, in imitating the works of nature as far as we are able, it is necessary for us to follow nature's own method in "incerating" <note>applying the process of ceration</note>.

<summary>This page describes the "fixation" of mineral ores and introduces the concept of "ceration," the process of softening hard substances so they can penetrate and transform metals. It argues that this must be done using an internal, fire-resistant moisture rather than common oils, following the natural principles observed in metallurgy.</summary>

<keywords>ceration, fixation, marcasite, magnesia, tutia, sublimation, Albertus Magnus, Elixir, alchemy, metallurgy</keywords>

<margin>The radical moisture <note>original: "humiditas radicalis," the fundamental life-fluid believed to exist within matter</note> of metals is the very mercury of the philosophers, just as sulfur is in <unclear>sevens</unclear> the salt of <unclear>nature</unclear> and <unclear>dryness</unclear>.</margin>
It softens, however, at the very root of the ceration of fusible materials by means of a moisture which, above all other moistures, can withstand the heat of fire. Therefore, it is necessary for us to use a similar ceration and moisture. In no other substances is this softening moisture found more effectively or more potentially than in these: specifically, in Sulfur and Arsenic closely, but even more closely and effectively in **Quicksilver** <note>mercury</note>. We do not see the moisture of these substances leave their "earth" <note>the solid, physical base of the mineral</note> because of the powerful union they formed during nature's own process of mixing. In all other things that contain moisture, however, you will find by experience that the moisture is separated from its earthy substance during resolution <note>the process of breaking a substance down into its component parts</note>; and after that separation, the substance is deprived of all its moisture. In the aforementioned **spirits** <note>the volatile substances: sulfur, arsenic, and mercury</note>, this does not happen at all. Therefore, there is no other way for us to achieve the desired softening except by accepting their use in the ceration process.

<margin>What the method of ceration is like</margin>
The method of ceration, therefore, is performed through these substances, so that their **sublimation** <note>the process of heating a substance into vapor and then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</note> is repeated over the material to be softened as many times as necessary, until they remain within that material along with their moisture, providing a good "fusion" <note>the ability to melt and flow like wax</note>. However, let this not be done before their perfect **cleansing** <note>original: "mundationem"</note> from every corrupting element.

Having explained the principles as the effective causes <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "effective" or "efficient" cause is the agent that brings something about—in this case, the alchemist’s initial operations.</note> of this art, he now approaches the material aspects, that is, the metals and the principles of metals from which the Elixir <note>original: "Elixir". Therefore, now that the discussion regarding the principles of this mastery has been delivered, it is necessary—as we promised—to pursue the intention of this art of ours completely, in language suitable to it. Likewise, we must consider the artistic processes through which we may know whether the perfection is complete. Once these things have been handed down, the entire knowledge of perfection will be delivered, according to the requirements of our art.

<margin>**Quicksilver** is the perfecter of the art.</margin>
<margin>**Arsenic** and **Sulphur** are more friendly to quicksilver than anything else.</margin>
...that it is the perfecter is shown by manifest experience. For we see that **Quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum|The liquid metal mercury, central to alchemical theory as the "mother" of all metals</term> adheres more to Quicksilver, and is more friendly to the same; after that, truly, to **Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"; often symbolized by the Sun</note>, and after that, **Silver** <note>original: "Argentum"; often symbolized by the Moon</note>. Therefore, from this it is left that the **Sun** and **Moon** <note>the alchemical names for Gold and Silver</note> are more of its own nature. Indeed, we do not see other bodies have such great conformity to it; therefore, we truly intimate that they participate less in its nature. And whatever things we see are saved most from <term>combustion|adustione; the process of being burned or oxidized by heat</term>, those we consider to have and possess more of its nature. And therefore it remains that Quicksilver itself is the perfecter and the savior from combustion, 
<margin><insert>See page 69.</insert></margin>
which is the ultimate of perfection. 
<margin>Preparation of quicksilver obtained through washing.</margin>
The second degree of its **cleansing** for its **coagulation** <note>the process of turning liquid mercury into a solid or "fixed" state</note> is that a washing away of its earthiness through purification should alone suffice for it. The method of which is this: let a glass or earthen dish be taken, and into it let the **Quicksilver** be placed, over which is poured a small quantity of **robes** <note>original: "robes"; likely referring to a red liquid reagent, vinegar, or a specific alchemical water</note>, or another similar thing which suffices to cover it. Afterwards, let it be placed over a slow fire so that it does not boil, and let it be stirred continually with the fingers over the bottom of the dish, so that the Quicksilver may be divided into the likeness of a most subtle white powder, until all the **vinegar** <note>original: "acetum"</note> evaporates, and 
<margin>Note the practice of the mastery, which is also in the chapter on the coagulation of quicksilver.</margin>
the **Quicksilver** itself returns. Afterwards, truly, when you see that the foul and black dross has emanated from it, wash it and throw it away; and multiply this by repeating the turn, until you see the color of its earthiness change perfectly into a clear state, mixed with a **sky-blue white** color—which is the sign of a perfect washing. When, therefore, it has arrived at that state, let the **medicine** of its coagulation be projected upon it, and it will be coagulated into a **Gold-maker** or a **Silver-maker**.
<margin>**Gold-maker** <note>original: "Solificum"</note> and **Silver-maker** <note>original: "lunificum"</note> are the **Elixirs** for Gold and Silver.</margin>

Regarding the other **spirits** <term>spiritibus|Volatile substances that can be vaporized by heat, traditionally mercury, sulfur, arsenic, and sal ammoniac</term>, it is necessary for us to provide the natural tradition. These are, namely, **Marcasite**, **Magnesia** <note>likely a reference to various ores like manganese or a form of lead/antimony</note>, and **Tutty** <note>zinc oxide, often collected from the walls of smelting furnaces</note>, which make a great impression upon metallic bodies. We say, then, that Marcasite has a twofold substance in its creation: that of Quicksilver—specifically, "mortified" <note>chemically altered or killed, meaning it has lost its liquid, flowing form</note> and approaching **fixation** <term>fixionem|The process of making a volatile substance stable and resistant to heat</term>—and that of burning **Sulfur**. For when it is **sublimated** <term>sublimatio|The process of heating a substance into vapor and collecting it again as a solid</term>, a manifest, burning sulfurous substance emanates from it; and even without sublimation, its sulfurous nature is similarly perceived. For if it is placed in the fire, it does not receive the heat until it is ignited and burns by the inflammation of its Sulfur. 

That it truly possesses the substance of Quicksilver is shown to the senses; for it grants the whiteness of pure **Silver** <note>original: "Argenti"</note> to **Venus** <note>the alchemical name for Copper</note>, just as Quicksilver itself does. In its sublimation, it also grants a **celestial** <note>original: "coelestinum"; a sky-blue or heavenly blue</note> color and a manifest clarity.

## On the Essence of Mars: Chapter 6.

If, however, the substance is a fixed, earthy sulfur mixed with an earthy Quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and both are of a leaden rather than pure white color, iron is formed. This occurs when the fixed sulfur is the dominant part, as its excess prevents the metal from melting easily. Therefore, it follows that <gloss>fixed</gloss> sulfur—through the process of fusion—loses the speed of its liquefaction more readily than Quicksilver does. In contrast, we see that sulfur which is not fixed melts even more quickly than Quicksilver.

From these things, therefore, the cause of the speed or slowness of melting in each of the metallic bodies is made clear. For that which has more fixed sulfur melts more slowly, but that which has more of the burning sulfur undergoes fusion more easily and quickly—a point we have left to be sufficiently proven by our own efforts. That <gloss>indeed</gloss> fixed sulfur makes melting slower is shown by this: it is never "fixed" unless it is calcined, and once it has been calcined, it allows for no melting at all. Therefore, it must hinder melting in all metallic bodies. 

That sulfur is not fixed unless it is calcined is clear from the experiment of anyone who tries to fix it without calcining: for he finds that the sulfur always "flees" <note>vaporizes or evaporates</note> until it is turned into earth, which has the likeness of true lime <note>original: "calcis"; the powdery residue left after heating</note>. This, however, happens very little with Quicksilver, for it can be fixed without being turned into earth, though it can similarly be fixed by being converted into earth. For by hastening its fixation—which is achieved through precipitation—it is fixed and changed into earth. Yet, through a gradual and repeated process of sublimation...

## On the essence of Venus. Chapter 7.

<margin>The generation and inner nature of copper; which I believe should be understood alchemically.</margin>
RETURNING therefore to our purpose, we say that if there should be an impure, fixed, and coarse Sulfur <term>Sulfur: in alchemy, one of the two primary principles of metals, representing the active, combustible, and coloring element</term> for its greater part—but for its lesser part, non-fixed, livid, and red—and if as a whole it neither overcomes nor is overcome, and falls upon coarse Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum uiuum"; the passive, metallic principle</note>: it is necessary that copper <note>original: "æs"; while "aes" can mean bronze or brass, in this alchemical context it refers to the metal of Venus: copper</term> be created from it. It is necessary to provide proof of all these things through the data of its own nature. For when it is placed in the fire for inflammation, you will be able to discern a sulfurous flame from it, which is a sign of non-fixed Sulfur; there is also a loss of its quantity through evaporation. However, fixed Sulfur is signaled in that metal by its ability to endure frequent burning. For from this comes the slowing of its melting and the hardening of its substance, which are signs of a multitude of fixed Sulfur within it. That it is red, impure, and joined to impure Quicksilver is signaled by the senses; hence it requires no other proof.

<margin>Calcination contributes greatly to the exact solution of bodies, because it makes their substance finer.</margin>
Therefore, you may draw out the secret by experiment: for you see that every thing changed into "earth" <note>referring to a powdered metallic oxide</note> by the action of heat is easily dissolved and reduced to the nature of water. This happens because of the refining <note>original: "subtiliationē"; the process of making the particles smaller or more "subtle"</note> of the parts by the fire. Therefore, a more refined thing, reduced in its own nature to this earthy state, is refined further, and thus more easily dissolved; and so, what is refined most is dissolved most.

<margin>Fixed and calcined sulphurs, if placed in the vapor of vinegar, "flower" <note>This refers to efflorescence, where a mineral forms a powdery or crystalline crust on its surface upon exposure to air or vapor.</note> and are easily dissolved with it, because they thus acquire an alum-like quality from which the solution occurs.

From where the blackness arises that appears in the preparation of sulphur.</margin>

Fixed sulphur reaches a state of melting <term>fusion: the process of turning a solid substance into a liquid by heat.</term> through the heat of the fire and the refining of its parts by that heat. Seek the suitability of the substance for dissolution; the sign of this is the exposure of these two bodies <note>Likely referring back to the "two bodies" mentioned in the previous page's context, typically iron and copper in this treatise.</note> to the vapor of vinegar. For through this, the alum-like quality of their sulphur blooms upon their surface, created by the refining heat. And if you place these two bodies into an acidic liquid, many of their parts will easily dissolve by boiling in it. If you look at the ores of these two, you will find a clear substance of this alum-like quality dripping from them and adhering to them; this quality is proven by its sharp taste and easy dissolution in water. For nothing else is found to be sharp and easily soluble except for alum and that which shares its nature. 

However, the blackness in each of these two bodies is created in the fire by unfixed sulphur, which is contained in them in great quantity—as in <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper.</term>—but in <term>Mars: the alchemical name for iron.</term> it is present in a small amount, approaching the nature of the "fixed" state <note>original: "fixi"; a "fixed" substance in alchemy is one that is stable in fire and does not evaporate.</note>. Therefore, it is not easily possible to remove such a mark from Iron. Thus, it has now become clear that melting occurs from unfixed sulphur, and melting is aided by it; whereas from fixed sulphur, melting does not occur and is instead hindered. Anyone who has been unable to keep sulphur in a melted state after its fixation knows this to be a necessary truth.

arguments, it follows that there is a twofold "sulphurity" <note>The quality of containing sulphur, which was thought to be the cause of combustion and impurity in metals.</note> in metallic bodies: one is found in the depth of the quicksilver, locked in at the very beginning of its mixture; the other is supervening. This is because it has already become one with the creation itself. This is proven by experiment: we see that combustible sulphurity is destroyed by fire, but fixed sulphurity is not. If, therefore, we say that bodies are cleansed by calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile impurities</term>, you must understand this as referring to the earthy substance, which is not united at the root of its nature.

# BOOK #

<margin>The cause of the hardness of metals</margin>
we see its entire color changed into lemon-yellow <note>original: "citrinum," a yellowish-orange color often signifying a specific stage of chemical transformation</note>. Jupiter's <term>Iouis|Tin</term>, however, changes into white during its calcinations <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or to oxidize it</note>. And thus, the path for investigating the cause of this work is opened to us: why, in calcination, is Jupiter hardened more easily than Saturn <term>Saturnus|Lead</term>? Yet, it does not reach its melting point more slowly than Saturn. This is because the true cause of hardness is fixed Sulfur and fixed Quicksilver <term>Argentum uiuum|literally "living silver," the common name for Mercury</term>. 

<margin>The cause of the melting of metals.</margin>
The cause of melting, however, is twofold: namely, Quicksilver and combustible Sulfur. One of these is sufficient for the perfection of fusion <note>melting</note> at each degree of heating, specifically regarding the Quicksilver. 

<margin>The Jupiter of the philosophers abounds in quicksilver that is not truly fixed.</margin>
Because there is a great quantity of Quicksilver in Jupiter that is not truly "fixed" <note>in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is stable under heat and does not evaporate</note>, it retains a high speed of melting, and this property is not easily removed from it. 

<margin>Jupiter is more easily hardened than Saturn, and why.</margin>
The cause of softness is likewise twofold: namely, Quicksilver and combustible Sulfur. Because the burning "sulfureity" <note>the sulfurous quality</note> is removed more easily from Jupiter than from Saturn, once that cause of softness is removed, it must necessarily harden quickly. Saturn, however, because it possesses the causes of both types of softness strongly joined together, is not easily hardened. 

<margin>The difference between softness caused by quicksilver not truly fixed, and that caused by combustible sulfur.</margin>
Yet there is a distinction in softness caused by Quicksilver and that caused by Sulfur. Softness from Sulfur is "yielding" <note>original: "cessiua," meaning it gives way under pressure or compresses</note>, while softness from Quicksilver is "extensible" <note>original: "extensiua," meaning it can be hammered out or stretched, like ductility</note>. This is necessarily proven by the fact that we see bodies containing much Quicksilver possess great extensibility, while those with little, have little. Therefore, Jupiter is more easily and finely extended <note>hammered thin</note> than Saturn; Saturn more easily than **Venus** <term>Venus|Copper</term>; Venus more than Mars <term>Mars|Iron</term>; and Luna <term>Luna|Silver</term> more finely than Jupiter.

### THIRD <note>original: "TERTIVS," likely referring to the Third Book of the treatise</note>

The Sun <note>original: "Sol," the alchemical name for Gold</note> is truly more subtle than the Moon <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for Silver</note>. It is clear, therefore, that since the cause of hardness is fixed Quicksilver <term>Argentum uiuum|Mercury, the liquid metal representing the feminine principle of receptivity and fluidity</term> or fixed Sulfur <term>Sulphur|The alchemical principle of masculinity, heat, and combustion</term>, the cause of softness will be the opposite. The cause of melting <margin>The cause of the melting of any [metal]</margin> is twofold: namely, non-fixed Sulfur and Quicksilver of any kind. But non-fixed Sulfur is necessarily the cause of melting without ignition <note>melting at a lower temperature without the metal becoming red-hot</note>, and you can clearly see the <margin>Note for practical application</margin> experience of this thing through the projection of Arsenic upon bodies that are difficult to melt; for it makes them easy to melt and without ignition. Indeed, the cause of easy melting is likewise Quicksilver. But the cause of melting with ignition is fixed Quicksilver. 

The cause, therefore, of the hindrance of any melting is fixed Sulfur; through this, you can indeed elicit a very great secret, since although bodies with a very large quantity of Quicksilver <margin>Metallic bodies are more perfect the more quicksilver they contain; however, the more sulfur they contain, the more imperfect they are.</margin> are found to be of the greatest perfection, and therefore bodies with a very large quantity of Quicksilver have diminished from perfection: it is necessary to approach closer to perfection. Thus, it happens that bodies with much sulfurous quality are in a state of great corruption. Therefore, from what has already been said, it is clear that Jupiter <note>The alchemical metal Tin</note> approaches most closely to the perfect, since it participates more in perfection. Saturn <note>The alchemical metal Lead</note> indeed less, and Venus <note>The alchemical metal Copper</note> even less still, and Mars <note>The alchemical metal Iron</note> least of all, <margin>From which perfection depends.</margin> because it depends on the perfecting [principle]. 

On the other hand, it happens differently regarding the medicine that completes <note>The "completing medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone</note> and supplies what is lacking, thinning out the imperfect, and cloaking the darkness of their substance with the depth of the bodies' density <term>spissitudinem|thickness or lack of porosity in a metal</term> and a shimmering brilliance <note>original: "subsplendentis fulgoris," a soft, underlying glow</note>. <margin>Which metals are more suitable to be perfected through the projection of the elixir.</margin> <margin>The same in chapter 12 of this [book?]</margin> For from this, Venus exists as the most easily perfected; Mars indeed less so; and Jupiter even less; and Saturn least of all.

->B O O K<-

<margin>Medicines are varied according to the variety of bodies that must be corrected and healed.</margin>
From these findings, therefore, through the investigation of truthful labor, it has been discovered that because of the diversity of physical bodies, it is necessary to prepare various medicines. One case requires a medicine for a hard, combustible <note>original: "ignibile," referring to a substance that reacts or burns in fire</note> body; another requires one for a soft and noble <note>original: "non ignobile," literally "not ignoble," meaning a body that is already somewhat purified or closer to a precious state</note> body. This medicine acts by softening and thinning into the depths of the material, maintaining the equality of its substance. Another acts by hardening and thickening what is hidden. Thus, it is useful for us to move on to medicines through clear practical experiments, showing us the reasons for the discovery of different medicines, what they leave incomplete, and what they bring to perfection.

### On the twofold medicine of any
### imperfect body and of Quicksilver,
### namely the white and the red. Chapter 10.

<margin>All medicine consists of spirits <term>spiritibus|volatile substances, such as mercury or sulfur, which can "penetrate" and change metals</term>.</margin>
We prove, therefore, that spirits are more closely assimilated to bodies because they unite with them more readily and amicably than anything else in nature; for nature attracts nature, and "like applauds its like" <note>A central alchemical maxim suggesting that substances with similar properties have a natural affinity for one another</note>. Because of this, it was first discovered that these spirits are the true medicine for the alteration of bodies. Therefore, we have applied ourselves with every kind of ingenuity to transform each of the imperfect bodies, through a firm and lasting mutation, into a perfect Lunar <term>Lunare|Silver-like</term> and Solar <term>Solare|Gold-like</term> body.

<margin>Diverse medicines are made from diverse spirits because of the different needs of the bodies.</margin>
Consequently, it is necessary to create different medicines from these same spirits, depending on the goal of the transformation. Since there are two kinds of alterable Quicksilver <term>Argentum uiuum|Mercury</term>—namely, that which can be perfectly coagulated <note>solidified or fixed into a stable form</note>, and the bodies that fall short of perfection...

### THIRD

<margin>
So that you may have knowledge of all these things which are held concerning medicines, know that in the Mastery <note>original: "magistro," referring to the alchemical *Magisterium* or Great Work</note> there are three principles: Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, which is called Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, and Mercury; and two Sulfurs, which are called Venus <note>Copper</note>, Sun <note>Gold</note>, Mars <note>Iron</note>, and Moon <note>Silver</note>. These, however, are medicines for each other, for Quicksilver washes and cleanses the Sulfurs, and likewise the Sulfurs purify the Quicksilver. This removal and cleansing has a triple degree: for either they mutually correct each other from accidental qualities—not in their fundamental root, but those that have come upon them—which happens in **preparation**; or from more radical qualities, as occurs in **composition** and digestion; or from all of them, as in the manifold **projection** <note>The final stage of alchemy where the "medicine" or philosopher's stone is cast upon base metals to transform them.</note>.
</margin>

bodies, and these indeed are varied. Some indeed are hard and ignoble <note>Base metals like iron and copper that were considered "lesser" because they oxidize or "perish" in fire.</note>, while others are soft but not ignoble. The hard and ignoble ones are Mars and Venus. The soft ones are Jupiter and Saturn; it is necessary that the perfecting medicine be similarly varied. For Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> needs one perfecting medicine, while the bodies to be transformed need another. And also some need the hard and ignoble ones, like Venus and Mars. Others need the soft ones that are not ignoble, like Saturn and Jupiter; and since both of these types differ from each other in nature, it necessarily follows that they require different medicines. For Mars and Venus are of one kind, namely of hardness. Yet they differ in a certain specific property. For the latter <note>Venus/Copper</note> is fusible <note>easily melted</note>, while the former <note>Mars/Iron</note> is not fusible. Therefore, Mars is perfected by one medicine and Venus by another; and while the former is entirely unclean, the latter is not; and while the former partakes in a certain dark whiteness, the latter partakes in redness and greenness, which similarly impose a necessity for diversity in the medicine. For the bodies of softness, namely Jupiter and Saturn, are of another kind. Since these differ similarly, it is necessary that they likewise require different medicines. For here Jupiter is indeed clean, but Saturn is not. But truly, all these four are changeable, being made now into **Lunar** <note>Silver</note> bodies, and now into **Solar** <note>Gold</note> bodies of perfection. Therefore, it is necessary that there be a twofold medicine for each one: one indeed yellow <note>original: "citrinam"</note> and changing into a yellow Solar body; the other truly white, similarly changing into a white Lunar body. Since, therefore, there is a twofold medicine for each of the four imperfect bodies...

### BOOK

<margin>
The author, therefore, in order to introduce obscurity <note>Alchemists often used "Trobar Clus" or closed speech to hide secrets from the uninitiated.</note> into his speech, specified various preparations of the three principles which hold the names of Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, Venus <note>Copper</note>, and Mars <note>Iron</note> according to their various degrees and colors, and thus he established eight medicines. However, the last two—through which the sum of the others are reduced into the Solar and Lunar body—constitute the true medicine. These are cast in manifold projection <note>The act of throwing the alchemical powder onto molten metal</note> and constitute the highest Elixir for the Sun <note>Gold</note> or Moon <note>Silver</note>. By this Elixir, we are excused from all other medicines whenever we possess it, because it achieves perfection in its fulfillment.
</margin>

might come, namely the Solar and the Lunar <note>Gold and Silver</note>. There will be, therefore, a total of eight medicines that perfect bodies into the form of noble ones. Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note> is likewise perfected into the Solar and Lunar, and for that reason, there happen to be two different kinds of medicine for altering it. Therefore, there will be ten medicines in all which we have found, which in their totality lead to the complete alteration of any imperfect thing; truly indeed, this is achieved through a long duration of time, persistent labor, and the industry of great investigation.

But we wish to be excused from the labor of finding these ten medicines through the benefit of a single medicine. For we have found through long and most laborious inquiry, and with certain experience, one medicine by which indeed a hard body is softened, and a soft body is hardened; the fugitive <note>Volatile substances, like Mercury, that evaporate when heated</note> is fixed, and the foul is illuminated with an unspeakable splendor, in a state that exists above nature. 

Therefore, it is expedient to provide a separate discourse on all these medicines with their causes and clear proofs of experience. First, indeed, the sequence of the ten medicines; then the principle of all bodies; then of Quicksilver; and finally we must move to the medicine of the perfection of the Mastery <note>original: "magisterii," the Great Work of alchemy</note>. 

However, since imperfect things require preparation—and lest we be bitten by the envious on account of the insufficiency of the tradition of our art—let us first bring forward a narrative concerning the preparations of the imperfect ones. We shall set down the necessity of the causes of their findings, by which indeed, through our art, they may be made suitable to receive the medicine of the perfection of Whiteness <note>The *albedo* stage, producing silver</note> and Redness <note>The *rubedo* stage, producing gold</note> in each degree, and from...

## On the administration and purification <note>original Latin: "mundificatione," a term for cleansing or refining a substance</note> of bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the solid metals</note>, diversifying according to the diversity of their essences. Chapter 11.

<margin>
On the consideration of bodies and spirits according to their hidden nature, which occurs in preparation.
</margin>
From the discourses already recounted by us, it appears what the works of nature leave behind as superfluous, or what is diminished, in each of those bodies which are imperfect. This has been discussed in sufficient part; however, regarding their completion, we shall here fully complete with sufficient discourse those things which we omitted in the previous sections.

<margin>
Diverse bodies demand diverse preparation.
</margin>
First, therefore, since it happens that the bodies of imperfection are of two kinds—namely, the mutable and soft ones, which are also not ignitible <note>meaning they do not withstand or require extreme fire to melt</note>, such as Saturn <note>the alchemical name for Lead</note> and Jupiter <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note>; and the hard, non-fusible ones, or those fusible only with ignition <note>high heat</note>, such as Mars <note>Iron</note> and Venus <note>Copper</note>. The former [Mars] is indeed not fusible, while the latter [Venus] melts with ignition. Nature, by its very shaping, has necessarily taught us to administer diverse preparations according to the requirements of that diversity of essences found at the root of their nature.

<margin>
Black lead, which is properly called lead, and white [lead], which is called tin.
</margin>
Thus, there are two necessary bodies of imperfection of one kind to be transformed: Lead, namely, which is called *melan* <note>original Greek: "melan," meaning black</note>, that is, black, and by the Art is called Saturn; and clattering <note>the "tin-cry" or sound tin makes when bent</note> Lead, which is called white, and in this science is called Jupiter. These are diverse from one another in the depth of their hidden nature, both innate and manifest from the root of their nature; for Saturn is dark, leaden-hued, heavy, and black, and being entirely without clattering, it is silent <note>original Latin: "mutus," contrasting with the "clattering" of tin</note>.

# BOOK THREE

<margin>The things that corrupt Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead</note> in its original root cannot be removed except by a medicine of the third order <term>medicine of the third order: a high-level alchemical agent capable of fundamental, permanent transformation, rather than a surface-level change</term>. Therefore, it is impossible to extract the Elixir from Saturn.</margin>

One [kind of corruption] is impossible to remove by a medicine of the first order <note>i.e., simple chemical processes or minor refinements</note> of any industry. The other, however, can be removed with a small amount of assistance. This indeed becomes impossible to remove because, in the principles of their own nature, these types of bodies were mixed into a true essence and became a true essence. And therefore, since it is not possible to remove the true essence of any thing in nature while the thing remains <note>original: "re permanente"; meaning the underlying object persists even if you try to change it</note>, it was not possible for them to delete these corrupting influences. For this reason, some of the philosophers thought that the Art <note>The "Art" refers to the Great Work of Alchemy</note> could not be achieved through this.

<margin>These things said in this place about the infection of both leads <note>original: "utriusque plumbi"; likely referring to Lead (plumbum nigrum) and Tin (plumbum candidum)</note> according to their root are to be understood regarding common lead and tin. From which it is impossible to elicit the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>.</margin>

But even we ourselves, inquiring into this science in our time, arrived at this same conclusion: that similarly, by no method of ingenious preparation, could we brighten the bodies with the completion of their clear brilliance without them happening to be totally infected and thoroughly blackened. Because of this, we too were brought to a state of stupor and hid away for a long time under the shadow of despair. 

Then, returning to ourselves and torturing ourselves with the afflictions of immense meditation and thought, we observed that bodies diminished from perfection exist as foul in the depths of their nature, and nothing radiant is found in them, since according to nature, it is not within them. For that which is not in a thing cannot be found in it. Since, therefore, nothing perfect is found in them, it follows by necessity that nothing superfluous remains to be found in them, regarding the separation of diverse substances within the depths of their nature. And thus through this we found that there was something diminished in them, which must necessarily be completed by a medicine.
