## Concerning the preparation of Saturn and Jupiter. Chapter 13. In general. <note>original: "De præparatione Saturni et Iouis. Ca. 13. in comuni."; Saturn and Jupiter are alchemical code names for Lead and Tin, respectively.</note>

<margin>Here we deal with the common purification of Saturn and Jupiter, that is, the chemical matter.</margin>
Saturn and Jupiter are therefore prepared with manifold preparations, according to the necessity of reaching a closer degree of greater perfection <term>perfection: "perfectionis"; in alchemy, the "perfection" of a metal means moving it closer to the properties of gold or silver.</term>, by both common and special modes of preparation. The common way involves multiple steps in the progression toward perfection.

<margin>Distribution of the operations necessary for purification.</margin>
For there is one degree of progression, namely, **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur"; here likely referring to the "spirit" or combustible principle of the metal</note> from a clean substance. Another is hardness with the heating of its fusion. A third is fixation <term>fixation: "fixio"; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</term> through the removal of volatile substance. Thus they are cleansed and made bright in three ways: either by cleansing agents, or by the method of calcination <term>calcination: "calcinationis"; the process of heating a metal in air until it oxidizes into a fine powder or "lime."</term> and reduction <term>reduction: "reductionis"; the chemical process of returning a powdered oxide or "lime" back into its metallic form.</term>, or by solution. By purifying things, they are cleansed in two ways: either reduced to a lime, or in the nature of their [metallic] bodies.

<margin>Cleansing of calcined Jupiter and Saturn through salts and other scouring agents.</margin>
When reduced to a lime, they are purified in this way: either by salts and alums <term>alums: "alumina"; a group of mineral salts used as astringents and fluxes in chemical processing.</term>, or by glass. And it is done when the body—namely Jupiter or Saturn—has been calcined; then, water of alums or salts is poured over their lime, or crushed glass is mixed into it and it is reduced back into a body. This should be repeated upon these bodies by alternating turns until they show themselves to be completely clean. For since salts, alums, and glass melt in a different fusion than the [metallic] bodies, they are separated from them, taking the earthy substance with them, leaving behind only the purified body.

<margin>Cleansing of the same in the nature of bodies.</margin>
In the nature of bodies, they are similarly purified by the same method. And it is done by filing these two bodies very finely; after this, they are processed with the same alums, salts, and glass, and afterward reduced into a body.

<margin>Purification of the said bodies by way of calcination and reduction.</margin>
And thus let it be repeated in alternating turns until they appear cleaner. They are also purified by a wash of **Quicksilver** <note>original: "Argenti uiui"; Mercury, often used in alchemy to "wash" or amalgamate other metals.</note>, the method of which we have already brought forward. Indeed, these bodies of both kinds <note>Referring to Saturn and Jupiter, or Lead and Tin.</note> are similarly purified by repeating the turn of **calcination** <term>calcination: "calcinationis"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state, usually into a powder.</term> upon them, and likewise **reduction** <term>reduction: "reductionis"; the process of restoring a calcined metal back to its metallic form.</term> with a sufficiency of its own fire, until they appear cleaner. For by this process, these diminished bodies are cleansed of their double corrupting substance: the one which is inflammable and fugitive <note>Volatile elements that evaporate or burn away.</note>, and the other which is foul and earthy. This is because the fire elevates and consumes every fugitive substance; and likewise, in the manner of reduction, the same fire divides all earthy substance according to its own proportion.

<margin>The *Book of Investigation* should precede this book of the *Summa*.</margin>
And we have written of this proportion in our other volume, which is entitled *On the Investigation of Perfection*, which according to the proper order precedes this book. For in that work, we wrote down whatever we investigated according to the reasoning of our mind. Here, however, we have completed the boundaries of our knowledge according to the order of science, regarding those things which we have seen and touched. <note>The author distinguishes between theoretical alchemy ("reasoning of the mind") and practical, experimental alchemy ("seen and touched").</note>

<margin>Purification of the aforementioned bodies through their solution and the reduction of the dissolved matter.</margin>
They are also certainly purified through the **solution** <term>solution: "solutionem"; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state.</term> of their substance, the method of which we have already stated. And likewise through the reduction of that which has been dissolved from them. For it is found to be cleaner and more perfect by this same mode of preparation than by any other kind of preparation. No other method is compared to this one, except that which is perfected through **sublimation** <term>sublimation: "sublimationem"; the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind.</term>, and therefore it is of equal value to it.

<margin>Another stage of approaching the perfection of the said bodies.</margin>
There is also a similar preparation in them: the hardening of their soft substance <note>Lead and tin are notoriously "soft" metals compared to gold or silver.</note> by the ignition of their fusion; and it is so that we might manage to mix into them the fixed substance of **Quicksilver** in their depths.

## On the preparation of Venus. Chapter 15.

<margin>Philosophical Venus is an enclosed sulfur, which is raised like a red smoke mixed with a white smoke, so that it appears lemon-yellow.</margin>
<margin>The cleansing of Venus is through quicksilver, the fire of calcination, and solution.</margin>

The method through elevation is indeed to take Tutty—with which Venus is more compatible—and let them be united through clever means. Then, indeed, let it be placed in its sublimation vessel to be raised, and through the most excellent degree of fire, its more subtle part may be elevated, which is found to be of the most brilliant splendor. Or let it be mixed with Sulfur into the smallest parts <note>original: "per minima"; ground finely and mixed thoroughly</note>, and afterwards raised through the method of its elevation already mentioned. Without sublimation, however, it is prepared either through things that effect cleansing, or in its ash <note>original: "calce"; the oxide or powder produced by burning a metal</note>, or in a body like Tutty, salts, and alums, or through a bath of Quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti vivi"; Mercury</note>, the method of which we have already brought forward. ## On the preparation of Mars. Chapter 16.

<margin>Philosophical Mars <note>The alchemical name for Iron</note> is a supervening sulfur, which is accustomed to being purified with a mixture of arsenic and quicksilver.</margin>
The preparation of Mars <note>Iron</note> is likewise multifaceted. For some methods are completed through sublimation <note>A process where a solid is heated into a gas and then cooled back into a solid to purify it</note>, while others are done without sublimation. That which is performed by sublimation is done with Arsenic, the method of which is this: let us devise as deeply as we can to unite non-fixed <note>Unstable or volatile</note> Arsenic to it, so that it melts together with it in fusion. Afterward, let it be sublimated in a vessel proper for sublimation; this preparation is found to be better and more perfect among the others. There is also another preparation of this same Mars, using Arsenic that has been sublimated from it many times, until a certain quantity of the Arsenic remains with it. For if this is reduced <note>Returned to a metallic state</note>, it will emerge white, fusible, clean, and prepared. There is also a similar third method of preparation for the same, through its fusion with Lead and Tutty <note>original: "Plumbo & Tutia"; zinc oxide collected from the flues of smelting furnaces, used in making brass</note>. For from these, it flows out clean and white.

## On the preparation of the substance of Quicksilver
<gloss>so that it may become a medicine according to the aforementioned properties.</gloss>
## in the projection of the medicine. Chapter 1.

<margin>How quicksilver may become a medicine possessing the aforementioned five properties.</margin>
IT REMAINS, therefore, for us to describe specifically its substance alone, the properties of that substance, and its differences. And since we have not found it possible to change its nature without careful management, we have similarly found that it must necessarily be prepared, since it cannot be mixed in the depths <note>i.e., at the molecular or internal core of a metal</note> without that specific method of preparation. And this is so that its substance may become such that it is mixed in the depths, even to the hidden parts of the body to be altered, without ever being separated again. 
<margin>Quicksilver must be refined <note>original: *subtiliari*</note> so that it may penetrate to the innermost parts.</margin>
This, however, does not happen unless it is greatly refined through the specific and certain preparation described in the chapter on sublimation <note>Sublimation is the process of vaporizing a solid and collecting the purified deposit.</note>. And its impression <note>The lasting change or "tint" it leaves on another metal.</note> likewise does not remain unless it is fixed, 
<margin>Quicksilver must be fixed, and brightened so that it may brighten and melt [others].</margin>
nor does it grant luster unless the most brilliant substance is drawn out from it, by the skill of its method and the manner of its operation through a suitable fire. And it does not grant a perfect fusion <note>The ability to melt and blend perfectly with other metals.</note> unless caution is used in its melting, since it has the power to soften hard things and harden soft things. It is such, however, that it boils with a sufficiency of its own proportioned humidity, according to the requirements of the fusion being sought.

## On the triple order of medicines.
### Chapter 2.

<margin>By this he understands [what was said] above; from this place he learns that medicine [comes] from imperfect [bodies].</margin>
<margin>Medicine of the 1st order, as held in the epilogue of the summary, is the preparation and cleansing of the matter from supervening accidental properties. For in particular instances, sulfur is the medicine of quicksilver, and quicksilver is the medicine of sulfur.</margin>
<margin>Medicine of the 2nd order is that which happens in composition, while sulfur is still better purified from quicksilver, and quicksilver from sulfur.</margin>
<margin>Medicine of the third order is that which occurs in multiplication.</margin>

WE HAVE indeed indicated that a triple difference of medicines necessarily occurs. For one is of the first order, another of the second, and another of the third. Now, I call a **medicine of the first order** any preparation of minerals which, when projected <term>projection<note>In alchemy, 'projection' (proiectio) is the act of casting a transformative substance—often a powder or elixir—onto a molten base metal to effect a transformation.</note></term> upon bodies that fall short of perfection, impresses an alteration that does not bring about a sufficient completion; instead, the altered thing happens to change and be corrupted along with the total evaporation of that medicine's impression. 

Such is every whitening sublimation of **Venus** <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for copper</note> or **Mars** <note>original: "Martis"; the alchemical name for iron</note> which does not undergo fixation <term>fixation<note>The process by which a volatile substance is rendered stable and resistant to heat, preventing it from evaporating.</note></term>. And of this kind is every addition of the color of the **Sun** <note>Gold</note> and **Moon** <note>Silver</note>, or of **Venus** mixed together, placed over a cementing furnace, and *zimar* <note>original: "zimar"; likely referring to verdigris or a specific mineral salt used in refining</note> and the like. For here it changes by a mutation that does not last, but rather diminishes itself through exhalation. 

Truly, we call a **medicine of the second order** every preparation which, when it is projected upon bodies falling short of perfection, alters them toward some degree of completion, though some modes of corruption are left entirely behind; such is the calcination <term>calcination<note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in a furnace to remove volatile components or reduce it to a powder.</note></term> of bodies, by which everything "fugitive" <note>volatile or easily evaporated</note> is destroyed. And medicine of this kind is that which perpetually turns the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> yellow <note>Giving silver the color of gold</note>, or even perpetually whitens **Venus** <note>Copper</note>, while other types of corruption remain in them. 

But I call a **medicine of the third order** every preparation which, when it is applied to bodies, removes all corruption through its projection, and with every [perfection of] completion... <note>The text ends mid-sentence here.</note>

For Venus and Mars, the medicine is the pure **whitening** <term>whitening<note>original: "dealbatio"; the alchemical stage of *albedo*, where impurities are removed to produce a white, silver-like state.</note></term> of their substance. Since reddening does not come to Venus and Mars with the medicine of the first order alongside the appearance of brilliance—because they are entirely unclean and not fit to receive the brilliance of redness—before a preparation comes to them which brings forth that brilliance. Let us therefore recount first all the medicines of Venus, and afterward those of Mars, which fall within the first order.

## On the difference of certain medicines.
### Sixth [Chapter].

It is necessary, therefore, to follow in order what remains. Since there are two kinds of medicines for the defects of bodies: one that **restores nature**, and the other that **evacuates** those things which have settled in a way not according to nature. Now, which of these treatments is more powerful requires few words. For what is lacking in nature should be supplied by medicines as the situation demands. A body that has been dried out requires moistening; one that is cold requires heating. In whatever state it has exceeded its nature, it must be corrected by its **opposite** <note>This refers to the classical principle of "allopathy" where a condition is treated with its opposite quality—e.g., treating a "fever" (hot and dry) with something cold and moist.</note>. Regarding those things which must be evacuated <note>In a medical context, this means purging humors; in alchemy, it refers to removing impurities or "dross" from a metal.</note>, since there are many kinds, and they are not all equally ready or available—some being contained in the whole body and others in a specific part—we shall speak of these instead. But before we approach that, it must be known that some physicians have used certain other techniques, which even some of those living now are fond of, and which can be of use to others. These are two: one which serves as a kind of warning for things to be treated, and the other which provides the aid for the treatment itself. Therefore, we shall speak of the first order first.

## On the medicines of Venus in the first order. Chapter 4.

<margin>First physical whitening of Venus in the first order by means of quicksilver <note>original: "arg. uiuum" (argentum vivum), which is mercury.</note>.</margin>
There is, therefore, a medicine that whitens Venus <note>In alchemy, Venus is the planetary name for copper.</note>, one through quicksilver, and the other through arsenic. Indeed, the whitening medicine is completed through quicksilver in this way. First, precipitated quicksilver is dissolved, and the calcination of Venus <note>The "ash" or oxide produced by heating the metal to a high temperature.</note> is dissolved in a similar manner; both of these solutions are mixed into one. Afterward, they are coagulated, and their medicine is cast upon the body of Venus itself. For this whitens and cleanses, yet it does not bring about a final completion, as it happens that the altered metal may be changed back or corrupted <note>meaning the "silvering" effect is unstable and does not penetrate the metal's core.</note>.

<margin>Litharge <note>lead oxide</note> and quicksilver, or rather mixtures and similar things.</margin>
<margin>Second physical whitening of Venus in the first order.</margin>
Furthermore, and in another way, precipitated quicksilver is dissolved, and litharge <note>original: "Litargirium," a secondary mineral form of lead oxide often used as a flux.</note> is dissolved, and both solutions are joined into one. Then the calcination of the body of Venus, which is intended to be whitened, is dissolved and joined with the aforementioned solutions. They are coagulated, and then they are cast upon its body: for it is whitened by this means.

<margin>Third physical whitening of Venus in the first order, which encompasses almost the whole preparation.</margin>
In another way, a quantity of quicksilver is sublimated <note>the process of heating a substance so it turns into vapor and then solidifies again</note> from its body in alternating turns, until a part of the quicksilver remains fixed with it, through complete ignition <note>firing the mixture at high heat</note>. From that point, it should be ground by frequently "imbibing" <note>soaking or saturating a dry substance with liquid</note> it with distilled vinegar, so that it may be better mixed into its depths. From here it is roasted, and finally, the quicksilver is sublimated from it in the same way, and it is repeatedly imbibed and roasted. And let the work be repeated upon it so many times until a great quantity of quicksilver rests within it, accompanied by complete ignition.

### Concerning the medicines of the Moon in the first order. Chapter 6.

<margin>The medicine that yellows the Moon <note>original: "Lunā" (Silver)</note>—that is, its external substance—is the sulfur enclosed within it that is natural to itself.</margin>
<margin>This variety leads to deception, although it can be verified in some way.</margin>
<margin>Vitriol, copperas, gum of copper, and the dripping of copper are names denoting enclosed sulfur.</margin>
Following the order of what was promised, let us speak with certain truth about the yellowing medicine for the substance of the Moon <term>Moon <note>The alchemical name for silver</note></term> in the first order. It is, namely, a yellow medicine that adheres to its depths and, by adhering, colors it, whether through its own nature or through the skill of this mastery <term>Mastery <note>The *Magisterium*, or the alchemical process of transformation</note></term>. We shall therefore speak of the medicine that adheres to it from its own innate root, and then of the skills by which we make a substance of any kind adhere with firm penetration. We extract it either from Sulfur, or from Quicksilver <term>Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note></term>, or from a mixture of both. But it is extracted through Sulfur in a more diminished way, whereas through Quicksilver it is done more perfectly. It is also extracted similarly through certain mineral things that are not of this kind: such as vitriol <term>vitriol <note>Metallic sulfates, often used to describe acidic or corrosive liquids in the lab</note></term> and copperas <term>copperas <note>Green vitriol or ferrous sulfate</note></term>, which is also called the gum of copper or the dripping of copper.

After this, dissolve a portion of the Moon <note>Silver</note>, and when it has been dissolved, mix the solutions together, and coagulate them, and cast this over the molten Moon; for it will yellow it with a very peculiar yellowness. If, however, the Quicksilver in precipitation has grown red to the perfection of its "projection" <note>the final stage of alchemical transformation where the medicine is added to the base metal</note>, the stated administration is sufficient without the mixing of a tinting substance into it.

# On medicines of the second order.
## Chapter 7.

<margin>Cleansed bodies are sulfurs prepared by a medicine of the first order.</margin>
IT REMAINS, therefore, to transition to the medicines of the second order, with the requirement of a discourse that is truly sufficient, supported by manifest proofs and true experience. Since there is one medicine for cleansed bodies and another for **Quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum <note>Literally "living silver," the alchemical name for mercury, considered the base of all metals.</note></term>—namely, the perfection of its coagulation—let us first completely describe the medicines for all metallic bodies.

<margin>What the medicine of the second order is.</margin>
From there, we shall proceed to the coagulable medicines of Quicksilver itself, intended for true **Gold-making** <term>solificum <note>From "Sol" (the Sun/Gold); a process or substance that transforms base metal into gold.</note></term> or true **Silver-making** <term>lunificum <note>From "Luna" (the Moon/Silver); a process or substance that transforms base metal into silver.</note></term>. A medicine of the second order is that which completes imperfect things solely by adding a specific difference of perfection. Truly, there are many causes of corruption in each of the imperfect bodies—as in **Lead** <term>Saturn <note>Alchemists associated the slow-moving planet Saturn with heavy, "dull" lead.</note></term>, for instance, there is a volatile sulfurousness and the "flight" <note>referring to evaporation or instability under heat</note> of Quicksilver, through which corruption necessarily occurs, along with its earthiness.

<margin>The medicine of the second order does not remove what is at the root of the bodies. See above, page 65.</margin>
Let a medicine be made, therefore, which either removes one of these entirely or conceals it by "cloaking" it <note>original: "palliando," literally to cover with a cloak; in alchemy, this refers to changing the appearance or outward properties of a metal without necessarily altering its internal essence.</note>, leaving only the other causes of imperfection behind. Because there is something immutable in metallic bodies which is innate at the very root of those bodies, it cannot be removed by a medicine of the second order; therefore, every medicine that removes that root from the mixture is called not a medicine of the second order, but one of the third and greater order.

<margin>What the duties of a medicine of the second order are.</margin>
And because the excess of volatile elements is found to be removed through the methods of **calcination** <term>calcination <note>Heating a metal in air until it turns into a powder or oxide.</note></term> and **reduction** <term>reduction <note>The chemical process of returning a powdered oxide back into a solid metal.</note></term>, which is called "earthiness," it was therefore necessary to find a medicine of the second order which might cloak what is innate, soften what is hard, and harden what is soft, and in hard things...

<meta>The catchword "scilicet" (namely) indicates the transition to the next page's detailed explanation of these transformative properties. The "second order" acts as an intermediary stage of refinement compared to the "first" (simple cleansing) and "third" (total transformation).</meta>

<summary>This page defines "medicines of the second order," which are substances that improve metals by concealing imperfections or altering physical hardness, though they stop short of the total elemental transformation achieved by the "third order." It specifically identifies volatile sulfur and "earthiness" as the corrupting factors in base metals like lead.</summary>

<margin>
The difference between the medicine of the second order and the medicine of the third order. The medicine of the second order is one regarding its ingredients, but diverse regarding its method of administration. This is because the sulfurs that harden quicksilver require a method of consuming fire, whereas quicksilver that softens sulfurs requires a method of fire that preserves moisture.

dullness of both kinds of bodies by masking it, transforming these into white <note>silver</note> and those into the most perfect lemon-yellow <note>gold</note>. Now, this medicine is not different from the medicine of the third order except by the imperfection of a lesser preparation; and it is not different from itself in what consists of the casting upon different bodies and the acceptance of pigments <note>the colors or "tinctures" that change the metal's appearance</note>, but in the method of preparation. For the medicine for soft bodies requires one kind of industrious preparation to thicken thinness, while the medicine for hard bodies requires another to thin thickness; the former by way of a consuming fire, the latter requiring the administration of fire that preserves moisture.

## Concerning the Medicines of **Quicksilver**, and Their Application. Chapter 10.

<margin>The medicine of the second order regarding <term>quicksilver<note>original: "argenti uiui"; mercury, the "living silver."</note></term> is drawn from the mercury itself: and it is noted in various chapters that both elements exist within the same substance.</margin>
<margin>Med: <unclear>gulan- genti uiv est jm quod in- putrã bicia i apparẽ sor e i m_ i. i. it ide itidẽ adser</unclear> <note>This marginal note is heavily abbreviated or damaged in the original transcription, making a full translation impossible, though it appears to refer to the "putrefaction" or preparation of the mercury.</note></margin>
Following the order previously established, it remains for us—as part of the completion of the work we promised to demonstrate from the beginning—to move into the description of the medicine used for **coagulating** <note>original: "coagulantia"; the process of solidifying or thickening a liquid substance so it can withstand heat.</note> Quicksilver. We say, therefore, that the medicine for that "stone" is drawn from the mercury itself, as has been noted in many chapters of this work. This is necessary because <term>quicksilver<note>original: "Argentum uiuum"</note></term> is "fugitive"—it evaporates easily without even being set on fire. It therefore requires a medicine that can pierce into its depths and bind to its tiniest particles instantly, before it can escape. This medicine must thicken the mercury and, through its own melting, preserve the mercury in the fire until it can tolerate a greater heat. This heat consumes the mercury's excess moisture and, through this benefit, transforms it in a moment into true **Solar** <note>original: "Solificum"; gold-making.</note> or **Lunar** <note>original: "Lunificum"; silver-making</note> material, depending on which one the medicine was prepared to create.

<margin>Understand that <term>arsenic<note>original: "arsenicum"</note></term> was joined with the quicksilver from the very beginning of its generation.</margin>
<margin>No <term>tincture<note>The "tincture" is the color-changing agent that turns a base metal into gold or silver.</note></term> is made without **sulfur**; the same is found in the chapter concerning the **Sun** (Gold).</margin>
Because no substance is found to share more with mercury than its own nature, we have determined that its medicine must be completed using itself. We have labored to provide a form for this medicine through <term>ingenious methods<note>original: "per ingenia"; the clever chemical processes or experimental devices used by the alchemist.</note></term>. Specifically, it must be prepared according to the methods already described, with the persistence of long labor. By this labor, the mercury's subtle and purest substance is perfectly manifested: it appears white for the **Moon** (Silver), but an intense yellow for the **Sun** (Gold). This cannot be completed—that is, it cannot create the yellow color—without mixing in a "tinting thing" that is of its own nature. From there, this purest substance of Quicksilver is perfected through the skillful methods of this mastery.

<summary>This chapter explains how to create an alchemical "medicine" to stabilize volatile mercury, preventing it from evaporating so it can be transformed into silver or gold. It emphasizes that the medicine must come from the mercury's own nature, combined with sulfur or arsenic.</summary>
<keywords>quicksilver, mercury, coagulation, gold-making, silver-making, arsenic, sulfur, alchemy, stabilization, volatile substances</keywords>

->[BOOK] FOURTH<-

...medicine for the spirits, which adheres most strongly to Quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo"</note> and melts very easily, and coagulates it, and converts it into a true Sun-maker <note>original: "Solificum"; a substance that produces gold</note> or Moon-maker <note>original: "Lunificum"; a substance that produces silver</note>, provided its preparation has been performed beforehand.

<margin>
The matter of the medicine of the second order is found in metals and in quicksilver extracted from metals; therefore, in these things, it is closer and easier to obtain.
</margin>

But it is often asked from what things this substance of Quicksilver can best be drawn out. In response, we say that it is extracted from those things in which it exists. It is present both in the [metallic] bodies themselves and in Quicksilver itself according to nature, since they are found to be of one and the same nature. However, it is more difficult to extract from the [solid] bodies. In Quicksilver itself, it is more "ready" <note>original: "propinquius"; meaning it requires less processing to reach the desired state</note> but not more perfect. Therefore, whatever kind the medicine may be—whether in the bodies or in the substance of Quicksilver itself—the medicine of the precious stone <note>referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note> is sought after.

<margin>
In what way quicksilver enters the substance in the medicine of the second order, and conversely, how the best mixture and alteration is achieved.
</margin>

But since it sometimes happens that the medicine mixes well, and sometimes it does not, we will describe the method of thorough mixing: namely, how each thing may acquire a most deep entry into a body, or why a medicine might not enter. The method is through the <term>dissolution</term> <note>the process of liquefying a solid to allow for mixing at a molecular level</note> of that which does not enter, and through the dissolution of that which does enter, and by the mixing of both solutions. For anything that is joined to another at the level of its smallest parts creates a point of entry. Furthermore, that which enters is perfected through solution; and through solution, fusion <note>melting</note> is achieved in things that are otherwise not meltable. Therefore, they are better suited to enter, penetrate, and alter [the substance].

<margin>
Calcination contributes greatly to solution; the same is mentioned in the chapter on calcination.
</margin>

And this is the reason why we <term>calcinate</term> <note>heating a substance until it oxidizes or becomes a fine powder</note> certain things that are not naturally of this kind: specifically, so that they may be better dissolved. Because of this, they are dissolved so that the [metallic] bodies may better receive an "impression" <note>a transformative change in their nature or color</note> from them, and likewise be prepared and cleansed by them.

<margin>Note, for this is how the practice of the medicine of the second order <note>The "second order" refers to a stage in alchemy where a substance can alter the qualities of a metal (like color or hardness) but is not yet the universal "Philosopher's Stone."</note> is carried out.</margin>

*Or we grant entry to those things which, because of their density, do not allow themselves to penetrate, by repeatedly raising non-inflammable spirits <term>Spirituum non inflammabilium: volatile substances like arsenic or mercury that vaporize when heated but do not catch fire</term> over them—namely, of unfixed Arsenic and Quicksilver <note>original: "Arsenici & Argenti uiui non fixorum"; "unfixed" refers to substances that are still volatile and have not yet been made stable under high heat</note>—or by the multiple repetition of the sublimation <term>Sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it turns into a gas and then cools back into a solid, used here to purify or "lighten" a substance</term> of that which lacks the power of entry. However, good care must be taken regarding the entry granted to mixable things, so that the body intended to be changed and altered by these means is dissolved <note>original: "soluatur"; meaning reduced to a liquid or fundamental state</note>, and that those things intended to enter and cause alteration are also dissolved. Yet, let there be a solution not of all the parts, but only of some; after this, let the same body, and no other, be soaked <note>original: "imbibatur"; a process of adding liquid to a solid until it is saturated</note> time after time. For through this benefit, the medicine necessarily gains entry into that body alone, whereas this does not necessarily happen with just any other body. Therefore, by these ingenious methods, it is necessary for any substance to both have entry—which depends on the favor of its nature—and to alter the body through the mixture discovered. Thus, by this discourse on the ten medicines, the number is completed with a sufficient explanation of its tradition.*

FOURTH BOOK

## On medicines of the third order, Chapter 11.

<margin>
The Solar and Lunar medicines are one in essence.
</margin>
Now, the <term>medicine of this third order</term> <note>This refers to the most potent class of alchemical preparations, often identified with the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note> is twofold: namely, Solar and Lunar. Yet, it is one in essence and similar in its manner of acting; for this reason, it is called a "single medicine" by our ancient predecessors, whose writings we have read thoroughly. There is, however, an addition of a <term>citrine</term> <note>original: "citrinitatis"; a lemon-yellow color indicating a specific stage of alchemical maturity</note> color, because it is perfected from the purest substance of fixed <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, combustible, and coloring principle of metals.</note>.

<margin>
The difference between the Solar and the Lunar.
</margin>
The difference between this one and that one—namely the Lunar and the Solar—is that the Solar contains that coloring principle within itself, while the Lunar does not.

<margin>
The order of the Great Work is the third order.
</margin>
This third order is called the order of the <term>Great Work</term> <note>original: "maioris operis"; also known as the Magnum Opus, the final goal of alchemy</note>, and for this reason: because it requires a more skillful industry in its administration, a greater preparation for its perfection, and a longer labor to reach the fulfillment of truth. Therefore, the medicine of this order does not differ in its essence at all, except through the most subtle stages of preparation during its creation and through a more persistent application of labor. We shall describe all these stages of preparation at the conclusion of this discourse, along with the complete mode of action, its causes, and manifest experiments; and from there, we will likewise describe several stages of administration for this third order. For the Solar medicine requires one stage for the complete preparation of its pigments, while the Lunar requires another; the Solar indeed requires the administration of the Sulphur that dyes it, but the Lunar does not.

<margin>
In the Lunar medicine, even if <unclear>one</unclear> adds sulphur, it still does not dye because it is not fixed as it should be; but in the Solar it dyes, because it is most absolutely fixed.
</margin>
Therefore, let us first describe the mode of administration for the Lunar medicine. It is thus: you should take its "known stone" and, through the method of separation, divide its purest part and set it aside.

<summary>This page introduces the "Third Order" of alchemical medicines, explaining that while Solar (gold-making) and Lunar (silver-making) preparations share the same essence, the Solar version is distinguished by the addition of "fixed sulphur" which provides its yellow-gold color. The author identifies this stage as the "Great Work," noting it requires superior skill and longer labor than previous stages.</summary>

### On the administration of the Solar & Lunar medicine. Chapter 12.

<margin>
The power and effectiveness of the **Lunar** medicine of the 3rd order.
</margin>

<margin>
**Sulfur** is necessary in both the Lunar ☽ <note>the Moon, representing Silver</note> and Solar ☉ <note>the Sun, representing Gold</note> medicine. Operations necessary for the **Solar** medicine <note>The "Solar" medicine refers to the final elixir used to produce Gold, the most perfect metal.</note>.
</margin>
And the intention of this process is that the **stone** <term>Stone: The *Lapis*, or the Philosopher's Stone in its developing state.</term> and its additive be most perfectly purified through the method of **sublimation** <note>original: "sublimationis"; the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then collecting the purified solid that forms upon cooling</note>. From this point, by way of skillful ingenuity, the volatile parts among them are to be **fixed** <term>Fixed: To make a substance resistant to heat so that it no longer evaporates or vaporizes.</term>; then, conversely, the fixed is made volatile, and the volatile fixed once more. Repeat this—making the fixed volatile and the volatile fixed—as many times as necessary until it allows for easy fixation even when heated to redness <note>original: "cum ignitione," referring to the point of incandescence</note>. In this sequence, the most precious **secret** <note>original: "archanum"</note> is completed: a secret that is above every other science in this world, an incomparable treasure. You must exercise yourself in this with the greatest persistence of labor and with the duration of immense meditation; for through these you shall find it, and without them, you shall not.

<margin>
The more often the **Medicine** is dissolved and **fixed**, the more its power is intensified, so that it may eventually possess the immense ability to convert all metals into gold, or rather, into a new and superior **Solar** medicine.
</margin>
For this medicine, the repetition of excellent administration, conducted with the skill of such great caution, can reach a point in the preparation of the stone where it may change **Quicksilver** <term>Quicksilver: Mercury (Argentum vivum)</term> infinitely into true **Solar** <note>Gold</note> and **Lunar** <note>Silver</note> substance. This achievement depends entirely upon the multiplication or the frequent repetition of its preparation.

<margin>
Thanks be to God.
</margin>
Now, therefore, let the sublime God of all natures be praised, blessed and glorious, who has revealed to us the sequence of all medicines. Through experience—which we sought by the goodness of His prompting and the persistence of our own labor—we have seen it with our eyes and touched it with our hands; its completion has been discovered through our **mastery** <term>Mastery: *Magisterium*, the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work.</term>.

<margin>
Why he has treated the **mastery** more obscurely.
</margin>
But if indeed we have veiled <note>original: "palliauimus," literally "cloaked"</note> this knowledge, let the **son of doctrine** <note>A traditional term for a student or initiate into the alchemical mysteries</note> not wonder. We have not veiled it for him, but for the wicked and the corrupt. We have delivered it in such language that the foolish will necessarily fail to understand it, yet it will entice the prudent to search for its discovery. Therefore, sons of doctrine, search, and you shall find this most excellent gift of God, reserved for you alone.

## Concerning the examinations by which it is known whether the mastery is in perfection.
### Chapter 13.

<margin>A proposal of things to be said.</margin>
Setting aside the manifest experiences, of which we make no account since they are known and certain to all—namely, weight, color, and extension by the hammer, which require no great ingenuity of wisdom—let us attempt the experiments of the craft with caution. We must see if the **projection** of the administration of this art brings about a completion with truth. These tests are, namely: cupellation, cementation, ignition, fusion, exposure to the vapors of sharp substances, the extinction of burning sulfur in the mixture, the trial of calcination, the reiteration of reduction, and the easy or difficult reception of quicksilver. Therefore, we must begin with the first things in order, and then seek to complete the others according to our promise, following the same order with their known causes.

<note>original: "cineritium, cementum, ignitio, fusio, super uapores acutorum expositio, extinctio adurentis Sulphuris in mixtione probatio calcinationis et reductionis reiteratio, & Argenti uiui facilis aut difficilis fusceptio."</note>

<term>Cupellation (Cineritium): A refining process where ores or alloyed metals are treated under high heat to separate noble metals like gold and silver from base metals like lead.</term>

<term>Cementation (Cementum): A process used to purify gold by heating it in contact with a "cement" (a mixture of salts and minerals) that reacts with impurities.</term>

<term>Projection (Proiectio): The legendary final step of alchemy where the Philosopher's Stone is "thrown" onto base metal to transmute it into gold.</term>

<term>Quicksilver (Argentum vivum): Mercury; considered by alchemists to be one of the fundamental "parents" of all metals.</term>

## On the examination by the ash-test.
### Chapter 14.

<margin>
Only the substance of silver and gold endures in the ash-test.
</margin>
We now present a discourse on the ash-test <note>original: *Cineritium*, a refining process also known as cupellation, where metals are melted in a cupel made of bone ash to separate precious metals from base ones</note>, with all its manifest causes and the method of its performance. It is, therefore, only the Lunar and Solar substance <note>silver and gold</note> that endures in the examination of the ash-test. We shall therefore investigate the true differences in the substance of these perfect bodies, along with the causes of the ash-test itself—namely, why some bodies endure more and others less in this examination of the mastery, among those things diminished from perfection <note>i.e., base metals that have not reached the "perfection" of gold or silver</note>. Moreover, we have sufficiently explained the secret of these two bodies in the depth of their substance.

<margin>
The reason why only the substance of silver and gold endures in the ash-test is the great quantity of the best quicksilver and its proper thickening.
</margin>
And the reason is this: because their primary root was a great quantity of quicksilver <note>original: *Argentum vivum*, or mercury</note> and its purest essence, being first very subtle and later thickened <note>original: *inspissata*, referring to the alchemical process of "fixing" mercury into a solid state</note>, until it could withstand melting under fire. Therefore, whatever things are diminished from perfection and possess more earthiness <note>original: *terreitas*, referring to the non-metallic impurities or dross within a substance</note> endure less in this examination; conversely, those with less earthiness endure more. For these latter parts adhere more closely due to the subtlety of their components, which are highly mixing and unifying.

<margin>
In both types of lead, proper thickening is lacking. In Venus and Mars, however, it is in excess.
</margin>
And those bodies which are likewise of greater thinness, such as the two types of lead <note>In alchemical nomenclature, "two leads" usually refers to lead and tin</note>, or on the contrary, those bodies of greater thickness, such as Mars and Venus <note>iron and copper</note>, than those which consist in perfection—these must be entirely separated from the mixture: for they do not share the same melting point, and therefore they are separated. And those which participate in a smaller quantity of quicksilver are more easily separated from the mixture. It is therefore evident that since they contain much earthiness,

### BOOK FOUR

<margin>By "Saturn" in this passage, some understand "added sulfur." <note>original: "sulphur superueniens"</note></margin>
<margin>Saturn [lead] has the greatest earthiness, little quicksilver, and is easily melted; therefore, it is used as the medium in the cupellation assay. <note>The "Cineritium" or ash-test used a cupel made of bone ash to purify silver or gold.</note></margin>
...of earthiness, it would be Saturn [lead], which has a small quantity of quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti uiui," referring to mercury, then thought to be a component of all metals</note>, melts easily, and is of the greatest thinness—qualities which are the opposite of the perfection required for the cupellation assay. Therefore, among other metallic bodies, Saturn lasts the least in the craft of the cupellation; rather, it is separated and yields most quickly. Because it yields more than other bodies that fall short of perfection, it is more suitable for this masterly assay. Because it yields so quickly, it drags each of the other imperfect metals out of the mixture along with it. For this reason, a larger quantity of the "perfect" metal <note>In this context, gold or silver.</note> is saved from the intense heat of the trial-fire, because the perfect metal does not remain exposed to the consuming assay for a long duration. Thus, by the assay of lead, the metal is burned less and purified more easily.

<margin>By the "substance of Jupiter," some mean to understand arsenic.</margin>
<margin>These things regarding the "Jupiter of the Philosophers" are to be understood if we pay close attention to what was said about the common variety on page 65. <note>Alchemists distinguished between "vulgar" metals found in shops and "philosophical" metals used in their experiments.</note></margin>
However, because the substance of Jupiter [tin] consists of a larger quantity of quicksilver and less earthiness—sharing in a greater purity and a more subtle substance—it is preserved in the mixture longer than Saturn. <insert>Jupiter</insert> adheres more deeply to the mixture. <unclear>And for that reason</unclear>, much of the perfect metal's quantity is destroyed before the Jupiter joined to it can be separated.

<margin>Venus <unclear>signifies</unclear> arsenic.</margin>
<margin>In distillation, the "perfect whitened sulfur" is first separated from the mixture. Then, with ignition, the arsenic departs. Finally, the quicksilver, or salt, is also raised and joined with its dregs.</margin>
Venus [copper], however, allows for melting with ignition; but because its melting point is slower than that of the perfect metal, it is separated from the mixture, though more slowly than Saturn, because of the glowing heat <note>original: "ignitionem"</note> of its meltable substance. Because it has a smaller quantity of quicksilver than Jupiter, and more earthiness and a thicker substance, it is removed from the mixture more easily than Jupiter, since Jupiter adheres more deeply than Venus does.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical refining processes, specifically focusing on "cementation," a dry method used to purify noble metals by burning away base impurities.</meta>

### FOURTH [BOOK]

<margin>The cause and purpose of cementation.</margin>
<margin>Undoubtedly the "Mercury of the Philosophers," as mentioned by Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy.</note> on page 56.</margin>
<margin>The degrees of the metals in relation to cementation.</margin>
Since "cement" <note>In this context, cement refers to a corrosive powder mixture used in a dry refining process to purify gold.</note> is composed of flammable substances, the reason for its necessary invention is clear: namely, that all combustible components might be burned away. Since there is only one incombustible body <note>The author refers to gold, which resists oxidation and corrosion in the fire.</note>, only that which is prepared according to its nature is preserved in the cementation. However, some metals endure longer in the cement and some less; which ones last longer or shorter is known from the causes already mentioned. Thus, Silver <term>Luna|The alchemical name for silver</term> lasts the longest; Iron <term>Mars|The alchemical name for iron</term> lasts less; Tin <term>Jupiter|The alchemical name for tin</term> lasts even less; Copper <term>Venus|The alchemical name for copper</term> even less than that; and Lead <term>Saturn|The alchemical name for lead</term> lasts the least of all.

---

<margin>The method of cementing the metallic bodies</margin>
<margin>What the flammable things are.</margin>
Let us therefore describe the method of cementation, since a knowledge of it is most necessary for us in the examination of perfection. We say, then, that its composition is made from flammable things. To this class belong all things that blacken, flee <note>original: *fugientes*; referring to volatile substances that evaporate or sublime when heated</note>, penetrate, and burn, such as Vitriol <term>Vitriol|A historical term for metallic sulfates</term>, Sal ammoniac <term>Sal ammoniac|Ammonium chloride, used as a flux and a source of chlorine in refining</term>, flower of copper <note>likely verdigris or copper oxide</note>, crushed old pottery, a very small amount of Sulfur (or none at all), male urine, and similar sharp and penetrating substances. 

<margin>Note the practice explained under the form of cementation</margin>
All these are mixed together with male urine and applied over thin plates of the metal that is intended for testing, so that the quality of the metal may be examined by this judgment. Afterward, the plates should be spread out upon an iron grate inside a closed earthenware vessel, arranged so that they do not touch one another, allowing the power of the fire to run freely and equally between them. In this way, they are kept in the earthenware vessel for three days in a strong fire. 

<margin>Chemists' "days" are sometimes taken to mean months.</margin>
However, caution must be exercised so that the plates are made red-hot but do not melt. After the third day, you will find the plates clean of all impurity if a [perfect] body existed in their perfection. If they were not perfect, you will find them entirely corrupted and destroyed by the burning of the calcination <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to cause thermal decomposition or oxidation.</note>.

## On the examination by the mixing of Sulfur.
### Chapter 20.

<margin>The property of burning Sulfur, regarding which see pages 51 and 56.</margin>
Whether the mastery <note>term: magisterium - the successful alchemical transformation or the "Great Work"</note> consists in perfection is similarly proven by the mixture of Sulfur; for in our experience, we have found that Sulfur mixed with metallic bodies burns some more and some less. We have discovered through our art that some bodies return [unchanged] from that combustion, while others do not. From this, therefore, a difference can be noted between those bodies prepared toward a counterfeit <note>original: sophistico</note> completion that are diminished from perfection. Therefore, since among the other bodies of every kind, we find that the Sun <note>term: Sol - the alchemical name for Gold</note> is burned the least by Sulfur; and after this Jupiter <note>term: Jupiter - Tin</note>, then the Moon <note>term: Luna - Silver</note>, and after this Saturn <note>term: Saturn - Lead</note>; and more easily than all these Venus <note>term: Venus - Copper</note>, and most easily of all Mars <note>term: Mars - Iron</note> is burned by the oiliness of Sulfur.

<margin>The order of metals by reason of this examination, which is greatly different from their ranking with respect to cementation <note>term: cementation - a process of heating a metal surrounded by powdered chemicals to purify it</note>.</margin>
Therefore, by this test it is noted which things approach perfection more or less. Furthermore, from the diversity of colors appearing after the combustion of the bodies, it can be investigated in what kind of genus the body consists, altered from the root of its own nature. For the Sun <note>gold</note> indeed produces <note>original: protendit</note> an intense yellow <note>original: citrinum</note> or a clear red color from combustion with Sulfur.

<margin>The colors of chemical bodies after calcination <note>term: calcination - the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its state or purify it</note> with sulfur.</margin>
The Moon <note>silver</note>, however, produces a black mixed with sky-blue. Jupiter <note>tin</note> produces a black mixed with a tint of moderate redness. Saturn <note>lead</note> produces a dark black mixed with much redness and a leaden-blue <note>original: liuiditati</note>. Venus <note>copper</note> produces a black mixed with greenness when there is a great deal of sulfurous combustion; but when there is little combustion, it produces a very bright green and a lovely violet.

## On the testing of calcination and reduction of bodies. Chapter 21.

<margin>
Perfect bodies prepared in calcination and reduction lose nothing. See pages 54, 56, etc.

One must next investigate the testing of repeated calcination <note>term: calcination - the process of heating a metal in air until it decomposes into a fine powder or "ash".</note> and reduction <note>term: reduction - the chemical process of restoring a metal to its solid, metallic state from a powder or ore.</note>. We have found, therefore, that when bodies are found to be perfect, they lose nothing of their color, weight, or quantity—of which one might be overly concerned—nor do they lose their luster during the repetition of calcination and reduction, no matter how many times the complexity of those operations is repeated upon them. Therefore, if through the repetition of the methods of calcination and reduction from the powder <note>original: "calce"</note>, any of the qualities of excellence are lost from any kind of altered metals, you should consider that the searching craftsman has investigated in a deceptive <note>original: "sophistice" - referring to 'sophistry' or fraudulent chemical practices.</note> manner. For this reason, you should practice other methods so that you may recognize them.

I do this so that you may better and more clearly understand the volumes that follow, and so that, once understood, and having been devised and examined with care, they may be more easily and promptly brought to a successful result. 

And because it is one thing in this art to investigate through reason, and another to attempt and prove the subtleties and techniques <term>ingenia|In alchemical Latin, this refers both to the practitioner's natural "ingenuity" and the specific technical "devices" or "tricks" of the trade.</term> of these matters, until by working, searching, and experiencing, one reaches the complete objective. Therefore, in this book of mine, I have written according to the logic of my mind whatever we have investigated through the accounts given—that is, the things that bring the art to perfection. 

Yet, let no one think that this investigation, or our book titled the *Summa of the Perfection of the Mastery* <note>original: "Summa perfectionis magisterij"</note>—in which we have completely defined in scientific order whatever we have seen and handled, based on experience and certain thought, and which we have noted and devised through our own examination of the various transforming effects of natural and mineral substances appearing in the work—[let no one think] that we have [contradicted] our previously composed science with this investigation

...to the assembly <note>original: *conuentus*</note> which we proposed to clarify regarding the art itself. Therefore, by right, this book precedes that one, since through this book I seek to investigate the logic of the perfecting thing. Since, therefore, this science treats the imperfect bodies of minerals <margin>The purpose of this work</margin> insofar as it is fitting to perfect them, we have first considered these two things: namely, imperfection and perfection. 

We base our intention around these two points. Regarding the things that perfect and those that corrupt, according to what we have investigated through our own experience, we compose this book—because opposites placed side-by-side shine more clearly. 

<margin>The thing perfecting metallic bodies, which we must look toward as a goal in the craft.</margin> Now, the thing that brings perfection in minerals is the substance of **Quicksilver** <term>Argenti viui|Literally "living silver," the common alchemical term for Mercury.</term> and **Sulfur** <note>In alchemical theory, all metals were thought to be composed of varying proportions and purities of Sulfur (the soul/fire) and Mercury (the spirit/liquidity).</note> combined in due proportion through long and temperate decoction <term>decoctionem|A process of heating or "cooking" a substance in a fluid, mimicking the natural heat of the earth.</term> in the bowels of clean earth; it is thickened and fixed while preserving its radical humidity—not a humidity that destroys, but one produced into a solid substance that is fusible <term>fusibilem|Capable of being melted by heat.</term> with proper firing and extensible under the hammer <note>meaning it is "malleable."</note>. 

Through the definition of this perfecting nature, we can more easily arrive at a knowledge of the corrupting thing. This is to be understood in the opposite sense: namely, an impure substance of **Quicksilver** and **Sulfur** combined without due proportion, or cooked either too little or too much in the bowels of clean earth; neither rightly thickened nor fixed; possessing a combustible and corrupting humidity; and being of a thin and porous substance. <margin>The thing corrupting and infecting metallic bodies.</margin> Alternatively, it is that which has a fusion without the proper firing, or none at all, and does not sufficiently endure the hammer. 

I found this first definition <note>the definition of perfection</note> embedded in these two bodies: namely, in **Sol** and **Luna** <note>original: *Sole & Luna*; the alchemical names for Gold and Silver.</note>.

### OF THE INVESTIGATION.

<margin>From these points, you understand that the Elixir <note>The "Elixir" here refers to the transformative substance, often called the Philosopher's Stone, capable of perfecting metals.</note> must be drawn from imperfect metals.</margin>

<margin>All metals consist of sulfur and pure quicksilver <note>original: *argento puris* (referring to Argentum Vivum/Mercury)</note>, and the Elixir can be drawn from all metals. Know, however, that Saturn <note>Lead</note> is foul in its root substance, and likewise Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, as the author says in Book 3 of the *Summa*, Chapter 13. Therefore, we cannot easily draw the Elixir from these primary sources. From Gold and Silver, however, the Elixir is drawn through a short work. From the remaining metals, the true and supreme Elixir is produced.</margin>

...they thought; which was never the intention of the philosophers <note>In this context, "philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemists who studied the secrets of nature.</note>. Yet they say many things by way of analogy. And because all metallic bodies are composed of Quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum|The liquid metal Mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" or "seed" of all metals.</term> and Sulfur—whether pure or impure by accident and not by their primary nature—it is therefore possible to remove those impurities through suitable preparation. For the stripping away of accidental qualities is not impossible. Preparation is, therefore, the removal of the superfluous and the supplying of what is lacking in imperfect bodies, which cannot be done without the assistance of labor and purifying substances.

<margin>Helpful operations.</margin>
For preparation is diversified according to the variety of things that are lacking. Experience has given us the methods of acting, namely: Calcination <note>Reducing a metal to a powder or "ash" through high heat.</note>, Sublimation <note>Heating a substance until it turns to vapor, then collecting it as it cools back into a solid.</note>, Descension <note>A method of refining where a substance is melted so it flows downward, often through a filter or into a lower vessel.</note>, Solution <note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note>, Distillation, Coagulation <note>The thickening or hardening of a liquid into a solid.</note>, Fixation <term>Fixionem|The process of making a volatile substance stable so that it no longer evaporates or changes when exposed to fire.</term>, and Ceration <note>The process of softening a substance until it has a wax-like consistency.</note>. We have given a sufficient account of each of these in the *Summa of the Perfection of the Magistery*. These, then, are the operations that assist in preparation.

<margin>Helpful materials.</margin>
The materials that assist in these preparations are these: namely, all kinds of salts, alums, atraments <note>Metallic sulfates or vitriols, often used for their acidic or coloring properties.</note>, and also glass, borax, and things of this nature, as well as the sharpest vinegar and fire. And with these, we propose to prepare the imperfect bodies:

<margin>
Salt among the Alchemists is considered the same as their quicksilver <note>original: *argento uiuo*</note>. However, different kinds of salts are established according to the various degrees of preparation of the aforementioned quicksilver.
</margin>

## 1. On the preparation of common Salt.

<margin>
The spring water should be distilled vinegar.
</margin>

Let common salt be burned; once burned, let it be dissolved in common water or clear, warm spring water. Once dissolved, let it be passed through a filter. Once filtered, let it be congealed <note>In this context, "congealed" refers to the process of evaporation and crystallization.</note> over a slow fire in a glazed dish <note>original: *paropside uitreata*</note>, or a lead-glazed earthen vessel, but never in a metal one. Once congealed, let it be calcined <note>Calcination involves heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or to oxidize it.</note> for a day and a night in a moderate fire, and keep it thus, for it is then sufficiently purified.

## 2. On the preparation of Salt of Glass.

Saltpeter <note>original: *Sal petræ*</note> is dissolved in spring water; once passed through a filter, it is congealed in a glass vessel until it reaches a crystalline fusion.

<margin>
The grease of nitre <note>original: *Sagimen nitri*</note> is the fatness of quicksilver, namely, the sulfurs.
</margin>

## 3. On the preparation of Salt of Nitre.

Salt of nitre is prepared in this way: dissolve the grease of glass <note>original: *sagimen uitri*</note> in aqua fortis <term>Aqua fortis|Literally "strong water," this is nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used to dissolve metals.</term>, pass it through a filter, and congeal it in a glass vessel, and in this way, it is most excellently clarified.

## 4. On the preparation of Rock Salt.

Rock salt <note>original: *Sal gemmæ*</note> is ground, dissolved, and congealed in a glazed earthen vessel, just like common Salt.

<margin>
Soda is a plant from which, when burned, an ash is produced that is necessary for the creation of glass. The same is called *Kali* or *Alkali* by the Arabs. Amatus <note>Likely referring to Amatus Lusitanus, a famous 16th-century physician and botanist.</note> thinks it is *ant-sillim* <note>An Arabic-derived botanical term for a salt-marsh plant.</note>.
</margin>

## 5. On the preparation of Salt of Alkali.

Salt of alkali is made from dissolved soda, passed through a filter, and boiled down to a third of its volume. In time, the salt will settle to the bottom of the vessel in the form of a crystal, and it is then prepared. Si-

<margin>Potash <note>original: *Cinis clauellatus*, literally "clubbed ashes."</note> and Quicklime denote the calcined chemical mass.</margin>
Similarly, alkali salt is prepared by some in this way: they take five or two weights of potash and one weight of quicklime, draw off the whole lye <note>Lye is a metal hydroxide traditionally obtained by leaching wood ashes.</note>, and then distill and congeal it. They repeat this once, and it is prepared. Or, like common salt, let it first be ground entirely, dissolved in warm common water, then distilled through a filter, congealed, and calcined with a slow fire.

## On the preparation of Sal Ammoniac. <insert>6</insert>

<margin>Urine signifies common quicksilver or metallic water. Sweat denotes chemical quicksilver, which is also called common salt. Let wood soot be sulfur.</margin>
Sal ammoniac <note>Historically ammonium chloride, highly valued in alchemy for its ability to help metals sublimate.</note> is made from five or two parts of human urine, one part of the same "sweat," one part of common salt, and one and a half parts of wood soot or sticks. These having been boiled together until they are consumed in this manner, sublime <term>Sublime|The process of heating a solid until it turns into a gas and then cools back into a solid, bypassing the liquid phase, used here to purify the salt.</term> the true and useful sal ammoniac. Dissolve this again into "sweat," congeal it, and sublime it from common salt once, and it is prepared. Or, let it first be ground with the preparation of cleansed common salt; afterward, let it be sublimed in a tall aludel <term>Aludel|A series of pear-shaped earthen pots used as receivers in the sublimation process.</term> until the pure substance has been totally extracted. Finally, let it be dissolved upon a porphyry stone <term>Porphyry|A hard, reddish-purple stone slab used for grinding or for "deliquescence"—leaving a salt to melt into a liquid by absorbing moisture from the air.</term> in the open air <note>original: *sub diuo*</note> if one intends to make its "water," or let the sublimated and sufficiently pure substance be preserved.

---

## On the preparation of Salt of Tartar. <insert>7</insert>

<margin>Wine denotes the reddening chemical mass.</margin>
Salt of Tartar <note>Potassium carbonate, often derived from the crusty deposits left in wine barrels.</note> is made from calcined and distilled wine dregs, or from dissolved and congealed calcined tartar, and it is prepared.

## 8. On the preparation of the Salt of Urine.

<margin>The dregs <note>original: *faeces*</note> of urine are the calcined chemical mass.</margin>
<margin>You have the same instruction in the beginning of the testament <note>A reference to a foundational alchemical text, likely the *Testamentum* attributed to the famous philosopher Raymond Lull.</note>.</margin>

SALT of urine is made from the dregs of distilled urine which have been calcined <term>Calcined|Reduced to a powder or ash by prolonged heating at high temperatures to remove volatile impurities.</term>, and it is dissolved again in its own water and congealed; it is of great assistance. Many authors treat the preparation of salts in various ways. We, however, through our own investigation, have found these preparations of salts to be shorter and more useful for achieving our purpose. Since salts are extracted from all truly calcined things through dissolution, they are required to be prepared by the aforementioned way; it is enough for us to proceed using these customary methods.

## 9. On the preparation of Ice or Rock Alum.

<margin>Alum signifies <note>original: *sig.*, for *significat*</note> the supervening sulfur; <unclear>it is used</unclear> in the first book of the *Summa*, chapter 17. Sometimes, however, it is also taken for salt, or for quicksilver <note>original: *arg. v.*, for *argentum vivum*.</note>.</margin>

ALUM of ice or rock <note>Ice alum (*alumen glaciae*) and rock alum (*alumen rocae*) are historical terms for purified potassium alum, often appearing as translucent crystals.</note> has a twofold method of preparation: one for washing calcined bodies, the other for sublimating spirits. The first method: Dissolve it in clear spring water, distill it through a filter, boil it down to a third of its volume, place it in glazed dishes <note>original: *parapsidibus uitreatis*</note>, and the prepared crystalline alum will settle around the sides of the vessel and at the bottom. The second method is that the alum be boiled in an earthenware vessel until the moisture has evaporated, and you will find a white, spongy, light alum, prepared for sublimations <term>Sublimation|The process of heating a substance so it turns from a solid to a gas and then back to a solid, purifying it in the process.</term> and various other works. Let the dregs remaining at the bottom of the vessel either be dissolved upon a stone, or in some humid place, or in water extracted therefrom, or be re-boiled.

### 12. On the preparation of black atrament.

### 14. On the preparation of Roman Vitriol.

<margin>Various things are necessarily extracted from imperfect bodies for the elixir.</margin>
Roman vitriol <note>original: *Vitriolum Romanum*. Historically, this often referred to blue vitriol (copper sulfate), though the term was sometimes used for high-quality iron vitriol.</note> needs no other preparation except that it should be kept in some ashes over a moderate fire until it turns red <note>This process of heating vitriol until it changes color is called calcination, resulting in "colcothar," used as a pigment or a polishing agent.</note>. It is certain that (as we have more fully considered) various things necessary to us are extracted from imperfect <term>Imperfect|In alchemy, "imperfect" metals are base metals like lead, tin, copper, and iron, which were believed to be "sick" versions of gold or silver.</term> bodies, and these are the aids to perfection in this case, which require preparation.

### 15. On the preparation of Ceruse.

CERUSE <term>Ceruse|Also known as white lead (lead carbonate). It was a common pigment and a staple in alchemical experiments involving lead.</term> must be dissolved in vinegar and then purified of its coarser parts; that which flows out like milk is to be congealed in the sun or over a slow fire, and it is then prepared.

### 16. On the preparation of Spanish White.

In the same way as described above for Spanish white, white tin <note>original: *stagnum candidum*. This may refer to refined tin or a specific tin-based pigment.</note> should be dissolved in distilled urine in the manner of ceruse, and thus prepared.

### 17. On the preparation of Verdigris.

<margin>In the art, verdigris is the same as arsenic.</margin>
Verdigris <note>original: *Viride æs*. Literally "green of copper," a green pigment (copper acetate) produced by exposing copper to vinegar vapors.</note> <note>The marginal note equating verdigris with arsenic likely refers to their shared "volatile" or corrosive properties in alchemical theory, rather than their modern chemical identities.</note> dissolved in distilled vinegar and clarified until clear, must be congealed over a very slow heat; and it is excellent.

### 18. On the preparation of Crocus of Iron. 18

<margin>Crocus of iron is the same as arsenic <note>The author makes a curious alchemical association here; "Crocus of iron" is usually iron oxide, but they equate its function or nature with arsenic.</note></margin>
Crocus of iron <term>Crocus of iron|A reddish-yellow powder, typically iron oxide (rust), named "crocus" for its resemblance to the color of saffron.</term> is to be dissolved in distilled vinegar and must be clarified. This reddish, saffron-colored water, once congealed, provides a suitable saffron substance, and the work is done.

### 19. On the preparation of Litharge. 19

Dissolve litharge <term>Litharge|A secondary mineral form of lead(II) oxide, often used as a pigment or in glassmaking.</term> in distilled vinegar, clarify it, and congeal it, for it is then well prepared. You may dissolve this again—just like the other substances named previously—and use them in this dissolved and congealed state. There is deep investigation in this, and this preparation is completed very quickly.

### 20. On the preparation of Antimony. 20

Antimony <note>original: *Antimonium*. In this period, this usually refers to stibnite, the sulfide ore of antimony.</note> is calcined <note>Heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile impurities.</note>, dissolved, clarified, and congealed, and it is then prepared.

### 21. On the preparation of Lapis Lazuli. 21

Lapis Lazuli <note>A deep-blue metamorphic rock used as a semi-precious stone and, when ground, as the pigment ultramarine.</note> is calcined, ground, and washed; thus it is purified of its earthy parts.

### 22. On the preparation of Hematite. 22

Hematite <note>original: *Lapis Ematitis*. An iron oxide stone, often called "bloodstone" because it leaves a red streak.</note> is heated until it glows and is quenched <note>original: *extinguitur*. ## On the preparation of Cinnabar.

Cinnabar <term>Cinnabar|A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury, used as a pigment and in the extraction of quicksilver.</term> is to be prepared once with common salt, and it is then in its best state.

## On the preparation of Tutty.

Tutty <term>Tutty|Crude zinc oxide that collects as a crust in the flues of zinc-smelting furnaces, used in medicinal ointments and alchemy.</term> is calcined <note>original: *calcinatur*; heated to a high temperature to drive off moisture and volatile components.</note> and dissolved in distilled vinegar, and thus it is prepared.
Various other kinds of salts, alums, and vitriols <term>Vitriols|Sulfate minerals, referred to in the text as "atramenta" (literally 'inks'), so named because they were used to make black pigments and inks.</term> are found, all of which are prepared and purified according to their specific types as already stated.

## On the preparation of Glass and Borax.

Glass and Borax <note>original: *baurachia*. This term refers to various alkaline salts used as fluxes to help metals melt.</note>, if they have been made in the proper manner, do not require further preparation.

<margin>Imperfect bodies possess three impurities: namely, superfluous moisture, combustible sulfurousness, and unclean earthiness.</margin>
...them. For they are prepared and purified by these means through the application of fire in this manner. These imperfect bodies <note>In alchemy, "imperfect bodies" refers to base metals such as lead, tin, copper, and iron, which were believed to be "diseased" versions of gold and silver.</note> possess superfluous moistures and a combustible sulfurousness, which generates blackness when they are mixed, corrupting the aforementioned bodies. <margin>These accidents occur only in Mars and Venus.</margin>
And because these superfluities occur in these bodies accidentally <note>The author distinguishes between "accidental" properties, which are external contaminants that can be removed, and "radical" properties, which are the essential building blocks of the metal.</note> and not fundamentally, and the removal of accidents is possible, we must use artificial fire to cleanse these bodies and remove all accidental superfluities, so that

only the substance of **Quicksilver** <note>original: *Argenti vivi*; Mercury.</note> and **radical Sulfur** <term>Radical Sulfur|Not common sulfur, but the internal, essential principle of combustion and color within a metal, believed to be one of the two roots of all metallic matter.</term> remains. This is the complete preparation and perfect purification of imperfect things; the improvement and refining of these, or of this remaining pure substance, is accomplished in many ways depending on what the elixir <term>Elixir|The "Philosopher's Stone" or transformative medicine used to "heal" base metals into gold or silver.</term> requires.

<margin>The general method of preparing imperfect metals: Calcination of the body, Solution, Coagulation, and Washing of the same.</margin>
Therefore, the general method of preparation and purification is as follows. First, all superfluous and corrupt moisture in their essence must be driven off with a proportional fire, as well as the subtle and burning superfluity; this is done by **calcining** <term>Calcining|The process of heating a metal or mineral to high temperatures in the presence of air to reduce it to a powder (calx).</term>. Then, the total remaining corrupted substance within their ash—containing the burning superfluous moisture and blackness—must be corroded away with the aforementioned cleansed, sharp, or very sharp corrosives <note>original: *corrosivis acutis*; likely referring to distilled vinegar or mineral acids.</note>, until the ash is white or red, or colored according to the nature and property of the body, and clean and pure from every superfluity.
