## Concerning the greater perfection of perfect bodies.

<margin>To chemists, "perfect bodies" are prepared sulfurs. Gold is indeed the internal sulfur, while Silver is that which is added. To make these even more excellent, they must be dissolved frequently and, once dissolved, thickened <note>original: *coagulanda*; turned from liquid back to solid</note>.</margin>
Truly, perfect bodies <note>Gold and Silver</note> do not need preparation to achieve perfection—since they are already perfect—but they must be prepared so that they may be further perfected, refined, and made subtle; such a preparation must be applied. Take Gold <note>original: *Sol*, literally "the Sun"</note> beaten into thin plates and place it with excellently prepared common salt, layered <note>original: *solariatim*; stacked in layers like the rays of the sun</note> in the calcination vessel. Place this in the furnace to be well-calcined for three days, or until it has been entirely consumed and reduced to a fine powder. Then, let it be removed, ground very well, washed with vinegar, and dried in the sun. Afterward, grind it well with half its weight of cleaned Sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note> and set it to dissolve until the whole substance, through the benefit of the common salt and sal ammoniac, has turned into a most clear water. 
<margin>This "most clear water" and ferment is arsenic distilled with its quicksilver <note>original: *argenti viuo*; mercury</note>.</margin>
This ferment is a perfect, precious elixir, and a true spiritual body <note>original: *corpus spirituale*; a solid metal that has been converted into a liquid or volatile state</note> made manifest.

...of modern teachers, and also with respect to the operations of nature, this truth is more quickly determined. Whence the Philosopher said:

# THE TESTAMENT OF GEBER,
## THE MOST CLEAR-SIGHTED PHILOSOPHER
## and King of India. Concerning the Salts of Animals,
## Fish, Birds, Vegetables,
## and others. Chapter 1.

<margin>Salt is made from all calcined <note>To "calcine" is to heat a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air, reducing it to a powder or ash.</note> things, whether they are fixed or volatile.</margin>
From all things—even from animals, fish, and birds—a fixed <term>Salt</term> <note>In alchemy, a "fixed" salt is one that remains stable and does not vaporize when subjected to high heat.</note> can be made, provided they are burned and reduced to ash. This is done in the same manner as one makes Salt from the ashes of wood, or from the lime of stone. And if the original substance was naturally red, such as blood is, then its salt will naturally be red as well. But the burning of these things ought to take place in a closed vessel.

<margin>10</margin> If the substance is blood, let it first be dried; it is no disadvantage if you dissolve two parts of common salt (which has been calcined in any furnace) into eight parts of the blood.

<margin>The method of burning things so that salt may be made from them.</margin>
Then, dry it again, and afterwards you shall burn it in a glassmaker’s or potter’s kiln, or in a reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace that reflects heat back onto the substance being treated.</note> for a day and a night, or intermittently for two days without the nights. However, if you are working with the flesh of some animal which cannot be easily dried, then burn it for two natural days in a vessel well-sealed with <term>lute</term> <note>A clay-based paste used to hermetically seal laboratory vessels.</note> so that it cannot breathe <note>Meaning the vessel is airtight to prevent the escape of vapors.</note>, without adding any salt.

<margin>20</margin> After the burning, boil the remains in four times their weight of rainwater until two and a half parts of the water are consumed. Then, let the mixture rest and filter it through a cloth until the water becomes clear and without any cloudiness. Then congeal <note>To "congeal" here means to evaporate the liquid until only the solid crystals remain.</note> it over a slow fire, or—what is even better—in the sun. 

<margin>25</margin><margin>Animal salt</margin>
By this method, you will have **animal salt**, which surpasses all others in its power of melting <note>original: "virtute fusiva." This refers to the salt's effectiveness as a flux to help metals melt.</note>. Then, dissolve it again in twice its volume of water...

### On the Salts of Metals. 2

<margin>The power of metallic salts</margin>
Salts are also made from metals after they have undergone calcination <note>Calcination involves heating a metal to high temperatures until it oxidizes and turns into a fine powder or "lime."</note>. These Salts have a power that is both penetrating and fixing <note>A "fixing" agent is one that makes a volatile substance stable under heat.</note> by reason of their refinement and sharpness, because they are made from things that are fixed and have been calcined in the fire for a long time. But because metals are calcined in the fire in various ways, we must first look at the calcination of those which are used for the red work <note>Alchemical operations intended to produce gold.</note>, such as Gold [Sol], Copper [Venus], Lead [Saturn], and Iron [Mars]. Finally, we shall look at those which are useful for the white work <note>Alchemical operations intended to produce silver.</note>, such as Silver [Luna] and Tin [Jupiter].

Then, extract its Salt with rainwater distilled through an alembic <term>Alembic</term> <note>A distillation apparatus consisting of a gourd-like container and a cap that catches and cools vapors.</note> once or twice by boiling it in a copper vessel. Use four parts water to one part lime <note>The powdered remains of the calcined metal.</note>. Finally, congeal it: and if you calcine it again...

<margin>Whiteness is beneath the redness</margin>
If you have performed calcination <note>Calcination is the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in a furnace until it is reduced to a fine powder, or "lime."</note>, the limes will be whitened in three days in a reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace where the heat or flame is reflected (reverberated) onto the material being worked, rather than coming into direct contact with it.</note>. Do not wonder at this, since every red thing, once its tincture <note>In alchemy, a "tincture" is the essential coloring principle or essence of a substance.</note> is removed, remains white: because beneath the redness, whiteness remains hidden, though it is not converted. And for that reason, because whiteness is beneath the redness, I say that if for ten days you calcinate those dregs <note>original: "fæces." In this context, it refers to the solid residue left over after a process.</note> alone without any mixture, and finally, as was said regarding the Salt, you extract the Salts, and afterwards you again calcinate those dregs remaining in the earth after the Salt is removed, they will be converted into whiteness. And if you reduce them, it will be true Mercury <note>original: "Argentum uiuum." Literally "living silver" or Quicksilver.</note>. I say therefore that if you return the Salt of the Sun <note>original: "Sal Solis." The Sun is the alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> to its dregs which have been converted into whiteness, an elixir <term>Elixir</term> <note>A potent substance capable of transforming base metals into noble ones or curing diseases.</note> is made both for tinting and for converting true Silver into Gold, and for tinting prepared bronze and Lead.

## On Jupiter. 2 <note>Jupiter is the alchemical name for Tin.</note>

# THE BOOK OF THE THREE WOR-
### ds by the most acute Khalid.

## On the quality of the Philosophical Stone.

### Chapter one. 1

<margin>
* The Elixir is constituted from one thing, which has three names based on the three things contained within it: namely, two sulfurs and a salt. Therefore, the "Book of the Three Words" concerns the Elixir, which has three names and is furthermore completed by three medicines; it possesses the three aforementioned principles: <term>arsenic</term> <note>often referring to yellow arsenic or orpiment in alchemy</note>, sulfur, and <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "arg. uiuum"; mercury</note>.
</margin>

This stone from which this work is made has all colors within itself. For it is white, red—indeed the reddest red—yellow—the most intense yellow—sky-blue, green, and heavy. In this stone are the <term>four elements</term> <note>the classical Greek elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. For it is watery, airy, fiery, and earthy. In this stone, in its <term>occult</term> <note>hidden or internal</note> state, there is heat and dryness; and in its manifest <note>outward or visible</note> state, there is coldness and moisture. It is necessary, therefore, for us to hide the manifest and to make that which is hidden manifest. 

However, that which is in the hidden state—namely heat and dryness—is an oil, and this oil is dry; that dryness <term>tints</term> <note>original: "tingit"; the process of permanently changing the color and nature of a metal</note> and nothing else, because the <term>alkali</term> <note>a salt-like substance derived from ashes</note> and nothing else tints. That which is manifest—the cold and the moist—is a corrupting watery smoke. It is therefore necessary that this moisture and coldness be made equal to the heat and dryness, so that it does not flee from the fire; because between that coldness and moisture there is one small particle that is hot and dry. It is therefore necessary that the cold and moist elements receive the heat and dryness that were hidden, and that they become one single substance. That coldness and moisture, however, is a corrupting and watery smoke, of which it is said that the watery and burning <note>original: "adustiua"</note> moisture corrupts the "body" <note>the solid metal</note> and tints it into blackness.

### On the hidden heat and dryness existing in that which is moist and cold.
### Chapter 3.

This wonderful *work of the three words* <note>original: "opus trium uerborum"; this refers to the title of the treatise attributed to Khalid ibn Yazid, symbolizing the three stages or principles of the work</note> *is the work of the precious stone, in which there is watery and burning coldness and moisture, and within the same, hidden heat. ## On the works of the planets and their manifestations in Mercury. Chapter 5.

I say, therefore, that in <term>Mercury</term> <note>In this context, Mercury refers to the "sophic" or alchemical Mercury—the fluid, transformative principle of the Work—rather than just the common metal</note> are the works of the planets and their manifestations <note>original: "imaginationes"; referring to the formative influences or "blueprints" the planets imprint upon matter</note> in their proper places, just as they work in the **fetus** in its parts and times. For in the fetus, in the first month when the seed is received by the womb, **Saturn** works by congealing and constricting the matter into a single mass through his coldness and dryness. In the second month, **Jupiter** works by his heat, digesting the matter into a certain fleshy mass called an **embryo**. In the third month, **Mars** works, acting upon the matter, and by his heat and dryness, he divides and separates that mass and arranges the limbs. In the fourth month, the **Sun**, as lord, sends in the spirit, and thus it begins to live. In the fifth month, **Mercury** works, creating the openings and breathing passages <note>original: "foramina & spiracula"</note>. In the sixth month, **Venus** arranges and orders the eyebrows and eyes, the testicles, and similar parts. In the seventh month, the **Moon** labors with her coldness and moisture to expel the fetus.

### Chapter 4.

**LET US NOW RETURN** to the explanation of the Three Words, in which the whole art consists. For **Water** is said to preserve the fetus in the womb for three months. **Air** nourishes it for three months. **Fire** guards it for just as many <note>That is, another three months, completing a nine-month cycle mirroring human gestation.</note>. All of this is said concerning **Mercury** <note>Mercury here refers to "Philosophical Mercury," the living spirit or transformative substance of the Stone, rather than common quicksilver.</note> by way of a metaphor. For there is one nature in a pregnant woman and another in Mercury; nevertheless, by the likeness of the heat found in the womb, the fire is estimated to be of thirty-two degrees. Whence that third word, of which it is said, "fire guards for just as many," is obscure, and many err in it, and enter an unknown land and region. This is because from three they take two degrees, and from these two degrees the remaining degrees are extracted; and this little book <note>original: "libellus"</note> is divided into 32 parts of the **Grid** <term>Craticulæ; a technical term likely referring to a graduated scale, a furnace grate, or a specific diagram used to regulate the intensity of alchemical fire</term>. In these degrees, the entire third word is fulfilled, of which it is said "just as many."

The first degree completes the water and the air. The second degree completes all of this which we have said, and "just as many." And this is the **gift of God** <note>original: "donum Dei"; a standard alchemical expression signifying that the final success of the Great Work requires divine favor as much as labor.</note>.

### Concerning the degrees of fire.

## Chapter 8.

The **Philosopher of the King of the Persians and of the Prince of the Romans** <note>A common way of citing ancient authorities like Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) or Khalid ibn Yazid, who were legendary figures in Latin alchemy.</note> said: thus divide the three words into two parts, and again let these two parts be divided into two parts; and upon those two, let thirty-two degrees be divided, which are the limits of fire and are called "particles of fire." These are found from the portions of the **ark** <note>original: "archæ"; likely referring to the alchemical furnace or a specific graduated vessel used for measurement.</note> which is divided into thirty-two parts, and these are called **almec** <note>original: "almec"; an Arabic-derived term likely referring to the divisions on a scale or a specific alchemical measurement.</note>. All these degrees are spread over the first two parts, which are the two limits; and being divided into four parts, the thirty-two degrees are distributed. 

Just as the first degree is one particle of fire, **albechir** <note>original: "albechir"; likely an Arabic term for the lowest grade of heat, similar to the "heat of a brooding hen."</note>, it is alone and simple, and is said to be almost nothing, as it is a very light fire. With this fire, we begin to grasp **Mercury** and lead it toward the **red stage** <note>original: "Mercurium ad rubeum"; the Rubedo, the final stage of the Great Work resulting in the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. The Persian masters lead it to "death" <note>In alchemy, "death" or mortification refers to the chemical breakdown and purification of a substance.</note> through the subtlety of their wit, and thus two words are completed in six **months** <term>maenchen; a phonetic rendering of the German "Monden" (moons/months), used here as a standard unit of alchemical duration.</term>. 

After this, the third word is fulfilled, which is obscure, and in which many err and lose their senses. The Philosopher of the King of the Persians said: let us divide this through the middle. One half consists of three **months**, and this half is governed with two degrees, which are two particles of fire. Thus these three words are completed in twenty-two **months**, and this is the first limit, and it is without error. The second limit consists of sixteen **months** and is governed with eight degrees of fire. The third limit is of twenty **months** and is governed with sixteen degrees, that is, particles of fire.

# AVICENNA ON THE
## CONGELATION AND BINDING
### of Stones.
### Chapter 1.

**Pure earth** does not become stone, because it cannot create a continuous bond, but rather remains fragmented. Indeed, the prevailing dryness within it does not allow it to be glued together. <note>Avicenna is applying Aristotelian physics here: stones require a "moist" principle to act as a binder; pure "dry" earth simply crumbles.</note> Stones are formed in two ways: by **binding** <note>original: "conglutinando"; the process of sticking earthy particles together.</note> and by **solidification** <note>original: "congelando"; the process of a liquid hardening into a solid.</note>. In some stones, earth is the dominant element; in others, however, water is dominant. Sometimes, mud is first dried out and becomes a substance that is midway between mud and stone, and then it becomes true stone. Viscous or sticky mud is the most suitable for this transformation because it is cohesive. On the banks of the **Geon** <note>original: "Geon"; a Latinization of the Gihon, one of the four rivers of Eden, often associated by medieval scholars with the Nile or the Oxus river.</note>, earth has been observed that appears to be converted into stone over a period of thirty-three years.

From water, stones are formed in two ways. The first is when water falling drop by drop solidifies <note>A description of the formation of stalactites and stalagmites in caves.</note>. The other is when a certain substance precipitates from running water and settles on the surface of the stream bed, eventually becoming stone. There are indeed certain places where water, when poured out, is converted into stones of various colors. Furthermore, there are waters which do not solidify if they are taken away from their source, but if they are poured out near their own natural channel, they do solidify and become stones. We know, therefore, that there is a **mineralizing power** <note>original: "uis mineralis"; a formative force in medieval science believed to reside in certain earths and waters that directed the growth of minerals.</note> in that earth which solidifies the waters. Therefore, the principles of stones are either created from a muddy or viscous substance, or from a substance in which water prevails, which by a certain mineral power con—

Similarly, certain plants and certain animals are converted into stones by a certain **mineral stone-forming power** <note>original: "uirtute minerali lapidificatiua"; a medieval scientific concept used to explain the existence of fossils—the belief that a specific "virtue" or force in the earth could turn organic matter into stone.</note>. This occurs in stony places or through a sudden disharmony of a certain power that emerges from the earth during an earthquake; this power turns into stone whatever it encounters at that hour. This transformation of bodies, plants, and animals is as swift as the transformation of waters. 

It is, however, impossible for a complex body to be entirely converted into a single element, because elements and compound things, when transformed into one another, pass into whichever element is dominant. Thus, what falls into salt-flats becomes salt, and what falls into fire becomes fire; but some things do so more quickly and others more slowly, according to the power of the active forces and the resistance of the passive ones. There is also a place in **Arabia** that colors all bodies within it with its own color. There also fell near Lurgea <note>Likely Jurjan (Gorgan), an ancient city in modern-day Iran, where a famous meteorite fell in the 10th century.</note> a piece of iron weighing one hundred Marks <term>Mark: a medieval unit of weight; one hundred marks would weigh approximately 50 pounds or 23 kilograms.</term>. Due to its extreme hardness, it was nearly unbreakable. Nonetheless, a piece of it was sent to the King <note>original: "Regi torati"; likely a scribal corruption of the King of Khwarazm, a region in Central Asia.</note> who ordered swords to be forged from it, but it proved to be both unbreakable and impossible to work. The Arabs say, however, that the "Alamanic" swords <note>original: "enses alemanici"; referring to Germanic or Frankish swords, which were legendary for their quality in the medieval Islamic world.</note>, which are the finest of all, are made from this very iron. When that mass fell, it bounced off the ground several times like a ball because it was composed of tiny fragments sticking together, each about the size of large millet grains. A similar process occurs among terrestrial stones.

## On the Causes of Mountains.

### Chapter 2.

**Mountains** also sometimes arise from an **essential** cause, and sometimes from an **accidental** cause. From an **essential** cause <note>original: "ex essentiali causa"; in medieval philosophy, this refers to internal or primary forces, such as tectonic activity.</note>, as when the earth is elevated by a violent movement of the earth and becomes a mountain. From an **accidental** cause <note>original: "causa accidentali"; refers to external or secondary forces like erosion.</note>, as when a deep excavation is made by the winds or the flow of water; this happens gradually until a vast depth is created. Consequently, a great height stands out next to the excavation, and this is a primary cause of mountains. There are also certain masses of earth which are soft, and some which are hard. The soft ones are dissolved by the flows of water and the winds, while the hard ones remain, and thus an eminence <note>A height or hill.</note> is formed.

Therefore, just as with the generation of mountains, so it is with the generation of stones; for as water continuously brings a viscous mud to these places, it dries out over a great length of time and becomes stone. Indeed, it is not improbable that there exists a **mineralizing power** <term>Mineralizing power: (Latin: "vis mineralis") a theoretical force believed by medieval scientists to transform water or earth into solid stone or metal.</term> which converts waters into stones. And for this reason, parts of aquatic animals and other creatures are found in many stones <note>This is a remarkably early and accurate observation of fossils as the remains of living organisms.</note>. Mountains have been formed, as it were, over many ages (as we said before), provided they are not currently decreasing. 

The muddy substances found in the heights are made of that stony matter, but they consist of what is worn away from the mountains, or of terrestrial matter, or of another substance added by waters along with muds and vegetation mixed with the **mud of death** <note>original: "luto mortis"; likely referring to organic sediment or the silt created by decaying matter.</note>. Or perhaps it is the ancient mud of the sea which is of a uniform substance, so that part of it becomes stone and part does not, but is instead softened and dissolved by some prevailing quality. There is also the retreat and approach of the sea <note>The ebbing and flowing of tides or the long-term rise and fall of sea levels.</note>, which hollows out certain places and lifts up others, and wh—

<summary>Avicenna explains that mountains are formed either by earthquakes (essential causes) or by the erosion of soft earth by wind and water (accidental causes). He also correctly identifies fossils as the remains of aquatic animals, preserved as mud is transformed into stone over vast periods of time.</summary>

## On the four species of mineral bodies. Chapter 3.

**MINERAL BODIES** are divided into four species: namely into **stones**, and into **liquefiable substances**, **sulfurous substances**, and **salts**. And of these, some are of rare substance and weak composition, while others are of strong substance; some are ductile <note>Capable of being hammered thin or drawn out into wire.</note>, and some are not. And of those which are of weak substance, some are **Salts**—such as those which liquefy quickly from moisture, like <term>Alum</term> <note>original: "Alumen"; a sulfate mineral used as an astringent and in dyeing.</note>, <term>Vitriol</term> <note>original: "Calcamentum" or "Chalcantum"; sulfate minerals used in medicine and to make ink.</note>, and <term>Sal Ammoniac</term> <note>original: "Sal Armoniacum"; ammonium chloride, often found near volcanic vents.</note>—and some are oily and do not liquefy easily by moisture alone, like <term>Sulfur</term> <note>original: "Sulphur".</note> and <term>Orpiment</term> <note>original: "Auripigmentum"; an arsenic sulfide mineral used as a yellow pigment.</note>. 

But <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argentum uiuum"; mercury. Medieval scientists viewed mercury as a foundational element of all metals.</note> belongs to the second category, although it is an element of ductile [metals], or similar to some ductile [metals]. Moreover, all liquefiable things are ductile; for the most part, those that are neither ductile nor liquefiable do not soften except through great force. And the matter of ductile [substances] is a **watery substance** mixed with an **earthy substance** in a strong mixture, and one cannot be separated from the other; its watery substance is congealed by cold after the action of heat upon it, which is <term>Boiling</term> <note>original: "epthesis"; from the Greek "hepsēsis," a term used in Aristotelian physics to describe the process of maturation or "cooking" through internal heat.</note>. And an example would be wine that has not yet frozen because of its oiliness.

...and therefore it is not **ductile** <note>Capable of being hammered thin or drawn into wire without breaking.</note>. However, stone-like things among mineral substances are materially composed of water, but they are not solidified by water alone, but also by **dryness**, which alters their water-like nature into an earth-like nature. There is no excessively oily moisture in them, and for this reason, they cannot be drawn out or hammered. Because their solidification comes from dryness, they are not easily dissolved, except by specific natural methods of dissolution.

**Alum** <note>original: "Alumen"; a sulfate mineral used as a fixative for dyes.</note> and **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: "Sal armoniarum"; ammonium chloride, often found near volcanoes.</note> belong to the category of **Salts**, because the portion of **fire** in Sal Ammoniac is greater than the portion of **earth**. For this reason, the whole substance is **sublimated** <note>The process where a solid turns directly into a gas when heated.</note>. It is essentially water mixed with a very subtle, hot smoke of high fieriness, solidified by dryness.

The wateriness of **Sulfurous substances** <note>original: "Sulphureorum".</note>, however, is mixed with earth through a powerful blending caused by boiling heat, until they become oily; afterward, they are solidified by cold. 

**Vitriols** <note>original: "Atramenta", literally "blackings" or inks; these were sulfate minerals used to make ink.</note> are composed of Salt, Sulfur, and stones. There is within them a mineral power derived from certain liquefiable bodies that are formed from them. For instance, **chalcantum** <note>original: "calcamentum"; a sulfate of copper or iron.</note> and **alachar** <note>A Latinization of an Arabic term, likely referring to a type of vitriol or mineral residue.</note> are produced from the larger grains of vitriol. Only its saltiness is dissolved along with whatever sulfurous component is present; afterward, it solidifies and takes on a mineral power from other bodies. Therefore, that which takes on a **ferrous** <note>Iron-like.</note> power will be red or saffron-colored, such as **alathar** <note>Likely another Arabic-derived term for a specific mineral residue.</note>. That which takes on a **cuprous** <note>original: "aeream"; copper-like.</note> power will be green. For this reason, it is possible for these two to be produced artificially.

**Quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum uiuum"; mercury.</note> is like water mixed with a very subtle earth in a powerful sulfurous mixture, to the point that it will not rest still on a flat surface. This is due to the great dryness inherent within it, and for this reason, it does not stick to whatever touches it. Its whiteness comes from the clarity of that water and from the whiteness of the earth...

->### OF AVICENNA ###<-

But bad **Sulfur**, and these parts not well ground, but composed as if of small fragments, and therefore it does not become such a substance. In heavy **Lead** <note>original: "Plumbi".</note>, however, the **Mercury** <note>original: "Argentum uiuum", literally "living silver".</note> is bad, heavy, and yellowish, and its **Sulfur** is bad, possessing a foul and weak vapor. For this reason, it does not solidify well. Artisans perform a solidification nearly similar to this artificially, although artificial things are not produced in the same way as natural ones, nor do they possess such certain likenesses; and therefore it is believed that the natural composition occurs in this way, or one close to it. But art is weaker than nature, and it does not truly follow it, even though it labors much. Let the practitioners of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimiæ".</note> know that the species <term>species: the essential nature or "blueprint" of a substance</term> of things cannot be transmuted. 

But they can make things similar to them, such as tinting a red substance with yellow so that it appears to be **Gold**, and painting a white substance with whatever color they wish until it is very similar to Gold or bronze. They can also, afterward, wipe away the impurities from **Lead**. Yet it will always be **Lead**, even if it appears to be **Silver**. In such a case, other qualities will be so excellently present in it that men are deceived, just as those who take **Salt** and **Sal Ammoniac** <note>original: "Salem Armoniacum", a salt used in alchemy, primarily ammonium chloride.</note>. Furthermore, I do not believe it is possible that the specific difference <term>differentia specifica: the defining characteristic that makes one species different from another</term> can be removed by human ingenuity, and it is not possible that one temperament <term>complexio: the unique balance of primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that constitutes a body</term> can be converted into another. This is because these sensible qualities are not the difference by which a species is transformed, but are merely accidents <term>accidentia: non-essential properties like color, smell, or weight that can change without changing the thing's essence</term> and properties. 

Their actual differences are not known; and since the difference is unknown, how can it be known whether it has been removed or not, or how it might be removed? But the stripping away of accidents—such as vapor, color, and weight—or at least their reduction, is not impossible, for reason does not stand against this; however, the proportion of these substances will not be the same

<summary>Avicenna argues that while alchemists can mimic the appearance of precious metals by changing their "accidents" (color and weight), they cannot change a metal's essential "species." ### OF KING ALEXANDER

...your work is directed just as I have granted my grace to you, when I described the species to you, which must be governed step-by-step, until **bodies become spirits** <note>In alchemy, "bodies" are solid, fixed substances, while "spirits" are volatile substances that can be vaporized or distilled. Turning a body into a spirit involves sublimation or dissolution.</note>, and then the wisdom of the art works so that nature may be altered and converted into another nature, and nature appears through nature. But after the accidents of nature itself, you must join two natures until you extract from them a clear and lucid nature, which when it ascends into the highest parts, is held, shines, and is joined together. 

And know that in this art I speak nothing [merely] philosophically <note>original: "philosophicè loquor." The author is asserting that these are practical, laboratory-based instructions rather than purely symbolic or abstract concepts.</note>, and in the **solution of liquefaction** <note>The process of reducing a solid to a liquid state, either by melting or by dissolving it in a solvent.</note>, caution must be applied above all else, so that in ascending you do not exceed the limit. For in liquefaction consists the whole **secret** <term>archanum: a hidden mystery or a powerful medicinal/chemical secret</term> of the alteration of all natures. 

Know how this is changed from nature into nature, until it becomes a substance that is neither fleeing <note>original: "non fugiens," meaning non-volatile; a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate when exposed to fire.</note> nor altering, but becomes fixed and constant, from which the entry joins the black ones <note>original: "nigros." A reference to the *nigredo* or "blackness" stage, the first phase of the alchemical Great Work, signifying putrefaction and the stripping away of old forms.</note>, since the part is discerned. And soon nature appears through nature. 

Therefore, the nature of rare fixed things joins together through liquefaction, and the water which is called the **Water of Wisdom** <note>original: "aqua sapientiae." A poetic term for the specialized alchemical solvent or "mercurial water" used to dissolve the base matter.</note> by the Sages; then the secrets which are tempered and moist, because unless you thin the natures and make them water, they will not be able to color; thus you shall moisten the body through watering. 

And know that **whitening** <term>albedo: the second major stage of the alchemical process, where the "black" matter is purified and washed until it turns brilliant white.</term> is found in the coagulation, and that the species are spirits, and they improve one another in turn. I tell you also, my son who desires to be improved, that you should not place raw and disordered species in it, but those that are putrefied and joined, ascending and descending <note>Refers to the process of "circulatory distillation," where vapors rise (ascend) and then condense and fall back (descend) into the flask, repeatedly refining the substance.</note>. I have without doubt discovered certain elevated, lucid, and illuminated ointments, and I found in them hidden secrets, which if you indeed govern well, the nature of those things which...

# A SMALL WORK
<meta>Catchword: Of the author</meta>

...you possess the hidden things; it has clearly appeared to you and will appear—that is, the **white earth** <note>original: "terra alba." In alchemy, this refers to the *albedo* stage, where the matter has been purified and washed of its impurities, turning into a white, shining substance.</note> by means of the clear and well-known **Silver** <note>original: "Argentum." While it can mean the metal silver, in this context it often refers to "Philosophical Mercury," the fluid principle of matter.</note>. And know that certain bodies require solution <note>Dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note>, and some require elevation <note>Sublimation or distillation, where a substance is heated until it rises as a vapor.</note> so that they may tinge <note>To "tinge" is to fundamentally change the color and nature of a substance, the goal of the alchemical transformation.</note> and become clear and illuminated, in which all bodies may be dissolved. Know also that according to nature, **secrets** <term>archana: hidden mysteries or powerful medicinal/chemical secrets</term> are hidden within them; and if the hidden nature is governed correctly, those things which appeared to **Hermes the Philosopher** <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> will appear to you, and it is the white earth near the Silver. Therefore, prepare the bodies which heal themselves when the earth is white, so that they may remain **fixed** <note>original: "fixa." A "fixed" substance is one that is stable and does not evaporate or change when exposed to high heat.</note>. Place it over the heat so that the fire does not burn it with its flame, but liquefy them just as melted wax is liquefied. And be mindful that this is called the **water entering again** <note>original: "aqua intrans iterum." This refers to the process of "imbibition," where a dry substance is repeatedly nourished with a liquid until it absorbs it and changes state.</note>.

Therefore, in your arts in which you study, believe that there will be **two hammers** <note>Metaphorical tools representing the active forces used to "strike" or shape the metals. Given the context of Sol and Luna, these may represent the Sulphur and Mercury principles.</note>, of which one is owed to the **Sun** (Gold) and the other to the **Moon** (Silver). Afterward follow two orders, which the "crown of our head" <note>original: "nostro capiti." This likely refers to the human mind or the "summit" of the alchemical vessel, suggesting the governance of the process requires both intellectual clarity and proper equipment.</note> represents appropriately enough for their governance. Behold, I have numbered them; I have revealed the celestial secret (*archanum*); I have illuminated the difficult and hidden science, and I have certified the perfect knowledge of the method of governance. I swear, therefore, that I have concealed nothing, nor have I described any other species with a foreign description, nor have I placed the genera in the wrong places.

Therefore, if you read and understand my letters, you will reach your goal and give thanks to God. If, however, there is one for whom the composition is weak and the understanding is brief, he will not reach his goal. Let him not blame a portion of his ignorance on me, nor say that I have erred, but rather blame himself, who will not reach his goal.

The SON OF RACHAIDIBI, Zetheibida, philosopher to the King of the Persians and the Prince of the Romans, said: The seed <term>Sperma: In alchemical terms, this refers to the 'prime matter' or the generative starting material of the Stone.</term> of the stone is cold and moist in its manifest appearance, and in its hidden nature it is hot and dry. He says, therefore: make that which is cold and moist hidden, and place that which is hot and dry in the manifest appearance. In this way, its coldness and moisture will be hidden so that they are never diminished; for if they were diminished, the Stone would also be diminished.

Therefore, when the coldness and moisture are hidden, act by that hiding so that you may compose that heat and dryness—which was previously hidden—into the manifest. Thus, from the spirit, a body may be made in two stages <term>Gradibus: Steps, degrees, or levels of intensity in the chemical process.</term>, and it shall become a mass <note>original: "globus"</note>, and blood, and flesh.

Rodianus says: The seed is white and liquid. This liquid, from the first [stage], creates a mass in its proper place within five days; and it receives flesh and blood, and limbs and an image, and the power of imagination from God most high. And it comes to its birth, and it shines and rises in its own time. These are the two stages and the seven <note>Likely referring to the seven stages of the work or the seven metals/planets.</note>. And now we speak of the second...

### FAUSTUS SABAEUS TO THE READER <note>original: "FAVSTVS SABAEVS AD LECTO [LECTOREM]"; Fausto Sabeo (c. 1475–1559) was a Renaissance scholar and poet who often wrote prefatory verses for alchemical and classical works.</note>

<warning>Handwritten annotations in the right margin and at the bottom of the page are heavily struck through with dark ink, making them largely illegible.</warning>

<margin>
<unclear>Struck-through vertical handwritten inscription</unclear>
</margin>

Female, male, neuter, its own father and creatress,
Both conceiving itself and giving birth to itself.
It lies hidden in these papers, though it shines brighter than a star,
And though soft in its own nature, it surpasses the Hundred-Handed giant <note>original: "Centimanum"; referring to the Hecatoncheires of Greek myth, giants of immense strength.</note>.
Suited to all names and all colors,
Dry land and flowing water, King, slave <note>original: "geta"; a common name for a slave in Roman comedy, used here to show the substance's lowly, "base" state before transformation.</note>, flame, and stone.
Who, by dying, brings forth life and salvation for others,
While it is pious to us, it is impious to itself.
It suffers the sword and fire like a martyr; suspended from the high
Air, while still alive, it is shut within a tomb.
From martyrdom it finally rises, gleaming with a crown,
Much stronger and better than it had been before.
Then it is made the victor over Kings and the tamer of Gods,
And it holds both peace and war in its own hand.
It is no wonder, therefore, if it is sought throughout the whole world—
That honor, that health, those riches, and that rest.
And it is less a wonder if it hides itself and fears all men,
It who just now was a thief, crafty and fleeting.
Certain to pay the penalty of death for its flight and theft
If it is captured; trembling for this reason, it remains hidden.

->THE END.<-
